stories.title: A Lawful Morsel
paragraphs: Even if the flour is fresh and the water perfectly clean, spoiled yeast will not produce sound dough; nor will sound bread come from such dough.
To raise a child of good character, one must nourish that child with lawful and honestly earned food.
— Imam al-Ghazali
Moral: A child’s moral formation begins with the food placed on the family table. Lawful earnings and honest nourishment help lay the foundation of sound character.

stories.title: Adversity and Blessing
paragraphs: If adversity brings you closer to God, it is a blessing.
If blessing takes you away from God, it is adversity.
Moral: A hardship that brings you closer to God is a blessing, and a blessing that takes you away from Him is adversity. The measure is not comfort, but direction.

stories.title: Blessings given by God
paragraphs: Whoever God has blessed, He will definitely look at how he uses that blessing:
If he has given you power - to your justice;
If he has given you position - to your mercy;
If he has given you wealth - to your morality;
If he has given you peace - to your gratitude;
If he has given you a life partner - to your loyalty;
If he has given you children - to how you raise them.
Moral: Every blessing is also a test. It is not what you have acquired that shows who you are, but how you deal with them.

stories.title: Church bell
paragraphs: In ancient times, there was a rule in a country: when a commoner died, the church bell was rung once, when a nobleman died twice, when one of the king's relatives died three times, and when the king himself died four times.
One day, a court where everyone sought justice unjustly convicted a citizen, and on this occasion the church bell was rung five times.
The people came to the church in confusion and asked: "Father, who is more important than the king that the church bell was rung five times?"
The priest replied: "Of course there is - justice. Today justice has died."
Moral: When justice dies, something greater than the king dies. Stand by the truth so that injustice does not go unpunished.

stories.title: Confidence is half the battle!
paragraphs: A school principal invited several of his fellow teachers into his office and said to them:

— Since you are our best, most capable teachers, we are entrusting you with a group of the most intelligent and capable students we have selected. Your task is to provide them with a very good education and raise them to a higher level over the next year. I wish you success.
Teachers, students, and parents considered this initiative a very good idea and were eagerly awaiting the end of the school year.
Finally, the school year ended. After the tests, it turned out that those students had shown higher results than other schoolchildren in the city.

The principal congratulated the teachers and said: “I have a confession to make. Those students we entrusted to you were not the most capable children at all - they were average. We chose them by chance.”
Hearing this, the teachers became proud and began to consider the students’ success a result of their professionalism.

The principal continued: “I also have a confession. You weren't the most capable teachers either! I picked your names at random from a bag of papers I had stuffed into a bag. You succeeded because you believed.”
Moral: Belief awakens the hidden power within a person; and high expectations are sometimes the first reason for high results.

stories.title: Dervish Spoons
paragraphs: One day, the dervish was asked:
— What is the difference between true lovers and those who only talk about love?
— Wait, I will show you now, — said the dervish.

He called several so-called lovers and set a table for them. After the guests took their places, hot soup was brought to the table, followed by unusually long spoons called “dervish spoons”. The dervish stated his condition:
— You will eat your soup by holding the ends of these spoons.

The people agreed. But the spoons were so long that it was impossible to bring the soup to their mouths — with every attempt, the soup spilled on them, and the people burned themselves. As a result, they left the table hungry and embarrassed.

Then the dervish called those who knew what true love was. People with radiant faces and eyes full of love came and sat down at the table. The dervish gave them the same condition. This time the scene was different: everyone filled their spoons and handed them to the person in front of them, and one person fed the other. The table was filled with joy, and everyone stood up with full bellies and gratitude.
After the guests dispersed, the dervish turned to the questioners:

— Have you seen it? Whoever sees only himself at the table of life remains hungry. Whoever thinks of his brother or friend and extends his hand to him is also satisfied. In the market of life, it is not always the buyer who benefits, but the giver.
Moral: Whoever thinks only of himself remains hungry at the table of life, while whoever feeds the person in front of him is also satisfied. The giver always wins.

stories.title: Dervish's Robe
paragraphs: One day, a wounded bird came to the king and complained that a dervish had broken its wing. The king immediately summoned the dervish.
— This bird is complaining about you. Why did you break its wing? — he asked.
The dervish tried to defend himself:

— Thank God, the king, I wanted to hunt this bird. I approached it, but it did not run away. I went up to it, but it did not move again. Thinking that it would surrender and trying to catch it, it tried to run away at the moment when I wanted to catch it — and its wing was broken.
The king turned his face to the bird:
— This man is right. Why did you not run away? It did not attack it suddenly. You could have seen it approaching and flown away in time. And now you come to me and complain.
The bird tried to justify itself:
— I did not run away because I saw it in the guise of a dervish. If it were a hunter, I would have flown away immediately. But I thought, "The dervish will not harm you, they fear God."
The king was silent for a moment, then he ordered:
— The bird is right. Break the dervish's arm!
The bird immediately protested:
Please, don't do that!
— Why? — the king asked.
— If you break his arm, he will do the same thing again after he recovers. It is best to have him remove his dervish cloak so that birds like me will not be deceived again.
Moral: Outward holiness does not make a person genuine. Look at the actions, not the clothes - clothes do not make a person a dervish.

stories.title: Drinking the syrup of martyrdom
paragraphs: During the Ottoman period, soldiers who were seriously injured in wars and were dying would drink syrup made from Zamzam water from small barrels they carried with them, so that their mouths would be sweetened before they became martyrs. The expression “drinking the syrup of martyrdom” originated from here.
Moral: Behind every expression, there is a history, a sacrifice. The words in our language carry the memory of our past.

stories.title: Fasting
paragraphs: A few young men see an old man sitting in a corner eating during Ramadan. They approach him and ask him jokingly:
— Come on, uncle, are you eating, aren't you fasting?
The old man: — Of course, I'm fasting, I just drink water and eat.
The young men laugh: — What kind of fasting is this?

The old man says: — Of course, I'm fasting. I don't lie, I don't look at anyone with a bad eye, I don't make fun of anyone, I don't waste, I don't insult anyone, I don't gossip, I don't covet anyone's property. Because I suffer from a certain illness, I can't force myself to fast, just because I have a stomach ache. — Then he turns to the young men and asks:
— And what about you, are you fasting?
The young men look embarrassed and lower their heads: — No, we're not fasting, we're just not eating.
Moral: If a person abstains from food and does not abstain from lying, backbiting, insulting, and evil deeds, he is not fully experiencing the spiritual spirit of fasting.

stories.title: Forty days
paragraphs: There is a custom in Turkic countries where the mother and baby do not leave the house for forty days after birth, and no guests come to their house. It is said that this is an ancient Turkish custom and dates back to the Goyturks.

When the time came, the child's fortieth birthday was celebrated as follows: the mother and child were invited to the house of one of their close relatives, and the owner of the house would give gifts in the name of the baby - SMALL MONEY so that he would be prosperous throughout his life; COTTON so that he would live long and have a soft heart until his hair turned gray; SUGAR so that his mouth would always be sweet and his face would always smile; WHEAT so that his house would be blessed; SALT so that his mouth would not run out of flavor; EGGS so that his stomach would be full and his back strong.
Moral: A blessing and love are hidden in each of our customs. The gifts given to a baby are actually beautiful wishes that are kept for his whole life.

stories.title: Friend of God
paragraphs: An old man sees a child without shoes, feels sorry for him and buys a pair of shoes for the child.
The child takes the shoes in his hands and looks at them for a while, then raises his head and asks:
— Are you God?
The old man's hands tremble, his eyes fill with tears:
— No, my child, I am a simple person.
The child thinks for a moment, then says quietly:
— Then you are a friend of God. Last night, while crying, I told God that I had no shoes.
Moral: Sometimes goodness does not come from heaven, but through the hands of good people. Perhaps it is in your hands to be the answer to someone's prayer.

stories.title: Hajj pilgrimage
paragraphs: When the time comes for a person on Hajj pilgrimage to throw stones at the devil, instead of throwing them, he starts hitting himself with them. A young man asks in surprise: “Uncle, why are you hitting yourself with stones?” The man replies: “Son, tell me, what do we have to do with the devil here? We need to stone the devil within ourselves, educate our souls, and purify ourselves.”
The heat is in the fire, not in the hair,
the miracle is in the head, not in the crown.
Whatever you seek, seek it within yourself,
not in Jerusalem, Mecca, or the Hajj.
Moral: The real struggle is not with the devil outside, but with one’s own soul. The miracle is not in the stones or crowns, but within one’s own soul.

stories.title: Haram money
paragraphs: One day, while walking on the road, a sum of money fell from the hand of a person walking in front of me. Usually, in such cases, I would warn him by saying, “You dropped your money,” but this time I followed the devil, picked up the money from the ground and put it in my pocket.
When I got home, I told my wife the story.
— Put some more on top, let's go to the cinema, — she said. “Let's do it.” I said. We decided to go to the cinema on the weekend.
The lady insisted: “You promise now, but then you suddenly refuse; it's better to buy the tickets online now so that we can be sure.” I said “Let's do it” and bought the tickets online.

I am a repairman myself. A paid client of mine called and said, “Come to my garden on Saturday, we have some work to do.” I asked, “Can I come on Sunday?”, but my client said, “No, it's not possible.” Since we bought the cinema tickets on Saturday, as if they were the other way around, I lost a lot of money from this.
In short, Saturday arrived. As my wife and I were getting ready to leave the house, we unexpectedly met my mother-in-law and father-in-law in front of the door.

I was about to say, “We’re going to the movies,” and continue on our way, when my wife quickly moved away from me and said, “We’re going to the movies, come on, come with us.” I realized how helpless I was.
Since my mother-in-law doesn’t like public transportation, we had to take a taxi to the cinema. Of course, I had to pay for the taxi.

We got to the cinema. I bought two extra tickets. Moreover, I had to buy a box of popcorn for everyone before the movie started — it couldn’t be otherwise, the groom has to entertain everyone, because he found money on the way! I didn’t even spend as much money on the sacrificial meat as I had spent on that popcorn. Since we quickly emptied the popcorn boxes, I had to go buy new ones during the movie. In short, I paid a lot for the money I found, but my punishment wasn’t over yet. Well, what we were going to see was still ahead of us.

Finally, the movie ended, and we went out into the street. We went out, but what a way! I ran into one of my old acquaintances. Since we had a long-standing enmity, my father-in-law and mother-in-law were with me, but he said a few harsh words to me. I couldn't stand it. A fight broke out. It broke out, it broke out! I hit him, he hit me. My father-in-law also got involved. In short, by the time the police arrived, my nose and my father-in-law's arm were broken. Although we ended our fight peacefully at the police station, I had to pay for both my and my father-in-law's hospital expenses due to the injuries we received.

Recently, I was walking along the road again. I saw someone buying doner in front of me. When the seller was giving me the change, the coins fell to the ground. The man bent down and didn't pick up the change. I couldn't bear it and said, “Oh brother, at least don't think about yourself, think about the person who will find this money; ”Don't put people in trouble, please take that money from the ground.“”
Moral: Money that is not earned by the sweat of your brow does not benefit a person; often you lose much more than you earn. Do not touch what is not lawful.

stories.title: He who eats little and walks upright
paragraphs: He who eats little has no business with the doctor, and he who walks upright has no business with the judge.
Moral: The best defense is not to get sick, and the best right is to be right. He who lives upright has no business with his body or his fate.

stories.title: Help Them Yourself, O Exalted God!
paragraphs: To the restless, left without a home,
to the orphan, left alone,
to the needy, left hungry and thirsty,
to the sick, left in hardship,
to the one whose heart is wounded, whose eyes wait on the road,
to the hopeless, left without a way,
to the heedless, left without light,
to the one who still has a wish, who still dreams,
to the faithless, left without You —
help them Yourself, O exalted God!
Moral: The last refuge of the helpless, the lonely, and the hopeless is the Creator. Prayer is the language of deepest need.

stories.title: If fate allows, we'll meet
paragraphs: The man who always says "we'll meet" now says "if fate allows, we'll meet." There's something strange here. I haven't changed, my attitude towards him is as warm as before. I would like to meet him again with great pleasure. But this "if fate allows" seems to be a barrier between us. I'm unaware of his fate, and he's unaware of mine. I wonder if these two fates know about each other, can they agree among themselves and make us meet?
Maybe we shouldn't expect anything from fate, and this is just the embodiment of the saying "out of sight, out of mind"?
I never liked this expression "if fate allows".
Moral: Don't let the coldness between you and your loved ones linger. Don't postpone it by saying "if fate allows" - meet today, take heart today.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

stories.title: Light of the Universe
paragraphs: British artist William Holman Hunt's "Light of the Universe" is on display at the Royal Academy in London. The painting depicts a man standing at a door at night with a lantern in one hand, looking philosophical. The man knocks on the door with the other hand, hoping that it will open.

An art critic who studied the painting asked Hunt: "It's a beautiful painting, but I don't understand its meaning. Will the door that the man is knocking on never open? Perhaps you forgot to pull the doorknob?"

Hunt smiled and replied: "This is no ordinary door. This door embodies the human heart. Since the door only opens from the inside, it has no outside handle. If that door is not opened for you from the inside, you cannot enter."
Moral: The door of the heart opens only from the inside. Love and goodness do not force their way in - you must let them in yourself.

stories.title: May prayer come and find you
paragraphs: Our elders have said that you —

be the one who holds the hand of a poor person, the one who caresses the head of an orphan, the one who covers the feet of a child, the one who is wide and the one who is strong, so that the prayer that you need may come and find you.
Moral: A person who extends a hand to the needy and caresses the head of an orphan is himself worthy of prayer. The hand you do good to will one day be opened to you too.

stories.title: My Alif Has Been Dotted
paragraphs: There is an expression in Turkish: “elifim noktalandı.” It comes from writing the letters “alif” (ا) and “ha” (ه) side by side in the old Ottoman script (اه). Because the “ha” after “alif” resembles a dot, people say “alifim noktalandı,” and metaphorically it means “my joy turned to sorrow.” The letter “alif,” with its long, thin appearance, expresses freedom and beauty, while the letter “ha,” with its bent, almost crushed appearance, expresses distress and collapse.
When these two letters come together, the cry “ah” appears.
Moral: Sometimes the change of a letter — of a moment — turns joy into sadness. Every expression in our language carries the trace of an emotion, a story.

stories.title: Not to deviate from the right path
paragraphs: One day, a man who was wasting his time in idleness, idleness, and eating inheritances got tired of this situation and went to the king to seek advice on how to live a righteous life without deviating from the right path and asked him to show him a way. The king thought for a while and ordered the man to do the following: "Take this jar full of olive oil and carry it from one end of the city to the other without spilling even a drop. If a single drop falls on the ground, know that your neck will be cut off." He also assigned two soldiers to the man to supervise.

The man gathered all his strength, used his intelligence, and carried the jar to the other end of the city without spilling even a drop. Then he returned and went to the king again and said, "May the king live, I have carried out your order perfectly." The king asked, "What did you see in the city, what did you witness?" There was a market in the city that day, and the crowd was so large that even a pin would not fall to the ground.

Nevertheless, the man replied to the king: "May the king live, I was so careful not to spill the oil in the jar on the ground for the sake of my life that I could not take my eyes off the jar for a moment to look around. For this reason, I did not see anyone or witness any event."

After this lesson, the king gave the man his advice with peace of mind: "If you are so careful in everything you do, in every task you are given, if you devote yourself to your work, and if you do not forget that God is always watching over you, you will never stray from the right path."
Moral: A person who approaches everything he does with full attention, and who does not forget that God is watching him, will never stray from the right path.

stories.title: O Allah, find a solution to our problems
paragraphs: In the name of the Most Gracious and the Most Merciful, find a solution to our problems,
In the name of the Forgiving and the Relenting, forgive our sins and accept our repentance,
In the name of the Provider, bless our sustenance,
In the name of the Healer, heal our sick,
In the name of the Opener, open the doors of goodness.
Moral: When a person realizes his weakness and prays sincerely, his heart finds peace. Prayer is the language of hope and trust.

stories.title: O God, first give to the mountains and stones
paragraphs: There was a prayer in ancient Turkic lands:
— O God, first give to the mountains and stones, give to the forest, animals, water. Then give to people, to my next door neighbor, to the needy. If there is any left, give to me last!
Moral: True generosity is to think of others first, then yourself. The culture of sharing of an entire people lives in this prayer.

stories.title: Pray while washing dishes
paragraphs: Pray while washing dishes. Be grateful that you have dishes to wash. Because it shows that you have something to eat, that you fed someone, that you cared for someone, that you prepared food and set the table.
Think of those who don't even have a dish to wash, who don't have anyone to set the table for.
Moral: Be grateful for the simple things you have: having dishes to wash means you have a table, you have loved ones. Gratitude goes a long way.

stories.title: Ramadan Prayer
paragraphs: May the Almighty God accept our prayers, bless our sustenance, heal our sick, forgive our sins, open doors of goodness for us, and fill our hearts with love and mercy!
May you have a blessed Ramadan!
Moral: Sincere prayer fills the heart with hope and mercy. The wish for blessings, healing, and forgiveness brings a person closer to the Creator.

stories.title: Sacrificial meat
paragraphs: I was in the 5th grade of school. We didn't need anyone. My father, who was a builder, had joined a cooperative that was under construction. We dreamed that “it won't take six or seven months, and we will move into our own house.”

One morning we woke up to a terrible shaking. There had been an earthquake. Thankfully, nothing bad had happened to us or to those around us. No one in our building was hurt. But although our house and our lives were safe, this event brought another trouble to our family: as a result of the earthquake, construction work had stopped, and my father was unemployed.
No matter how hard we tried to save, the money my father earned from the repair jobs he found from time to time was not enough to support our household.
My father couldn't find work all winter. He would go with hope and return sad.

There were a few days left before Ramadan. My father came home happily - he had found a job. “Prepare your documents, come,” they said. He announced the news with joy and left the house at lightning speed. “I have to deliver today,” he said.
A few hours had passed when our neighbor came in with a panicked expression on his face.
“Don’t be afraid, but your father has had a minor accident,” he said.

When we arrived at the hospital, my father’s face was pale. His arms and legs were bandaged. A car speeding through a red light had hit my father. When we prayed that he was alive, my father tried to hide the tears that were flowing from his eyes, embarrassedly saying, “Why did I survive? I made your burden heavier.”

After a while, my father came home. Our stove wasn’t burning, our house was cold. Several of our neighbors had called the municipality and asked for coal for us. “No way,” they said — we had to register in advance.
And so, our “sugar-free” Ramadan holiday came and went. Despite all the difficulties, the weather had warmed up a little, the bandage on my father’s arm had come off, but his leg was still bandaged.

Then came Eid al-Adha. I thought to myself: “There are twelve apartments in our building, many of them will sacrifice. At least they will give us a share, and my mother will cook my favorite meat dishes.” As I watched from the window, the sacrificial animals were slaughtered, skinned, and bowls of meat were carried to the houses in the empty area opposite. Every time the door was opened, the delicious smell of meat being roasted in the houses spread to our house. But unfortunately, no one brought us a piece of meat.

Meanwhile, my grandmother called from the village to congratulate us on our holiday. She sensed that I was worried by the sound of my voice as she spoke. She asked insistently and anxiously: “Has your father gotten worse?”
“No,” I said slowly. “The neighbors didn’t give us sacrificial meat.”
In the summer months, we would go to the village to my grandmother. She had a cow and five or six chickens. Her cow gave good milk. When she milked it, my grandmother would sing songs to her.

On the third day of the holiday, there was a knock on our door early in the morning. It was my grandmother who came. We welcomed her with joy. She hugged us all, crying. “My lambs, my lambs, I brought you a lot of meat,” she said.

We filled the refrigerator to the brim with meat. My sister quickly chopped the meat. The delicious smell of the meat cooking further fueled my appetite, which had been growing for two days. My mouth was watering as I stood at the stove. I had no patience to wait for the table. I picked up the fork and dipped it into the meat. I was whistling as I brought the skewer to my mouth when my father’s words to my grandmother almost pierced my ears:
— Oh, mother, oh! Why did you slaughter that cow?
My heart was pounding, my head was spinning. I threw the fork in my hand and ran outside. My grandmother's hope, the cow she milked while singing songs, had been dashed because my soul craved meat?

The table was set, they pulled me by the arm and insisted on making me sit down. I reluctantly and shyly dipped my fork in again. The skewer was stuck in my throat. Tears fell from my eyes. “What happened, what's wrong with you?” they asked.
— My tooth!… — I said. — My tooth hurts a lot.
Moral: A holiday is a real holiday when it is everyone's holiday. It is humanity's duty not to forget those who do not see meat in their homes, those who are in need, in the midst of abundance.

stories.title: Stoning the Devil
paragraphs: When the time comes for a person on the Hajj pilgrimage to throw stones at the devil, instead of throwing them, he starts hitting himself with them. A young man around him asks in surprise:
— Uncle, why are you hitting yourself with a stone?
The man replies:
— Son, tell me, what do we have to do with the devil here? We need to stone the devil inside us, educate our own souls, and purify ourselves.
Moral: The real struggle is not with the devil outside, but with one's own soul. Purifying oneself is more difficult than condemning others, but it is more valuable.

stories.title: The Dervish's Dress
paragraphs: The Dervish was asked:
— Why is your dress so untidy?
The Dervish replied:
— Since I am constantly busy improving my interior, I have no time to improve my exterior.

Moral: A person who beautifies his inner world does not make external defects a criterion for measurement. Because what makes a person beautiful is not his clothes, but the purity of his heart and the light of his soul.

stories.title: The Idle Devil
paragraphs: A dervish was lost in thought when he suddenly saw the devil next to him. "Why are you sitting so harmlessly?" he asked the devil.
The devil, tired, raised his head and answered the question with a question: "You people cause so much harm and pain to each other that I have no work to do?"
Moral: People oppress each other so much that the devil has no work to do. Most evil comes not from outside, but from within us.

stories.title: The most beautiful blessing
paragraphs: The dervish was asked:
— What is the most beautiful blessing that can happen to a person?
The dervish said:
— It is to meet someone who wants to listen to you.
Moral: The most beautiful blessing that can happen to a person is a person who wants to listen to you sincerely. Being listened to is another name for being loved.

stories.title: The Mullah and the Scholar
paragraphs: A scholar from another country comes to Tamerlane; after much talk through an interpreter, he says he wishes to meet the scholars of this land. Tamerlane gathers all the scholars. None of them dares to debate the foreigner. At last, seeing their fear, the Mullah takes the debate upon himself.

A gathering is held. The foreign scholar draws a circle on the ground and faces the Mullah. The Mullah thinks a moment and divides the circle in two. Seeing the scholar silent, he draws another line, divides it into four, pulls three parts toward himself and acts as if giving one part to the foreigner. The scholar agrees. Then the scholar holds out a fist with the back of the hand toward the ground and waits. The Mullah answers by turning his hand the other way, fingers pointing down. The scholar agrees to that too.

A third time the scholar gestures as if eating. The Mullah quickly takes an egg from his pocket and flaps his arms like bird wings. The scholar laughs, kisses the Mullah’s hand, and the Mullah leaves.
Through the interpreter Tamerlane asks the scholar: “We understood nothing of these signs.”

The scholar says: “Views of the world differ. By drawing that circle I meant that the earth is round, and I wanted your scholar’s opinion. Mashallah — he quickly drew the equator, then divided the globe into four and showed that three parts are water and one is land. Then I asked about the life of plants on the globe. Your scholar answered rightly again — that all plants live by rain and the sun’s rays.”
“As a third question I wanted his view of humans and animals; with an egg he quickly reminded me that birds too belong to that kind.”
After the scholar left, Tamerlane called the Mullah and asked him about the exchange.

The Mullah said: “Ah, the scholar… I thought he was truly a deep man. Turns out he was a simple glutton… First he drew a circle on the ground and said to me, if only there were a pan of omelette here now. I quickly halved it and said they wouldn’t give it all to you — we’re here too. I saw my friend wasn’t satisfied. I quickly split it again and took three shares myself, so he’d see what greed gets you. The man saw the omelette slipping away and agreed. The second time he raised his hand to the sky as if to say: how about a pot of pilaf?

I held my hand palm-down and said: if there’s any black on top, I’ll eat it. The third time he showed me his belly and said: I’ve come from the road, I’m hungry. I quickly took the egg from my pocket and said: for your sake — I’m hungrier than you, and I’ve only one egg in my pocket; don’t insist, I can’t give it.”
Moral: The same sign is read differently in each person’s world. We often see the other in the mirror of our own thoughts.

stories.title: The Pleasure of Allah
paragraphs: Haja Ubaydullah Ahrar says:
"I have examined all the paths that lead to the pleasure of Allah; I have found that the shortest is to please people.
I have examined all the paths that lead away from the pleasure of Allah; I have found that the most dangerous is to break a heart."
Moral: The shortest path to pleasure is to please people, and the most dangerous path that leads away from it is to break a heart.

stories.title: The power of truth

stories.title: The Price of a Miracle
paragraphs: (A True Story)

Lisa was eight years old when she heard her parents talking about her younger brother, Oliver. All the little girl knew was that her brother was very sick and that her parents had no money for his treatment.
Only a very expensive operation could save Oliver. There was no one to lend them money. Lisa heard her father whisper helplessly to her tearful mother, “Only a miracle can save him now.”

The girl went into her room and took out a glass jar that she had kept in a secret place in the closet. She poured out all the money in the jar on the floor and counted it carefully—she did this several times. When she was finished counting, she carefully put the coins in the jar, closed the lid, and went out the back door to the pharmacy.

As soon as she reached the pharmacy, she went inside and patiently waited for the pharmacist to pay attention to her. The pharmacist was busy, his mind was busy talking. Although Lisa tried to get his attention with various movements and sounds, the man remained silent. Finally, the little girl took some of her money out of the container and slammed it on the glass counter. The pharmacist was startled:
— My daughter, what do you want? — he asked nervously and, without waiting for her answer, added: — I am talking to my brother right now, whom I have not seen for a long time.
— I also want to talk to you about my brother, — Lisa answered with the same nervousness. — He is sick... I need a miracle to cure him.
— What? You want a miracle? — the pharmacist became even more irritated.
— His name is Oliver, and something bad is growing in his brain. My parents say that now only a miracle can save him. Tell me, how much does a miracle cost?
— We do not sell miracles here, my daughter. I am sorry, but I cannot help you, — the pharmacist said in a slightly soft voice.
— Look, I have money. If it is not enough, I will find the rest and bring it. Just tell me the price of a miracle.
A smartly dressed man who had been watching the conversation from the sidelines until now—the pharmacist’s brother—leaned down and asked Lisa:
— What kind of miracle does your brother need?

— I don’t know,— Lisa answered.— All I know is that he is really sick, and my parents say he needs an operation. Since my parents don’t have the money for an operation, I decided to spend my own money.
— How much money do you have?— the man asked.
— One dollar and eleven cents,— Lisa answered slowly.— That’s all I have, but I can add a little more if necessary.
— One dollar and eleven cents... What a wonderful coincidence,— the man smiled.— That’s exactly the price of the miracle your little brother needs.
The man took the money from the girl, took her hand, and said:
— Take me home. I want to see your brother, talk to your parents. Let’s see if I have the miracle your brother needs.
This handsome man was Dr. Carlton Armstrong, a renowned neurosurgeon.
The operation was free of charge, and soon Oliver was back home. Mom and Dad were overjoyed. Mom whispered to Dad, “This is a real miracle. How much did the operation cost?”

Lisa’s lips parted, and she smiled with satisfaction. Because she knew exactly how much this miracle had cost: one dollar and eleven cents—plus the little girl’s belief in the existence of a miracle that could heal her brother.
Moral: Faith is a powerful force. Sometimes, when a child’s pure faith meets the kindness of a human being, a miracle is born.

stories.title: Where does misfortune come from?
paragraphs: The dervish is asked:
— Where does misfortune come from?
The dervish says:
— Check your eyes, have you looked at what is forbidden?
— Check your tongue and ears, have you listened to gossip and gossip?
— Check your hands, have you reached out to what is forbidden and added something forbidden to your livelihood?
— Check your feet, have you gone where you should not have gone?
Moral: The root of what happens to us can often be found in our own actions. Check your eyes, your tongue, your hands, and your steps.

stories.title: Why are you waiting for the end of the world?
paragraphs: One day, a professor at a university in America addressed his students as follows while starting a class:
— Imagine for a moment that today is the last day of the world. Tomorrow at this time, everything will be over. You have no chance of salvation. What would you do if that were the case?
The students gave different answers:
— I would pray, ask God to forgive my sins.
— I would say goodbye to all my loved ones.
— I would dedicate the rest of my time to my family.
— I would visit my mother or father.
— I would eat all my favorite foods for the last time.
— I would sleep until I was full.
— I would walk in the forest for the last time, enjoying the greenery.
— I would watch the sunrise and sunset for the last time.
— I would watch the stars in the evening.
— I would prepare my favorite meal, invite all the people I love to dinner.
— I would go to the place I wanted to go most in life, and wait for death there.
— I would look for and find the people I have hurt, I would apologize to them so that they would forgive me, and so on.
The teacher writes all the answers on the board, then laughingly says:
— Children, why are you waiting for the end of the world to do all this?
Moral: Don't wait for the end of the world to do good deeds. Do loving, forgiving, and valuing today, right now.

stories.title: Work with your hands, hope in God
paragraphs: Once upon a time, there was a dervish. He spent most of his days in solitude and worship. However, he did not like being in need of people, so he would devote part of his day to work: he would work a little, buy bread with the money he earned with his hands, and distribute the excess to the poor.

One day, while he was still engaged in worship in the desert, his eyes fell on a fox. The fox's legs were crippled, and he could barely move forward. The dervish thought to himself: "I wonder what this fox does for a living? Wild animals live on hunting, and for hunting they need sharp feet. This poor thing has no feet. I wonder where God provides for him?"

While he was thinking this, he saw a lion from afar bringing a gazelle he had hunted in its tusks. The lion puts down its prey, tears it apart, eats it to its heart's content, then leaves the rest there and walks away. The crippled fox, who had been lying in wait for a while, crawls towards it, eats the meat and fills its stomach.

The dervish is amazed at this. He praises Allah, who provides sustenance to the fox through the lion's hand. Then the following thought comes to his mind: "Since this fox earns its sustenance without doing anything, why shouldn't Allah provide for me? I cut off the hours I would have set aside for worship and spend them on work. However, I can also worship my Lord during those hours and earn rewards. From now on, I will not work. Allah, who sent the crippled fox's food to the lion's feet, will also provide for me in some way."

From that day on, the dervish abandons work and devotes himself to worship day and night. But no matter how much he waits, sustenance does not come. No one knocks on his door, no one brings him a piece of bread. The dervish melts away day by day, leaving only skin and bones.
Finally, one day when he was exhausted, he heard a voice from the unseen:

— I gave you a healthy body, strong arms, and sharp legs. But you have compared yourself to a crippled fox. Why do you compare yourself to a fox and not a lion? Why do you look at someone else's surplus? Get up, work like a lion, earn your own livelihood. Let the helpless and the helpless rely on you. Eat yourself and feed the needy.

The dervish is ashamed of what he has done, repents, and returns to his previous life. He earns his livelihood again with the labor of his own hands, and gives up the idea of ​​being a burden to others once and for all.
Moral: A person who looks at the share of the needy despite having the strength is not trusting in Allah - he is simply covering up his laziness with faith.

stories.title: A Festive Gift

stories.title: A Mother’s Love
paragraphs: Erich Fromm
I am one year old—completely happy, because my mother is always beside me.
I am two—my mother is with me only sometimes. I wonder what is happening.
I am three—my mother is at work, and my nanny is with me.
I am five—my mother is in a meeting, and my grandmother is with me.
I am seven—my mother is at a seminar; I am at school with my teacher.
I am thirteen—a teenager. My mother still has to work, and my friends are beside me.
I am seventeen—my mother comes home exhausted. I am at school, in class, or at a café with friends.
I am twenty—young and confident. My mother is not at home, but my friends are with me.
I am twenty-three—I have started working. My mother is home now, while I am at work.
I am thirty—and I wonder: when did my mother and I last spend real time together? Something is wrong.
I am thirty-five—married. My mother lives in her home, and I in mine.
I am forty—my mother waits for me just as I once waited for her as a child.
I am fifty—I have grown older, yet one wish never ages: to press my heart to hers, embrace her, and rest my head on her tired knees.
I am fifty-five—another mother is always beside me now, the mother of my children. My own mother has passed away, and I live with the ache of missing her.

In the rush of ordinary life, one of our gravest failures is not giving enough time to our children and those we love. Children are the most precious characters in the extraordinary film of life unfolding before us. If we fail to notice them growing, those passing moments can never be recovered.
Life has no stop, play, forward, or rewind buttons that can show us its vanished scenes again. May we understand this before it is too late.
Love your child today. Hold them, take their hand, and remain beside them. Do not miss today’s episode, because tomorrow a new scene of childhood will already have begun.
“A mother’s love is a selfless, protective, and warm refuge. Precisely because it is unconditional, it cannot be obtained by force.”
Moral: A mother’s love is unconditional and irreplaceable. Make time for those you love today, because time is the most precious thing we can never recover.

stories.title: Fakir Baykurt's unforgettable mother's advice
paragraphs: One day, Fakir Baykurt (Turkish writer, 1929-1999) asked his mother for tea: "Mom, my heart wants tea, come and have some tea," he said. The mother did not let her son down and took him to Topal Hüseyin's nearby teahouse and called out, "Master, please bring a cup of tea for my child."

After the tea arrived, Fakir Baykurt, who was so excited at that moment and did not know how to drink the tea, took a big sip of the hot tea and suddenly threw the cup on the ground as it was near his mouth.

Although the tea cup did not break because it fell to the ground, Fakir Baykurt thought that his mother would slap him. But that did not happen. His mother called Topal Hüseyin and asked him to bring another cup of tea.
Baykurt drank the second cup of tea this time in a slurping motion. For years, he asked his mother why she didn't slap him that day, but his mother left this question unanswered every time...
Fakir Baykurt's mother answered this question years later at the village school where her son taught. Fakir Baykurt remembers that day when his mother, Elif Khanum, attended his son's lesson:
— I got angry, excited, and roared during class! When the lesson was over, I asked my mother outside: "Mom, how was it, did you like my teaching?"
And my mother said: "Oh, what can I say, son, it wasn't bad."
— Mom, the inspectors come, they like it, and they give good grades. And you say "it wasn't bad." How can this be? — I asked.
And my mother said these words that can be a lesson to everyone: "For years, you asked me why I didn't slap you. Now I'm telling you, open your ears and listen!

If I had been angry the day you poured tea on me, the lion inside would have raged. If I had beaten him, that lion would have died! Then you wouldn't be a teacher like that. You should act like me, be calm. Don't try to kill the lion inside these children with a stick."
Moral: Don't kill the "lion" inside a child — his self-confidence — by beating him. True education is not given with fear, but with patience and love.

stories.title: Father and son
paragraphs: The son had left home after a heated argument with his father. The father, who was heartbroken, was also angry and forbade his son's name to be mentioned in the house. The mother, however, would sit on her son's bed every night and go to sleep sniffing his pillow.
— I miss my son. What can I do, let's go find him and bring him home, — she said, but the father did not agree.
A long time had passed.
One day, seeing that the mother was constantly in tears, the father felt sorry for her; he took a piece of paper with his son's address written on it from his pocket and handed it to the mother:
— Go, you can find him at this address, — he said. — But never tell him that I gave him the address.

Although the father said a few more words, the mother did not seem to hear him; all that was left in her mind was the address. She was overjoyed. She immediately got ready, set off and reached the address written on the paper. It was a repair shop. Her son was working in overalls. The mother stared at her son with tearful eyes for a few minutes, then finally walked towards him. The son, who had been unaware of his family for a long time, thinking that everyone had forgotten about him, was at first surprised when he saw his mother, then hugged her tightly.
He asked everyone except his father, asked how he was, and finally:
— How is that man, is he still angry? — he asked his mother.
The mother left this question unanswered:
— Come on, son, let's go home, — he said.
— No, mother, I won't go. I can't live in the same house with that man again, — he said and started walking towards work.
The mother, who had been watching her son for a while, called out to give him the sweets she had prepared.
The son took the gift:
— What's wrong, mother, don't insist, I won't come. I can't live in the same house with a man who hasn't even looked for me once, isn't interested in me, — he said.
The mother, with her neck bent, said:

— Well, son, it's best that you know. I see that your decision is firm, you will not return home. But your father ordered you to stay away from the person you have been friends with for the past month - he will not do you any good. Let him reconcile with his old friend, - he said.
Hearing this, the son froze in amazement.
The mother returned home and rebuked the father:
- Man, if you knew where he was, why did you hide it from me? So, that's why you were so relaxed?
The father, who always seemed nervous, broke down, tears flowed from his eyes:
- He is my soul, my soul, - he said.
- How long have you known? - the mother asked.

- Since he left. Sometimes during the lunch break, I would go and watch from afar to see what he was eating and drinking. This was also the reason why I sometimes came home late: I would go and watch our son in the evenings to see what he was doing, who he was sitting with, - the father replied.
While the elders were hugging each other and crying, there was a knock on the door. The mother wiped away her tears and went to open the door.

The son had returned home. He kissed his parents' hands and hugged them. He had understood - the father he thought had forgotten him, torn him from his heart, had actually never taken his eyes off his son.
Moral: Don't hide your love, show it. Sometimes a timely step can prevent years of resentment.

stories.title: From the wise father's advice to his son
paragraphs: O my beloved son!
Every human being should have a mind that can help them to establish different relationships with others. This mind is the inexhaustible source of all happiness and joy.
Life cannot be satisfied; its short or long life does not diminish its value.
Fruit only falls beautifully from the branch when it is ripe. Similarly, people have always preferred those who have seen the light and experienced.
The son of man usually commits the wrongdoings he commits in his youth without thinking about it. But when he remembers them later, these sins pierce his heart like a dagger and torment him.
Those who follow the right and good path in their youth will be respected and honored in their old age in return.
It is good to be strong and powerful. However, strength must be given to the command of the mind.
The Almighty God, the creator of the worlds, did not send the son of man to this world to live forever, but wanted him to taste death at the end of his life.

Know this well: God Almighty has thoroughly tested and accustomed me to two things that have kept me healthy up to this age. One of them is to eat little, and the other is to walk around to digest what I eat.
I also want you to know this: there are three types of people in this world:
The first is those who have their minds and thoughts in order, and who can see and think more or less about the future;

The second is those who are far from knowing whether their path is right or wrong, but who fall into this state not of their own will, but due to the influence of those around them. When they are advised, they accept and listen to words.
The third is those who neither know anything themselves, nor listen to the advice given, but think they know everything. These are the most miserable of all.
O son!
If God Almighty has created you from the people I have listed in the first place, I will be happy.
If you are from the second, I advise you to listen to the advice given to you.
Definitely do not be from the third. They are in no good standing with God or man.
Moral: Wisdom is the source of happiness, and strength is the servant of wisdom. He who listens to advice will be exalted; but he who thinks he knows everything will perish.

stories.title: Grandfather and Grandson at the Market
paragraphs: A grandfather comes to the supermarket with his grandson. They walk the aisles, choose groceries, and fill the basket. Meanwhile the grandson keeps shouting, “Buy me this, buy me that!” and turns the shop upside down. Each time the grandfather says, “Be quiet, Arif — we’ll go home when we finish shopping.” The child reaches the limit of his frustration, takes a Kinder Surprise from the shelf, puts it under his foot, and crushes it. Again the grandfather says, “Be quiet, Arif — we’ll go home when we finish shopping,” then, crestfallen, turns to a nearby worker: “I’m so sorry — I’ll pay for this too.”

At last they pay at the checkout and leave. A woman who has watched the whole scene follows them, approaches the grandfather, and says: “I was impressed by how you behaved with Arif. You are a very patient man. Well done!” The old man thanks her and smiles: “The child’s name is Rafiq — I am Arif.”
Moral: Being able to control yourself in a tense moment is a sign of true strength. Keeping calm sometimes means mastering yourself, not others.

stories.title: Hold my hand
paragraphs: A little girl and her father are crossing a bridge. The father, a little worried, asks his daughter to hold his hand:
— My sweet daughter, hold my hand tightly so that you don't fall into the river.
The little girl replies:
— No, father, you hold my hand.
The father, a little confused, asks curiously:
— What's the difference?

— It's a big difference, — the little girl replies. — If I hold your hand and something happens to me, I might let go of it. But if you hold my hand, I'm sure that no matter what happens, you won't let go of my hand.
Moral: The power of love is not letting go. Instead of waiting for the hand of those who love you to hold theirs, hold theirs tightly.

stories.title: I'm tired, mom
paragraphs: — I'm tired, mom...
— What, son?
— I'm tired of everything: of working, of friends, of traveling, of always being responsible for pleasing someone, I'm so tired.
— Put your head on my knee and relax, son, forget everything for a moment... give me your pain...
— Thank you, mom, it's good that you're here; with you I forget my age, my life. Be there, mom.
— Mom is the giver of life, son, I'm always with you.
— Mom, we tire you out a lot too, forgive us.
— You don't tire me out, son. My tiredness is my motherlessness. I don't have a "mother's knee" to rest my head on, son... Don't get tired, appreciate what you have...
Moral: A mother's lap is the most comfortable refuge in the world. A mother always finds a place to put her tiredness - appreciate what she has.

stories.title: Mother and son
paragraphs: The man put the suitcases he was carrying against the wall. Then he stood up, took a deep breath, and said to his mother, “Mom, this is a very beautiful place.” “Of course, it is beautiful, my son,” the old woman replied. For a while, they were both silent, carefully examining the room.
Then the woman opened her small suitcase and took out her nightgown, slippers, a few towels, and a framed picture. She placed the picture on the table next to her bed.
A boy in a school uniform, with a soldierly posture, was looking out of the picture. A child with full eyes and pursed lips...

The man approached the window and opened the curtain. A pale daylight filled the room. It was freezing outside. He leaned his hands on the heater and watched the muddy cars passing by for a while. Then, without even turning his head, he asked, “Is this closet enough for you, Mom?”

The old woman was lost in thought, so she didn’t even hear her son. She was leaning slightly to one side on her bed, her eyes fixed on the boy in the worn frame, his eyes fixed on the boy with a frightened look.
It was a picture they had taken on the first day of school.

The woman suddenly went back years ago. The day before, she had spent hours explaining how wonderful school was, but she had barely managed to get her son into the classroom. He had been at school all day, and every break she had gone to him and said, “I’m here, son, I’m waiting for you.” But the boy had clung to his mother’s hand even tighter and cried, “Don’t leave me, mom, I’m so scared.”
The sun was setting. The man took his hands off the heater and leaned them against the window, sweating. “Open your other suitcase too, let’s put your things in it, mom,” he said.

“Don’t delay, son, I’ll put them in myself. I don’t have much stuff anyway,” the old woman said. She reached out her trembling hands and took her son’s hand. She seemed to be about to say something, but then she stopped. She swallowed: “The children will be worried too.”

The door slammed shut. The old woman was left alone in the room with the peeling paint and the soldier-like look in the picture with her son. After sitting on the bed for a while, she put on her slippers and went to the window with the curtains open. Her son was getting into the car.
The old woman was afraid. Despite the fact that she had listened for hours the day before to how beautiful this place was, she was still afraid.
Her son's handprint was still on the window glass. She carefully rested her cheek against the mark on the glass. Her eyes were full, her lips were pursed.
“Don't leave me, son, I'm so scared,” she whispered.
The words seemed to melt on the sweaty glass and flowed towards her son, who was sitting outside in his car, waving at her.

Those who lived on the same floor as the old woman heard a sobbing sound that night. The only thing they were used to in the nursing home was the sound of sobbing that echoed through the corridors at night.
Moral: Life is a circle: a child who holds onto his mother's hand one day may leave her the next. True loyalty to a parent is not physical care, but love and attention.

stories.title: Only my mother cries

stories.title: Parenting
paragraphs: In a family, there was a boy who did not listen to his parents. Whatever they said, the boy did the opposite. The boy did poorly at school. He neither studied hard nor completed his homework. Even though his mother got angry and beat him, it did not help. Even though his father locked him in his room and punished him, he could not cope with the child.

One day, when the mother, who was left helpless, took the child to school, she came across a “bear trainer” on the way. The trainer, surrounded by people around, was playing a tambourine, while the bear with a ring on its nose was jumping and playing.
The woman stopped and thought. She said to herself: “I can’t raise this child, but look how this man raised his bear!”
Then she approached the bear trainer and asked: — I can’t raise my child, how do you raise this wild animal?
The man smiled: — There is a way to everything. I also have my own way of raising him.
The woman said: — Please help me.
The bear trainer looked at the boy and said: — There is no difficult task. Entrust him to me for a week, I will make him obedient, — he said.
The woman was happy and started taking the boy to the bear trainer every day.

Although only a few days had passed, the boy's behavior slowly began to improve. He no longer protested against his mother. After a week, the boy became exactly as the woman wanted. The woman was very happy. She expressed her approval to the bear trainer and prayed for him many times.
The neighbors were very surprised by this. That disobedient, rebellious boy was gone, and in his place was a calm, peaceful, well-mannered boy.

The teacher at school was also pleased with this change in the boy and congratulated the mother. However, the change did not last long. Although he was not as ambitious and angry as before, this time the boy began to steal his classmates' things, do secret things and lie openly. The teacher called the boy's mother and said: “I don't know what you are going to do, but your boy has become very strange. He started stealing and lying.” The woman was very sad. Although she went to look for the bear trainer in despair, she could not find him. The man had left.
Seeing the parents’ helpless state, her wise neighbors said: “Don’t worry, I know a wise man with a big heart. If you want, go to him and explain the situation.”

The woman agreed. She took her child and took him to this wise man. After the man got acquainted with the situation, he said: — Give me this beautiful young man for a week, I will see what I can do. — The woman accepted the offer.
He started taking the child to this wise man.

After only two meetings, the man became very upset. He said to the child’s mother: — What have you done to this child? I see animal traits in him. — The woman was surprised: — I didn’t do anything, I just used to take him to the bear trainer because the child was very naughty.

The man became very angry: — Do you think an animal trainer can educate a child? Animals are educated with fear, and people with conscience. Animals are sometimes disciplined by beating, cursing, and punishing; if that doesn’t help, they are put in a dark room and left helpless. How can you entrust your child to an animal trainer?

Then he continued: — Remember that education is not about going after a child, but about entering his heart and influencing him with compassion. Take your child and go. Be close to him, kiss and hug him, listen to him, do not withhold your love from him. The more love you show your child, the more he will soften, he will see that he has parents who love him, his trust and love for you will increase.
— Your child’s cure is neither the bear trainer nor me; only you — the parents, — the wise man concluded.
Moral: A child is educated not with fear, but with love. It is not a teacher or an outsider who educates a child—it is a loving parent.

stories.title: Puppies for sale
paragraphs: A little boy entered the shop after seeing a sign in the window saying “We have puppies for sale.”
“How much do you sell puppies for?” he asked.
“Between thirty and fifty dollars. Each one has a different price,” said the shopkeeper.
The little boy reached into his pocket, took out all the money he had, and placed it in front of the shopkeeper, then counted it all carefully. Finally, in a disappointed voice, he said,
“All I have is thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents,” he said. Then, taking a deep breath, he asked,
“Can I at least see the puppies?”

The shopkeeper smiled and called to his lady in the back room to bring the puppies. A moment later, the lady came out of the room, followed by five fluffy, plump puppies. However, one of the puppies was walking with great difficulty. The boy looked at the puppy:
“What’s wrong with him? Why can’t he walk?” he asked.
“Our vet said that his tibia was congenitally deformed. He will never be able to walk comfortably, - the shopkeeper replied”.
Hearing this, the boy was excited:
“I want to buy this puppy,” the shopkeeper said:
“I don't think you want to buy it, my son. If you want, I'll give it to you.”
The little boy was very angry. He looked the shopkeeper straight in the eye and said:

“I don't want you to give him to me. That puppy is as valuable as any other. I can give you thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents now, but I'll bring you five dollars every week until I get thirty dollars,” he said.
The shopkeeper said:
“You really don't want that puppy, my son. He won't be able to run and play with you like the others,” the little boy said:

“But we have to give him a chance, he's as valuable as any puppy,” he rebelled. Then he bent down and slowly pulled up the hem of his trousers and showed his leg, which was injured by polio, and the iron supports on it. Then he turned to the man and said in a soft voice:
— Uncle, I can't run and play either. This little one and I need friends who will understand and support us.
Moral: Every living thing needs a friend who will understand and support it. The one who is different is just as valuable as the others; we need to give him a chance.

stories.title: Rotten Seed
paragraphs: A father who called his little son, who was constantly suffering from illnesses after his wife died, despised him and gave him to an orphanage.
Years passed.
One day, this man saw his grown son in front of a school. He could not believe his eyes. The father, who looked at his son's shining eyes and healthy body with regret, said with excitement:
— I did not believe that you would recover, that you would become a man. You have become a strong warrior. How did this miracle happen? How did you get rid of your illnesses? — he asked his son.
The boy looks at his father, who once despised him, with his moist eyes, and points to the old woman who has adopted him, who is approaching him from the opposite side, smiling and saying:

— After you said, “Rotten seeds do not germinate” and gave me to the orphanage, this woman took me in as her son and never left her compassionate hands on me, saying, “Every seed watered with love will germinate.”
Moral: Words either build or destroy. It is possible to elevate or destroy someone with a single word—every seed watered with love will germinate.

stories.title: Spinach
paragraphs: We lived in a remote village. We didn’t even have a proper road to get around. My mother was addicted to spinach. After my father’s death, I suspected that she had lost her mind when I was a child...

“You need to eat a lot, it gives strength to the body,” my mother would say, and for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, she would only feed us spinach, with a little cornbread on the side. I hated spinach already, I couldn’t stand to see this vegetable.

One day I told my mother: “When I grow up and have a job and start a family, I will never buy spinach at home. I won’t cook spinach at home.” She promised that she was looking forward to those days, and that she would even play at my wedding, no matter how old she was.

The day came, I moved from our village to the city to study in high school. I somehow managed to make ends meet with the small scholarship I received. Once a month, when I came home, I didn't want to eat a spoonful of the spinach dish my mother put on the table. I only wanted to go back to the dormitory and eat delicious food.

I studied. By the time I graduated from university, my master's degree, and my doctorate with government loans, my mother was already a bent old woman. When I came to the village and got married to the girl I was going to marry, my old mother both cried and played at my wedding, as she had promised years ago. At that time, I couldn't understand why my mother shed tears when she played.
Years passed. My mother passed away two years ago.

One day, I found the notebook my mother had kept at that time in an old chest. On one page of the notebook, my mother had written: “I only had spinach seeds left. I constantly planted spinach and a little corn. I didn't have any on hand or in my pocket. I cooked this dish so that my children wouldn't go hungry. But I didn't rebel. ”Spinach is very useful, so I give it to you three times a day,“ my heart ached when I said. This was all I could do for my children. I love them with all my heart.”

I loved eating spinach at the age of fifty. My wife asks me in surprise why I buy spinach so often, she thinks I love spinach. But she doesn't know that every time I smell that food, I remember the sacrifices my mother made to raise me, how she played at my wedding while crying...
Moral: We often understand a mother's sacrifice in the face of impossibility years later. Love is sometimes hidden in a plate of simple food.

stories.title: Teeth falling out
paragraphs: A king saw in a dream that all his teeth had fallen out, so he called a dream interpreter and asked him what it meant. The man replied: “May the king live, this means that all your relatives will die, and you will be the last to die.” The king was angry and dismissed the man, called another and asked him the same question, and received the answer: “May the king live, you will be the longest-lived in your family.” The king was very pleased with this answer and rewarded the man and sent him on his way.
Moral: The same truth can be expressed both harshly and delicately. Words can both hurt and heal - how can one say it?

stories.title: The best gift
paragraphs: For a father — honor,
For a mother — respect,
For a child — compassion,
For a spouse — love,
For a friend — loyalty,
For society — service,
For the deceased — prayer,
For the world — humanity,
For the hereafter — goodness in the world.
Moral: Every relationship has its own best gift: honor for a father, respect for a mother, loyalty to a friend, service to humanity.

stories.title: The nest builder
paragraphs: The female bird builds the nest.
Moral: It is the woman who builds the nest and keeps the family afloat. Her hard work should be seen and appreciated.

stories.title: The Value of Your Family
paragraphs: One evening, a son came to his father and said he wanted to ask him a question. The father agreed. The son got straight to the point and asked his father how much money he earned in an hour of work. The father was troubled by this question and wanted to know why his son was asking such a question. The son said he was just curious and waited for an answer. Finally, the father gave in and said that he earned a hundred dollars an hour.

Hearing this, the son lowered his head, was silent for a moment, and then asked his father to borrow fifty dollars. This request angered the father; he refused, thinking that his son would spend the money on a meaningless toy or something unnecessary, and told him to go to his room and sleep. The son went to his room without protesting, quietly closing the door.

The father tried to calm down by pacing the room. After a while, he calmed down and admitted to himself that it was wrong for his son to get angry without asking why he wanted the money. The father, tormented by a guilty conscience, went to his son's room, knocked lightly on the door, and asked if he was asleep. The son replied that he was still awake.

The father entered the room and apologized for his harsh behavior. He admitted that he had taken the stress of the day out of his son, handed him fifty dollars, and told him to spend it as he pleased. The son thanked him joyfully, took out the money he had hidden under his pillow, counted it, and looked at his father. Seeing this, the father became angry again and asked his son why he had asked for more money when he had money.

The son explained that the money he had saved before was not enough to buy what he wanted, and now he had exactly one hundred dollars. Then he asked his father if he could "buy" a watch for him - he asked him to come home from work early tomorrow and have lunch with him.
These words deeply moved the father, and his eyes filled with tears. He hugged his little son and apologized to him.
Moral: The greatest need of children is the attention, love, and time spent with them by their parents.

stories.title: Waiting for the teeth
paragraphs: On a cold winter evening, an elderly couple walks into McDonald's and sits down at a table. The man goes to the cashier and buys a hamburger, a large box of fries, and a large Coca-Cola. He cuts the hamburger in half and puts half in front of his wife, counts the fries one by one, and gives her half. After a while, he opens the Coca-Cola bottle, takes a sip first for himself, and then for his wife.
The people around them watch them, saying, "Two people share a meal for one, poor things."
After a while, they see that the hamburger and fries in front of the wife are still the same. The wife watches her husband eat with appetite, occasionally taking a sip of the Coke...
Finally, one of the young employees loses patience and approaches the couple and asks the man:
— Uncle, excuse me, I've been watching you for a while: you're eating, and your wife isn't touching the food. If he doesn't like it, let me bring him something else...
The old man:
— Thank you, young man, but we are happy with our situation... We have been married for sixty years and we share everything like this, — he says.
Not satisfied with this answer, the young man turns to the woman this time:
— Auntie, why don't you eat your hamburger and fries, what are you waiting for?
The old woman points to her husband and replies:
— Teeth...! I'm waiting for teeth, baby.
Moral: No one should be left in need of the one they love. May God not leave anyone helpless, even in their own family.

stories.title: Weeds need to be uprooted
paragraphs: When we were in school, we would spend our summer holidays in our garden with our family. My late father wanted to get us used to hard work. He would assign us garden chores on the days he was at work. He had planted a melon, and it was our duty to water it. Since the water in our well was not suitable for drinking, we would carry drinking water from the well in our neighbor, Uncle Aghasalim's garden.

We had learned to harrow the land. We also did weeding: we would turn the soil upside down with the help of a harrow, and crush and destroy the weeds. But they were not so easy to remove. One day, my father called us to him and explained: "If you want to destroy a weed, hit it deeply with the harrow; the work is not finished until you pull out its roots."
Moral: If you do not uproot both the problem and the bad habit, the appearance of cleanliness is deceptive - after a while it will reappear.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

stories.title: A loved one is a person who gives his love to others
paragraphs: Many years ago in China, a girl named Li-Li got married and started living in the same house with her husband and mother-in-law. However, she soon realized that it was very difficult to make ends meet with her mother-in-law. The two have completely different personalities, which causes them to argue frequently. According to Chinese traditions, this is not a pleasant situation and leads to discontent among those around her.

A few months later, the endless quarrels between the daughter-in-law and the mother-in-law turn into hellish torment for both the young woman and her husband. Believing that something must be done, the young woman runs to her father's old friend, a spice merchant, and tells him about her troubles. The old man prepares a medicine from herbs and instructs her to add a little bit of it to the food she cooks for her mother-in-law every day for three months. The poison will be given little by little so that it will not be known that the daughter-in-law killed her mother-in-law.

The old man instructs the young woman to treat her mother-in-law very well and to cook the most delicious dishes for her so that no one, especially her husband, suspects. Returning home with joy, Li-Li applied exactly what the old man had said.

Every day, she cooked the most delicious dishes and dripped “poison” into her mother-in-law’s bowl. She treated her very well so that no one would suspect anything. After a while, her mother-in-law had changed a lot, and she looked at her as her own daughter. Feeling a heavy burden, the young woman went to the spice shop, feeling regretful and begging the old man for a medicine that would cleanse the blood of the poison she had given her mother-in-law. She no longer wanted the old woman to die.

The old man looked at Li-Li standing in front of him and started laughing and said: “Dear Li-Li, what I gave you was only vitamins. The real poison was in your own brain. As you treated her well, that poison melted and gave way to love; thus you became a real mother and child.”
Moral: The real poison is often in our own brains. As you treat others with love, hatred melts, and enemies turn into friends.

stories.title: Advice for Those Who Marry
paragraphs: Wise elders offered the following counsel to a young couple beginning married life:
“Do not compare your marriage with anyone else’s. Do not say, ‘Look at what that person’s husband is like,’ or ‘Look at what that person’s wife is like.’
Do not seek perfection; none of us is flawless. Do not investigate each other’s past—it is called the past for a reason.
Do not expect your spouse to read your mind. No one can. Speak openly about your wishes and concerns, and try to resolve difficulties through conversation.

Accept that alongside your shared life, each of you has a private world. Hedgehogs draw only as close as their spines allow; if they move too near, they hurt one another. Respect each other’s personal boundaries.
In marriage, be neither owner nor servant, but companions on the same road.
Do not promise, ‘Everything will always be wonderful.’ Say instead, ‘When life becomes difficult, I will be beside you.’
Even if you have been upset with each other during the day, remember to say good night before sleeping. Let tomorrow begin with reconciliation.”
Moral: A happy marriage rests not on comparison or the pursuit of perfection, but on open communication, mutual respect, and care for each other’s personal boundaries.

stories.title: Don't let your hearts separate
paragraphs: Why do people shout when they argue? If the person is right next to you, why do you need to shout? Can't you talk to him calmly? Why do you shout when you get angry?

When people are unhappy with each other and argue, their hearts move away from each other. To overcome this distance and hear each other, they have to shout. The more angry they are, the louder they shout.
But what happens when people fall in love?
They don't shout, but they speak softly. Because their hearts are very close, and the distance between them is very small.
What happens when their love grows stronger?

They are silent, but they whisper to each other, and this love brings them even closer. In the end, even whispering becomes unnecessary for them - they just look at each other and understand everything without words. This happens only between two people who love each other.
Therefore, when you argue, don't let your hearts separate, don't say words that can increase the distance between you. Because one day this distance may become so great that you cannot return.
Moral: Screaming is the sound of the distance between hearts. Do not say words in an argument that will increase that distance, otherwise the return will become difficult.

stories.title: Early Marriage
paragraphs: I had just graduated from university and started working as a teacher at a school. One day, I was sitting in the teachers' room, reviewing the students' exam papers. I was correcting the wrong answers of the female students so that they could get a good grade in order to move up to the next grade.

At that moment, a person entered the teachers' room and curiously asked why I was changing the girls' exam papers. I said, "If these girls fail the exam, their fathers will take them out of school and marry them off at the age of twelve or thirteen. But if they move up to the next grade, their marriageable age will be at least fifteen or sixteen. During this time, even the laziest student will definitely learn something in class."
About half an hour later, our principal called me over and asked what I was doing in the teachers' room. I said that I was reviewing the exam papers.
— Did you meet someone in the teachers' room? What did you say to him? — he asked.
— Did that person complain to you about me? — I asked.
— Not at all! The man came to me and said that he had come to inspect the school, but there was no need for it.
— Why? — I was surprised.
— Because you have a wise young teacher. Please convey my thanks to him, — he said.
Moral: A teacher's small care can change the fate of a girl. Early marriage deprives children of education; let's not turn a blind eye to this.

stories.title: Friendship and love
paragraphs: — Write the quarrel on the leaves of the tree so that when autumn comes, the leaves dry up and fall, and the quarrel disappears.
— Write the anger on the clouds so that it rains, the clouds disperse, and the anger disappears.
— Write the hatred on the snow so that the sun rises, the snow melts, and the hatred disappears.
— Write the friendship and love on the hearts of newborn babies so that they grow up, and friendship and love spread throughout the world.
Moral: Write the quarrel, anger, and hatred on temporary things so that they disappear; write the friendship and love on the hearts so that they remain forever and spread throughout the world.

stories.title: I kiss your eyes
paragraphs: Do you know why it is said "I kiss your eyes"?
It is the eyes that suffer the most from longing; therefore, they are the ones who deserve the most farewell.
Moral: The one who longs the most is the one who deserves the most farewell. Love repays the one who works hard.

stories.title: I Love You
paragraphs: They say a nightingale fell in love with a white rose… Every night he would go and perch beside her and declare his love. But the white rose ignored his feelings and paid no heed to his devotion.

One day the nightingale gathered all his courage, perched beside the white rose again, and said he loved her madly. But the rose snapped: “Leave me alone — I don’t love you!” and hurt him. However much he insisted, the rose rejected him.

The love was so strong that the nightingale, shaken by despair, begged the rose’s forgiveness, pulled a thorn from her, drove it into his own heart with all his strength, and dyed the pure white rose red with his blood!

The rose understood, though late, that the nightingale had truly loved her. But what good was it? It was already too late. Under the branches of the rose now dyed red, the nightingale closed his eyes forever.
Since that day, red roses have meant “I LOVE YOU.”
Moral: True love is sometimes understood too late. Value the one who loves you in the moment — fear having to say “too late.”

stories.title: Love from a distance
paragraphs: Two friends meet. The following conversation takes place between them:
— I think I have a crush on a girl.
— How wonderful! Does she know?
— No.
— Why don't you come closer and confess?

— I would, but I'm afraid of disrupting the order. Suddenly, right where I am, I start to fall in love with someone. We start going to the cinema, the theatre, walking around holding hands. This can lead to resentment, reconciliation, and questions like "why did you look at that?" "why did you filter that?" If there's going to be a breakup in the end, why is there a need for all this fuss?
That's good, I love that girl from a distance.
Moral: Sometimes people are afraid to express their love for fear of losing her. But unrequited love is also a loss.
