stories.title: Purple chepken
paragraphs: In ancient times, there was a custom in Turkish villages: a purple chepken was added to the dowry of girls getting married, along with other items. The chepken was placed at the very bottom of the dowry chest, and it was hoped that the woman would never wear it.

A purple chepken was a garment that could be a threat to men. Because if a woman wore that chepken and went out onto the roof of the house, the chimney, the village square - a place where everyone could see it, it would mean "I don't love my husband, my husband is hurting me, I got married against my will, I want to get a divorce, I am in a difficult situation, help me." In such a case, the village people would help the woman, but would condemn her husband. This was considered a great shame for the man.

For this reason, men would try to solve their problems with their wives without resorting to violence, with love and respect, and, moreover, by making important concessions to the woman. Otherwise, they knew that the woman would wear a purple turban.

A man whose wife wore a purple turban would not only be forced to divorce, but would also not be able to easily remarry. Because everyone knew that a man who made his wife wear a purple turban would never become a husband. No one would give a girl to a man who did not respect a woman and was violent, and it would be very difficult for him to remarry. It is said that this is why the number of women subjected to violence was almost non-existent.

If a woman wore a purple turban, then the flowing waters would stop, the hands that milked cows, spun wool, and wove rugs would stop; old mothers and grandmothers would stop their work and come to the defense of the woman who was forced to wear a purple turban.

At that time, if there were no weddings, no flutes, no other entertainment around, everyone would be silent. Because for a married woman to wear a purple turban or fall into a difficult situation was considered death.
The husband of a woman wearing a purple turban cannot leave the house, cannot go to the teahouse, and no one will look at his face.
Moral: Violence against women is unacceptable. When society considers it a duty of conscience to protect women, there is no room for oppression.

stories.title: Rose
paragraphs: If you water a rose too much, it will rot; if you water it too little, it will wither; if you water it right, it will live.
Moral: In love and in upbringing, moderation is key. Neither excessive pressure nor indifference — moderate care keeps it alive.

stories.title: Take Care of Those You Love
paragraphs: On a sunny day in the park, a woman told the man beside her that the boy in the red shirt on the swings was her son. The man smiled and pointed to the boy in blue: that was his son, Jamil.
After a while, he checked his watch and called:
“Jamil, it is time to go home.”
“Five more minutes, Dad, please!”
The father agreed. Later he called again, but the boy asked for another five minutes. Once more, the man said yes.
The woman remarked admiringly:
“You are a very patient father.”
The man answered with a sorrowful smile:

“This is not patience. Last year my older son Kamal was struck nearby by a drunk driver. I had never given him enough of my time. Now I would give anything for five more minutes with him. I promised not to repeat that mistake with Jamil”.
“My son thinks he gains five more minutes of play. In truth, I am the one who gains — the happiness of watching him five minutes longer.”
Moral: Every extra moment with those you love is a gift. Before it is too late, give them five more minutes today.

stories.title: The eraser in marriage
paragraphs: A story takes place between a father and his newly married young son.
The father asks his son to bring a white piece of paper, a pen, and an eraser.
— Why? — the son asks.
— You bring it, — says the father.
The son brings a pen and paper, but he can’t find an eraser.
— Go and get an eraser, — says the father.
The son is very surprised, but he goes and buys an eraser, brings it, and sits next to his father.
— Write, — says the father.
— What should I write?
— Write whatever you want.
The son writes a sentence.
— Erase it now, — says the father.
The son erases it.
— Write another sentence.
— For God’s sake, father, what do you want?
— Write something again.
The son writes. His father again erases what he has written.
After this writing and erasing has been repeated several times, the father asks:
— Is the paper still white?
— Yes, it is white, father. What does all this mean?
The father puts his hand on his son's shoulder and says:

— Yes, my son, marriage is something that cannot be done without an eraser... You need to carry an eraser with you to erase some of the things you will see and dislike in your wife. And your wife should have such an eraser to erase the unpleasant things you will do. Because if you don't do this, your marriage page will be black and white in a few days...
If you expect mutual love and respect in your life, both of you will show it to each other. And you will never forget the eraser!
Moral: Marriage is the art of forgiveness. For love and respect to continue, both parties must be able to "erase" each other's flaws.

stories.title: The Mother-of-Pearl Flower
paragraphs: The situation of an eighty-year-old couple who were being tried for divorce in the courtroom was painful for everyone… The judge, looking into the eyes of the stubborn, silent grandmother, sunken from crying, addressed the old woman in a full voice:
— Tell me, aunt, why do you want a divorce? — he asked.
After taking a deep breath, the old woman began to speak in a choked voice:
— This man has worn me out; for exactly fifty years he has made me tired of life…, — she said and fell silent.

A long silence fell on the hall. The silence was broken by a journalist’s photo flash. Who knows what headline the newspapers would give this event after fifty years of life together. Many journalists were watching the trial. What would the woman say? Everyone was listening to her. The old woman’s eyes filled with tears and she continued: — I had a mother-of-pearl flower that I loved very much… He doesn’t know… It was fifty years ago. I had planted that flower by taking a leaf from the flowers he had given me. We had no children, but I considered this flower my child. After a while, I saw that the flower had begun to wither.

At that time, I promised that I would wake up every night before sunrise and water this flower. For fifty years this man never once got up at night and said, “Let me water this flower.” Until last night… Last night I lay down exhausted and could not wake up… I spent fifty years with such a man. I gave my life, my hope, my everything. I saw nothing from him. I assure you, I can live my life better without him.
The judge turned to the elder:
— Do you have anything to say, grandfather? — he asked.
The old man leaned on his staff, turned to the judge with a guilty expression on his face, and began to speak:

— I spent my military service as a gardener. I worked hard to make that garden grow beautifully and healthily. I met Fatima there. I gave her bouquets of the most beautiful flowers. When we were newly married, she complained of neck pain, so I took her to the doctor. The doctor said, “If she sleeps too long without waking, the muscles in her neck will stiffen and her condition will worsen. She should break her sleep every night, wake up, and walk around.” The lady did not listen to the doctor’s words… I did not listen to her either… In those days our flower accidentally started to wither. I told her, “If you get up and water the flower at night, it will come back to life.” I asked her to promise, and she promised…
I woke her up every night and watched her. I watched the woman I loved watering the flower she thought of as her child. Every night, it was as if I was that flower…
Grandfather paused for a moment and continued:

— Every night, after she went to bed, I woke up to empty the water from the pot. Mother-of-pearl does not like to be watered at night, Your Honor… And last night… what can I say, this old age… I could not wake up either… The flower could have gone thirsty, but my wife would have faced health complications… She blamed me for not waking her… I did not raise my voice; I remained silent…
At that moment everyone in the hall, including the journalists, was in tears…
Moral: Sometimes love is hidden not in words, but in the care that is silently borne for years. Let us protect those we love, and stay away from breaking hearts.

stories.title: The red dress
paragraphs: The red dress was hanging in my mother's wardrobe. It seemed to shine next to the worn, faded clothes she had worn all her life.
I went to touch my mother and the moment I saw it, I realized that she was living the last moments of her life.
Seeing the red dress, I said to her:
— Mom, what a beautiful dress! I have never seen you wear it before, — I said.
— I have never worn it, — she said softly. — Sit down next to me, my beautiful daughter, I want to teach you a lesson before I leave this world.
I sat down on the edge of the bed. My mother took a deep breath. “I don’t have much time left,” she said and continued:
— While I thought I had always taught you good things, I now realize that I have taught you very wrong things.
— What is that word, mother?

— Listen to me. I have always believed that a good woman should not think of herself first. I should have thought of others before myself. I should have always fulfilled everyone's wishes, this, that. My desires were crushed under the desires of others. Who knows, maybe one day my desires would come true too. But that day never came. My whole life was spent in sacrifices—for your father, for your brothers and sisters, for you.
— That's right, mother, you did everything a mother could do.

— Oh, my daughter, what I did for you or for them didn't benefit me. Do you understand? I never wanted anything for myself! Your father is now in the next room, staring at the walls, annoyed. When the doctor told him that I was living my last days, he came to me and said:
— You must not die, do you hear me? What will I do after you? — he said.

— My daughter, I have always worked hard for you. Seven days a week... I was always the first to wake up in the house and the last to go to bed. I always ate the burnt bread, the smallest pieces. I spent every penny I had saved on your clothes, on your books—even if they were often unnecessary. I have never gone shopping and bought myself anything nice. I just bought that red dress you saw last year. I had some money saved up to fix the washing machine. When I got home with the dress, my father was very upset:
— Where are you going to wear this dress? Are you going to the opera or something? — he said.
In fact, he was right. I never wore that dress except when I tried it on in the store.

— Oh, my daughter, I used to think that if a person does not think about himself in this world, he will be happy in the next. But I don’t believe that anymore. I think God wants us to fulfill our desires in this world and now. If a miracle could happen now and I could get out of this bed, I would be a very different person.
These were my mother’s last words to me:
— My daughter, — she said, — don’t follow my path. Promise me.
I promised my mother and she breathed her last.
Moral: A person who always forgets himself will one day find that he can't live for anything. Love others, but give yourself the right to live too.

stories.title: True Love
paragraphs: There was an island where all the feelings lived.
One day news spread that the island was sinking. The feelings began to prepare in haste to leave.
Love was in no hurry to leave. She waited until the last moment, as if sure a miracle would save her. When the island was almost gone, Love finally decided to ask for help.
At that moment Wealth was sailing away in a very large boat.
Love asked: “Wealth, can you take me with you?” Wealth said: “No, I can’t. My boat is full of gold and silver — there is no room for you.”
Love then turned to Arrogance, sailing in a beautiful sailboat, and asked for help: “Arrogance, please help me.”
Arrogance replied: “I can’t help you, Love. You’re too wet — you’ll ruin my sail.”
Sadness was nearby. Love asked him too: “Sadness, may I come with you?”
Sadness said: “Oh, Love, I am so sad that I need to be alone.”
Happiness was not far from Love, yet so excited that she did not hear Love’s call.

Suddenly a voice said: “Love, come with me.” Love felt so lucky and happy that it did not even occur to her to ask who was reaching out. When they reached the shore, the one who had helped Love left her there and went on.
On the shore, realizing how much she owed, Love told a wise person what had happened and asked: “Who was it that helped me?”
The wise one answered: “It was Time.”
“Time? But why did Time help me?” Love asked.
The wise one smiled: “Because only Time knows how important and precious Love is.”
Moral: Only time knows the worth of true love. Time keeps sincere love alive and lets the false fade into forgetfulness.

stories.title: What did a woman suffer in this world...
paragraphs: What did a woman suffer in this world...
Even in fairy tales, they made her either a witch or a stepmother...
What was not said about a woman in stories.
She could never be herself; whereas in this world, her name should have been someone who gave life, nurtured, and loved unconditionally.
Woman...
They told her that her hair was long and her mind was short.
Your hands are full of flour, stay put, don't interfere with anyone, they told her.
Oh woman, what did you suffer in this world.
Few people knew your worth.
Few people could see your love, your heart, your goodness.
When you asked for your rights, you were evil, but when you were silent, you were pure.
When you showed your love, some thought you were a master.
Sometimes, those you raised to the heavens with your love preferred to stay there and forgot about you.
They didn't ask if you were okay, if you weren't okay, how were you.
They didn't say if you were there or not.
They forgot that you had a soul.
They forgot that you were human.
They made you sick, they crushed you, they ignored you...
And you had no intention other than to beautify, help, and improve.
Your soul wandered in this world in need of love.
They talked about heaven and made you experience hell.
They looked into your eyes and denied even what they saw there. They did not hear the cry that came from within.
She loved being a mother the most, she loved looking into her child's eyes with love. In this world, only her child's embrace felt sincere to her.
Moral: There can be no peace or love where a woman is not valued. It is the duty of society to see her work and heart.

stories.title: What is loyalty?
paragraphs: It is not forgetting,
Not turning your back on a difficult day,
Not closing the doors...
Not laughing when your friend is crying,
Loyalty is sharing every pain with him...
It is not just a word...
Loyalty means being with your friend,
Balm for the wounded,
Water for the thirsty,
And finally, loyalty is "understanding", not throwing away a rose because of its thorn.
Moral: Loyalty is not abandoning on a difficult day, not throwing away a rose because of its thorn. It is not a word, but a deed.

stories.title: Will a broken heart love again?
paragraphs: Someone asked the dervish:
— Will a broken heart love again?
— Yes, it does, — said the dervish.
The man said to the dervish: — Have you ever drunk water from a broken vessel?
Dervish: — Tell me, have you ever stopped drinking water because the vessel is broken?
Moral: Even if the heart is broken, it does not stop loving. Just as one does not stop drinking water because a vessel is broken, so too does a person continue to love.

stories.title: Woman and the mirror
paragraphs: A woman wakes up in the morning and looks in the mirror. She sees that she has three strands of hair left on her head.
“Hmm... — she says. — Today I’ll braid my hair…” She braids her hair and has a great day...
The next day she wakes up and looks in the mirror again... She sees that she has two strands of hair left on her head.
“Hmm... — she says. — Today I’ll part my hair in two…” She does what she said and has another great day...
The next day she wakes up and sees that she has only one strand of hair left on her head.
“No problem, that’s fine... — she says. — Today I’ll do a ponytail too...” She does so and has another great day...
Another day she looks in the mirror and sees that she has no hair left on her head.
“Oh my!… — she shouts happily. — How great, I don’t have any hair problems today!”
Moral: Everything depends on the perspective. Those who cannot create happiness within themselves cannot take it from others - they can walk even in the rain.

stories.title: Yellow and Red Flowers
paragraphs: In earlier times, yellow flowers placed in a house window meant, “Someone in this home is ill; please do not make noise as you pass.” Red flowers conveyed a different message: “A young woman who has come of age lives here; please mind your words.”
Moral: A culture of considerate communication, expressed through subtle signs, teaches people to show respect without unnecessary words. A warning does not always have to be loud.

stories.title: A Compliment
paragraphs: Maria lived with her mother in a small apartment in New York and worked as a secretary for a large company. Her life was quiet, ordinary, and rather dull. At work, hardly anyone noticed her.
One morning, on her way to the office, Maria saw a newly opened hat shop and went inside out of curiosity. A woman and her young daughter were there, along with another customer looking for a hat.
Maria tried on several hats. One appealed to her more than all the others. The moment she put it on, the little girl exclaimed with delight:
“Mom, look how beautiful that woman looks in the hat!”
The girl’s mother turned to Maria and said:
“Madam, that hat suits you very well.”
The other customer joined them:
“It really does. You look wonderful in it!”
Maria stepped in front of the mirror. For the first time in her life, she liked her reflection so much. Smiling, she went to the counter and paid for the hat.

When Maria left the shop, an entirely new world seemed to open before her. The flowers looked brighter than ever, and the fresh air smelled especially sweet. Even the sounds of traffic and passing voices seemed to form a harmonious melody. Maria felt beautiful and happy.

At the office entrance, the security guard opened the door and wished her good morning. In the elevator, someone asked which floor she needed and pressed the button for her. Throughout the day, her colleagues admired her and told her how lovely she looked, as though they were seeing her for the first time. Her manager even invited her to lunch to ask for her opinion on a new project.
When the magical workday ended, Maria was still smiling. She thought about how suddenly her life had changed and was certain that she owed it all to her new hat.
Maria took a taxi home. Her mother opened the door, stared at her in amazement, and said:
“Maria, you look wonderful! Your eyes are shining just as they did when you were a child!”
“Yes, Mom, it is all because of my new hat. I have had an amazing day!”
“What hat?” her mother asked, puzzled.

Alarmed, Maria touched her head. The hat was gone. She wondered whether she had left it in the taxi, at lunch, or in the office. Then she replayed the scene in the shop: putting on the hat, hearing the compliments, walking to the counter, taking out her purse, and setting the hat down beside the register…
Suddenly she understood. She had forgotten the hat in the shop and walked out without it, her eyes still shining with joy.
The hat had not made Maria happy. It was the confidence and delight awakened by other people’s kind words. The world had not changed; Maria’s way of seeing it had.

Moral: A single kind word can change how a person sees themselves—and sometimes how they see the entire world. Happiness is not found in outward possessions, but within us and in the sincere attention we offer one another.

stories.title: A Glass of Milk
paragraphs: A poor boy who sold small goods from door to door to pay his tuition discovered one day that he had no money left and was desperately hungry. He decided to knock on the next door and ask for something to eat.

A young woman answered. Embarrassed, the boy could not bring himself to ask for food and requested only a glass of water. Seeing that he was hungry, the woman brought him a large glass of milk instead.
After drinking it slowly, the boy asked:
“How much do I owe you?”
“Nothing,” the woman replied. “My mother taught us to do kindness without expecting anything in return.”
The boy could say only:
“Thank you from the bottom of my heart.”
As he walked away, he felt stronger not only physically, but also in spirit. His faith in God and in other people had been renewed.
Years passed. One day, the same woman became seriously ill. Unable to determine the cause of her illness, the local doctors sent her to specialists in a large city.

Dr. Howard Kelly was called in for a consultation. When he heard which town the patient came from, he immediately went to her room. The moment he saw her, he recognized the woman who had given him a glass of milk years before and rekindled hope in his heart.
Dr. Kelly personally took charge of her treatment and resolved to do everything he could to save her. After a long struggle, the illness was overcome and the woman recovered.
When the time came for her discharge, Dr. Kelly requested the final bill. He wrote a few words along its edge and had it delivered to the patient’s room.
The woman opened it anxiously. She feared that she would never be able to pay the amount and would spend the rest of her life repaying the debt. Then she noticed a sentence written in the margin:
“Paid in full with one glass of milk.”
Signed: Dr. Howard Kelly.
Moral: A selfless act of kindness is never lost. It is entered into an unseen account and may return to us one day—often when we least expect it.

stories.title: A Handful of Roasted Chickpeas
paragraphs: A boy entered a nut shop with his mother and kept insisting, “I want some roasted chickpeas.” The shopkeeper saw that the mother did not intend to buy any and felt sorry for the child:
“Come here, son. Take a handful for yourself.”
“No, I will take them only if you give them to me,” the boy replied.
The shopkeeper handed him a generous handful and asked:
“Why did you not take them yourself? Why did you want me to give them to you?”
The boy smiled:
“Because your hand is bigger than mine.”
“What a clever child you are!” the shopkeeper said with a laugh.
Moral: Sometimes who you ask matters more than what you ask for. When the giver’s hand is larger, the gift may be larger too.

stories.title: A Pair of Boots
paragraphs: One day, a schoolteacher asked her pupils to write a story on any subject and promised a pair of boots to the author of the best one. Every child completed a story and handed it in.
The teacher read each piece and liked them all. Unable to choose the best, she decided to draw the winner by lot.
Each pupil wrote a name on a slip of paper, folded it, and placed it in a box on the teacher’s desk. After mixing the slips, she drew one and announced:
“Amina!”
The classroom erupted in applause. Amina pressed the boots to her chest and could not hold back tears of joy.
That evening, the teacher returned home and tearfully told her husband what had happened. He was puzzled:
“You found a wonderful solution. Why are you crying?”
The teacher replied:
“Because not one slip bore the writer’s own name. Every child had written Amina—the pupil from the poorest family in the class. They all wanted her to receive the boots.”
Moral: The finest victory is to value another person’s joy above one’s own. True compassion is revealed in the willingness to surrender an opportunity for someone else.

stories.title: Being lonely
paragraphs: I went to visit an acquaintance. I entered his house, I went into his room. He was sitting silently with his head bowed. He looked sad.
— Are you sad? — I asked. He raised his head, looked into my eyes and: — No, I'm lonely, — he replied.
Moral: The biggest pain is to feel lonely even among people. Seeing the loneliness of someone next to you is true sensitivity.

stories.title: Discussion and Conflict
paragraphs: As every day, Javid Bey and his team gathered in the meeting room to discuss the status of the project they were working on. Everyone briefly reported the successful results of the previous day as well as the difficulties they had encountered.

It was Kamal’s turn. Like the others, he reported on the work he had done, but — as if hoping for help from his colleagues — he spoke in more detail about the problem he faced. As soon as he finished, Nadir accused him in front of everyone: “You are to blame; because of you our work has stopped and we can do nothing.” The room froze. Kamal was deeply embarrassed and did not know what to do.

As project manager, Javid Bey immediately intervened so the talk would not turn into a conflict, and said to the team: “Friends, if you like, let’s end the discussion for today and settle this matter another time.” Everyone dispersed.

Javid Bey knew exactly what to do: meet one-to-one and talk as friends. He invited Nadir to the company café under the pretext of a cup of tea; after some small talk he finally came to the point and said calmly, without losing composure: “My son, your behaviour toward Kamal today was very wrong. It is unacceptable to accuse someone without knowing the truth of the matter — and in front of others. Put yourself in his place. He expected help from us and was met with blame. I am sure Kamal hoped we would sit together, think it through, and find a solution as a team.”
Nadir lowered his head in shame. Javid Bey’s counsel had worked; it was a good lesson for Nadir — he understood he had done wrong.
Later, whenever the moment arose, he would recall that conversation and say he was always grateful to Javid Bey. Importantly, no one else in the company ever learned of that talk.
Moral: Conflict asks who is right; discussion asks what is right. If you want the truth, discuss — do not quarrel.

stories.title: Everyone Is the Same Here
paragraphs: A newly appointed young head of the district municipality decided to walk around and learn the situation. After walking the area alone, he entered a teahouse on a side street and ordered tea.
Just then a twelve- or thirteen-year-old child said:
— Uncle, shall I polish your shoes?
Though his shoes were already polished, not wishing to hurt the child’s heart, he said:
— All right, come polish them. If you do it well, I’ll give you twice what you ask. — Then the child replied:
— I polish them the same way for everyone.
The official said:
— What do you mean?
The child answered:

— Our teacher told us: “Children, whatever you do, treat everyone the same — do not discriminate.” With this money I will buy medicine for my sick mother. If I serve you differently, that medicine will not heal her!

The young official had learned one of the most important lessons of his life. He was deeply moved and gave the child the largest note in his pocket, and his card as well. He promised to look after this fatherless boy who both studied and cared for his sick mother.
He also went to see the teacher who had instilled that honesty in the child, and thanked him separately.
So as not to forget what he had heard from the shoe-shine boy, and to apply it always in his work, he had the sentence “Everyone is the same here” written on the back of the nameplate on his desk.
Though it was hard, he always tried to put it into practice.
Moral: Treat a person the same because they are human, not because of their rank. Society is changed by those who choose what is right in small moments.

stories.title: Forgiveness
paragraphs: Forgiving someone does not mean loving them; it does not mean having to talk to them, continuing the relationship; it does not mean accepting that they are innocent, right.
Forgiving someone means getting out of the prison of disappointment, resentment, hatred, and no longer feeling the pain of the wound inflicted on you.
Forgive and be free. Forgive, but never forget, otherwise you will be hurt again.
Moral: Forgiving is not about justifying the other person - it is about freeing yourself from the prison of hatred and resentment. Forgive and be relieved, but do not forget the lesson.

stories.title: Getting to know and getting to know
paragraphs: For some, we can only say this:
We met - we were happy, we got to know - we were sad.
Moral: Acquaintance is happy, but getting to know is not always pleasant. Seeing a person as they are sometimes brings disappointment.

stories.title: Go away, but come again
paragraphs: An Ottoman custom: when a guest came to the house, the host would place their shoes in front of the door with the toes pointing towards the house. This way, the guest would walk around as if he were walking; this meant "go away, but come again".
Moral: A subtle gesture can convey great kindness. The value given to a person is often seen in small moments.

stories.title: Gossip
paragraphs: A bitter, impolite man was summoned to the village elder, accused of spreading gossip.
— It was a joke, just a joke, — he denied the accusation. — Others misunderstood my words, I am not guilty!
But the victim of the gossip stood firm:
— You have tarnished my clean name. I demand justice.
The culprit retreated as he was pressed:
— I take back everything I said, I ask for forgiveness.
The elder listened silently. It crossed his mind: “This man has not yet realized the gravity of what he has done. Time will pass, and he will repeat the same sin again.” Then he said to the man:

— Go and bring a feather pillow to the market square. Cut it, scatter the feathers around. Then collect all the feathers one by one and bring them to me. If you cannot do this, there is no forgiveness.

The man reluctantly accepted the elder's condition. “The old man has lost his mind,” he thought, and then he formed and cut the pillow. The feathers scattered in a single blow and flew in all directions. The man ran to the right and left, chasing the feathers; but no matter how hard he tried, in the end only a few feathers remained in his palm.
He lowered his head and returned to the elder:
— I could not collect the rest.
Then he sighed deeply:
— Just like the words I spread. I cannot take them back.
Moral: A word that is spread is like a feather thrown to the wind - it cannot be collected again. Therefore, stay away from gossip.

stories.title: How to overcome insults
paragraphs: (An instructive story from the life of the samurai)

There was a wise and wise samurai. He taught his students the secrets of wisdom and martial arts. One day, during the next lesson, a warrior known for his rudeness and cruelty entered the class. This warrior would insult his opponents and get them angry, and then, taking advantage of the mistakes made by his angry opponent one after another, he would defeat him. This time, he used the same tactic, saying a few insults to the samurai to provoke him into a fight. The samurai ignored the insults and continued his lesson.
After repeating his insults several times, the warrior, who could not get any response from the samurai, left the class in a state of anger.
The students, who were watching this scene carefully, asked their teacher:
— Master, why did you tolerate these insults? Why didn’t you challenge him to a fight?
The wise samurai answers:
— If someone brings you a gift and you do not accept it, then to whom does the gift belong?
— To the previous owner, — the disciples answer.
— Envy, hatred, and insults should be viewed in the same way. If you do not accept them, such “gifts” remain with those who tried to address them to you.
Moral: An insult that you do not accept returns to its owner — just like a gift that is returned. Do not return evil for evil, but with moderation.

stories.title: Humanity
paragraphs: He studied for years, worked hard, and finally the day of the exam that would determine his fate arrived... His father, Kazim, was a rather demanding man, always closely interested in his son's studies and thought that he would definitely succeed in this exam...

Kamal entered the building and found the class where he would take the exam. Although he was excited when the question and answer sheets were distributed, he was very relieved when the exam began... He answered the questions easily, and he was completely sure of the correctness of the answers... There was half an hour left before the exam ended. He was so confident in himself that...
Suddenly, he fixed his eyes intently on the classroom window. Without thinking about what he saw, he got up and ran towards the door...

— Go back! Otherwise, your exam will be canceled, a year will be wasted, my son, — the teacher who was taking the exam called out to him. But he did not stop, he ran out the back door of the building...

His father, who came home a few hours later, first scolded Kamal, and then even slapped him in the face. Kazim was very upset. Even though he asked why he had left the class and why he had left the exam unfinished, Kamal kept quiet because he knew that his father would be even more angry... If he had said so, he would not have understood...
Kazim scolded and reprimanded his son all that year. Although Kamal was hurt by this situation, he did not listen, he kept his head down and focused on his studies.

The following year, he took the exam again and was accepted into the medical faculty... He became a very good doctor. Despite living in the city for many years, he asked for a voluntary assignment to a remote village hospital. After working there for a year, his family came to visit him at his house... The exam issue between him and his father had long been forgotten...

On a snowy and cold evening, Kamal's home phone rang. The caller said that there was a patient in one of the nearby villages. When he picked up his bag and set off, his father Kazim did not want to leave his son alone on the mountain roads, so he decided to accompany him. They walked for about an hour under a heavy blizzard and reached that village. They found the house and knocked on the door. An old man opened the door, said that his wife was sick, and invited the doctor in with his father...

Kamal examined the patient and prescribed the necessary treatment. The old woman thanked the doctor and said in a trembling voice: "You have helped us in this cold, my son. What would this world be like if there were no good people like you? Being a human is not easy... Listen."

"Years ago, I went to the city. Suddenly, in the middle of the road, I felt bad, I was in severe pain. There was no one around, the roads were empty. By the way, there was an exam that day. Less than five minutes later, a young man approached me in excitement. He took me to the hospital in half an hour in that heat. I was pregnant, and I was trembling with fear that something would happen to my child. The doctor in the admissions department said that if I had been ten minutes late, I could have died... That day my son was born.

I learned the name of the boy who brought me to the hospital - he said it was Kamal. He said, "I was in the exam, I saw you when I looked out the window, and when I realized that you were alone, I left the classroom and came to your aid. Even though I lost a year because I gave up the exam, I did not regret it at all.

I named my son Kamal. I raised him with the story of that kind boy, I always advised him to be a person like Kamal. Now he is a teacher... He tries to raise his students as human beings first and foremost... Oh, I wish I could find that boy and get halal from him... Anyone can be a doctor, teacher, engineer. The most difficult thing in this world is to be a human being... What a wonderful person that young man was. He did not leave me alone in the middle of the road." Hearing this, Dr. Kamal said: "It is halal, mother, don't worry...".

Although his father Kazim was a handsome man, he did not want to show his tears. However, when he left the house, tears wet his cheeks. Even after he set off, Kazim's tears did not stop. He said in a trembling voice, "Kamal, my son," but he couldn't continue because he was sobbing.
Moral: It's possible to have a profession, but the real challenge is to be a human being. A kindness done in a young person's time becomes a blessing that lasts for generations.

stories.title: I want a friend
paragraphs: I want neither wealth nor possessions,
I want a true friend.
Which possession will show mercy to its owner when he dies?
I want a friend who will show mercy to me.
Moral: Neither wealth nor possessions are the true wealth of a person, but a loyal friend. A friend who will show mercy to his owner after death is more valuable than any possession.

stories.title: I was ashamed, by God
paragraphs: It was during the COVID-19 pandemic. Your sword, as they say, was cutting both the branch and the front. After a long break, the following conversation takes place between two people who meet:
— Hello, seagull, what's up? It's been a long time since you've seen each other. Where have you been?
— No! I had COVID.
— What? What is COVID?
— What do you mean, what is it? You don't know what COVID is?
— By God, I have no idea.
— So you don't know. So you're saying you've never had COVID?
— No, by God, I've never had it.
— Shame on you. But don't you know that in this day and age, it's considered a shame not to have COVID?
— No, by God, that's not possible, are you right?
— May there never be a dawn!
— Thank you very much for opening my eyes. Then let me go and get COVID too, or I'll be a disgrace to the community. I was ashamed, by God.
Moral: It is ridiculous to follow everything the crowd says is "shameful." Wisdom lies not in the gossip of the crowd, but in one's own thoughts.

stories.title: If the road is not tiring, it is because of your husband
paragraphs: My mother used to say: "I married your father when I was very young. I could neither cook a proper meal nor pick up a needle and embroider. One day, when my mother-in-law—your grandmother—was getting ready to go to the neighbor's house, she spread out a blanket in front of me that she had washed and dried, and said, 'You can finish sewing this before I get back.' I started sewing, but I couldn't do it. The needle wouldn't go through the blanket. I started to sew. On the one hand, the needle was digging into my hand, and my eyes were watering from the pain, and on the other hand, my tears wouldn't stop because I didn't know what to say to my mother-in-law.

At that time, my father came home for lunch. Seeing me crying, he picked up the needle, finished sewing the blanket in a short time, and put it aside. Then he ate his meal and went to work. He didn't say anything to my mother-in-law. When the woman returned home, she saw that the blanket was completely ready and was very pleased."
It's not for nothing that they say: "If the road doesn't tire you, it's because of your companion."
Moral: It's not the road that tires you or lightens your load, but the person next to you. A true companion makes even the hardest task easier.

stories.title: Interfering in the lives of others
paragraphs: May God never leave anyone so unemployed that they interfere in the lives of others!
Moral: Unsolicited advice is not a help, but a burden. Interfering in the lives of others under the guise of "kindness" often brings harm.

stories.title: Know your friend
paragraphs: If you want to know your friend, see him in trouble, in hardship, in strife; touch his advantage once, and then see him again.
Moral: A friend is known in trouble, in hardship, and in the test of advantage. Everyone is a friend in good times; a true friend is revealed in adversity.

stories.title: Mercy
paragraphs: It was a cold winter night. I was returning home from work. I saw a man in front of me who looked like a drunk. He was leaning back and forth, weakly clinging to a pole next to him. I approached him. He was over thirty. He was very clean and neatly dressed. Some of the passers-by were talking loudly about the dangers of alcohol, while others were laughing mockingly.
— Are you okay, do you need anything? — I asked the man.
In a voice that sounded like a groan coming from his lips:
— I am sick!… — he said.

I held him by the waist with my arm so that he wouldn’t fall and led him to the taxi stand. We started waiting for a taxi. The snow that had stopped in the evening was falling again; there were no signs of life except for stray dogs racing each other on the slowly icy roads.
I had given up hope of finding a taxi when a taxi stopped next to us. I explained the situation to the driver and told him that we were in a hurry.
We put the patient in the back seat and headed to the hospital. Thankfully, the doctors did everything they could right away, administered medication; we waited at the man's bedside.

The doctor on duty said that we had at least saved the patient from freezing. The young man, who could not speak yet, just looked at us and smiled. The driver was with me... Our patient came to his senses after a while. We put him back in the car and took him home.

His wife, knowing that he often fell into diabetic comas, had gone out into the street with her son in a terrible panic. When they saw us, they ran to us excitedly. The family members hugged each other tightly, their eyes full of joy.
There was no trace of our fatigue that had lasted for hours; our eyes were filled with the happiness of that family that did not know how to thank us.
When we said goodbye, I asked the driver what I owed him.
He shook his head:

— You are not in debt, on the contrary, you have a debt, my friend! — he said. — You have made me a partner in such a good thing. I am indebted to you for giving this wonderful feeling to a person who has probably forgotten what it is to cry for twenty years.
I did not feel the cold of the night as I hugged the driver and left, and decided to walk home.
Who knows? Maybe another person would come across me on my way who needed my help?
Moral: Humanity is built on compassion. Compassion is not crying with the crying person, but finding a way to stop the tears.

stories.title: People who are in need of you
paragraphs: Instead of feeling offended by people who "only seek you out when they are in need," you will feel much more at ease if you think that they are in trouble, that they may need your help, and that is why they are seeking you out.
Moral: Instead of feeling offended by people who only seek you out when they are in need, you will feel much more at ease.

stories.title: Permission or Apology
paragraphs: There is a saying attributed to Rear Admiral Grace Hopper that says, “It’s better to ask for permission than to ask for it.”
This saying is used in the sense of “Ask for permission first to do something — do it, and then apologize if you’re not happy.”
Sometimes waiting for permission is a missed opportunity. Do what you know is right, and apologize later if necessary.

Imagine that a company has a clear problem that is slowing down the work process. For example, every week the same information is manually transferred to several different spreadsheets, which takes hours. An employee realizes that this can be solved with simple automation.

If he first tries to get permission at length, the issue can be passed from one manager to another, waiting for weeks for a response, and the opportunity can be lost. However, the employee, realizing that the risk is small, sets up a separate test system without damaging the existing data, automates the process, and shows the result. If the system is successful, everyone benefits from it. If someone is unhappy that a procedure was not agreed upon in advance, the employee can say, “I was just trying to speed things up. If I broke a rule, I apologize.”

Moral: The point here is not to “ignore the rules.” The point is that in situations where the outcome is reversible, the risk is low, and the benefit is clear, expecting too much permission can kill the initiative. Sometimes it is better to act responsibly and show results than to expect endless approval.

stories.title: Relationship with people
paragraphs: Let your relationship with people be like your relationship with fire:
don't go too far away lest you freeze;
don't come too close lest you burn.
Saadi Shirazi
Moral: Keep your distance in your relationship with people: neither go too far away lest you freeze, nor too close lest you burn.

stories.title: Ridicule is unacceptable
paragraphs: We should teach our children from a young age that it is unacceptable to ridicule or humiliate other people for their differences or appearance.
Moral: It is humiliating to ridicule someone else's differences or appearance. We should teach this to our children from a young age.

stories.title: Spend time with people
paragraphs: My father had to transfer money, so I had to spend an hour with him at the bank. Finally, I couldn't wait any longer and said to him:
— Dad, let's do your banking online. What do you think?
— What will this give me, son? — my father looked at me in surprise.
— You won't have to waste an hour at the bank to transfer money anymore. The internet will even allow you to do your shopping online. Everything will be very easy and convenient, — I quickly replied.
I was very excited about the idea of ​​getting my father involved in the world of the internet.
My father asked:
— If I do what you say, then I won't have to leave the house. Is that right?
— That's right, dad.
I told him that even the groceries he would buy could be delivered to his door, that Amazon delivers everything to the buyer's home.
My father's answer left me speechless:
— My son, in the hour I spent at the bank, I saw four of my friends, and I talked to bank employees who have known me for a long time.
You know, I'm lonely... I need to see people. I like to come to the bank dressed up. I have enough time, and I always enjoy live communication.
Two years ago, when I was sick, the salesman from the nearby store where I always bought fruit came to see me. He was very upset that I was sick, sat by my bed and sympathized with my condition.
Some time ago, when your mother fell during her morning walk, the grocer in our neighborhood picked her up, put her in his car, and quickly drove her to our house. Because he knew where we lived.
If everything goes online, won't I be deprived of these human feelings?
After all, why should I only communicate with a computer so that everything can be delivered to my house?
I want to get to know the person I'm communicating with instead of an "electronic salesman." I want a live connection, a relationship.
Can Amazon do that too?
Technology is not life.
Spend your time with people, not devices, son.
Moral: Technology provides convenience, but it does not replace life. The real value is in live communication, in the warmth between people.

stories.title: The Friendship of Horses
paragraphs: There are two horses on a farm near my house. From a distance, they look nothing like the others. But when you get closer, you see something very interesting: one of the horses is blind. The owner has built a safe and comfortable stable for him. This alone is quite an amazing step.
As you approach the horses, you will hear a bell. This sound comes from the other small, healthy horse, which has a bell on its bridle, and the blind horse can hear where that horse is and follow it.

If you watch these two friends carefully, you will see that the horse with the bell always checks where the blind horse is; the blind horse, in turn, listens to the sound of the bell and slowly follows the healthy horse.
Every evening, as the horse with the bell returns to the stable, he stops and looks back to make sure that his blind friend is close enough to hear the bell.
Moral: The Lord does not leave us alone in difficult times; When we need help, it sends it through the hands of a human being. Sometimes it falls to us to be that helper.

stories.title: The sound of the doorbell...
paragraphs: I was laid off last winter. To make ends meet, I had to work as a newspaper carrier temporarily. Since the mailbox of one of the houses I delivered newspapers to was sealed, I had to knock on the door. An old man opened the door.
— Uncle, why did you seal the mailbox? — I asked.
— I sealed it on purpose, — he replied.
Then he smiled strangely and continued:
— I ask you, every day when you bring the newspaper, please knock on the door or ring the bell and give it to me personally.
— Of course, but it’s inconvenient for both of us, a waste of time, — I was surprised.
— No problem, I’m at home every day, — he said and added:
— My wife has passed away, my son is abroad, and I live here alone. Who knows how long I have left to live?
At that moment, I saw the old man’s misty, moist eyes.
— Have you subscribed to read the newspaper? — I asked.
— I never read the newspaper... I only subscribed to the sound of the doorbell.
Then he clasped his hands together and said:
— Young man, please do me a favor! Here is my son's phone number. If one day you don't hear from me when I knock on your door, call my son and let him know.
Moral: For some people, one ring of the doorbell, one greeting, is worth the whole world. Let's not forget to knock on the door of the lonely.

stories.title: Those who will not be friends
paragraphs: — Do not be friends with an arrogant person! He does not know the state, the mood, the heart; you will be upset.
— Do not be friends with someone who thinks he is very smart! He talks a lot, talks nonsense, and talks little; you will be upset.
— Do not be friends with a coward! He does not know courage, the heart does not know, and friends do not know; you will be upset.
Moral: Only regret remains from friendship with an arrogant, self-satisfied and cowardly person. Choose your friend according to your heart.

stories.title: Welcome, sir
paragraphs: When my late father Hafiz Ali was in Çanakkale, I was still in my mother's womb, seven months old. I never saw or recognized my father. There was not even a single photograph of him.
Those were very difficult days. Mobilization, occupation, liberation, poverty, hardship...
Our childhood was spent constantly running around in search of bread, filled with pain.
Whenever my mother wanted to go somewhere, she would always come to me and say:
— Son, I'm going to the market. If your father comes, let me know right away!
— I'm going to Khalangil. If your father comes, let me know right away!
— I'm going to the neighbor's. If your father comes, let me know right away! — she would say.
My mother waited for my father on the road with her eyes wide open.

I grew up, became a business owner, and opened a shop. As always, when my mother went somewhere, she would come to the shop, tell me where she was going, and say: "If your father comes, let me know, huh!" he would add.
Years passed. My mother grew old. Despite this, she would still come to me, remaining true to her custom and leaning on her stick: "If your father comes, call me, huh!" She would say.
One day, she became ill and fell into bed.

On her deathbed, she said goodbye to us: "You took good care of me, grant me your rights." She slowly turned to me and said: "If your father comes, tell him that my mother has always waited for you." Suddenly, she raised her head, looked towards the door, smiled and said: "Welcome, sir, welcome!" and gave up her spirit.
From the memoirs of Cevdet Algalp, an old shoemaker living in Balıkesir.
Written by: researcher and writer, geography teacher at Bursa Çınar Anatolian High School Mustafa Doğru.
March 18 is the day of the Çanakkale Victory.

If Çanakkale had fallen in 1915, fictitious states would have been established in Anatolia, the peoples living here would have been turned into enemies and exterminated, and the country would have become a colony of the British, French and Italians.
May the souls of all martyrs, including our Azerbaijani soldiers who were martyred in Çanakkale, rest in peace! May no mother lose sight of the road!
Moral: A mother's lifelong loyalty and longing are the purest expression of love. The memory of those who died for the homeland and mothers who lost their sight of the road is sacred.

stories.title: Why do people shout when they argue?
paragraphs: One day during class, a teacher asked his students:
— Why do people shout when they argue?
— Because they can’t control their temper, — one student answered.
— After all, the person you’re arguing with is right next to you, so why shout? Can’t you just talk to him calmly? If you’re angry, why should you shout? — the teacher deepened his question.
Each of the students gave an answer, but none of them satisfied the teacher. Finally, he said:

— When people are unhappy with each other, their hearts move away from each other. They have to shout to hear each other from this distance. The louder they shout, the further their hearts are from each other.
After a moment of silence, the teacher continued:

— But what happens when people love each other? They don’t shout, on the contrary, they speak softly. Because their hearts are very close to each other, the distance between them is small. But what happens when there is stronger love? Then they don't even speak softly, they whisper and get a little closer to each other. As their hearts get closer, they don't even need to whisper — they just look at each other and understand everything without words... My dear students, when you argue, don't let your hearts drift apart, don't say words that could increase the distance between you.
Because one day this distance may grow so much that you won't be able to find your way back.
Moral: Screaming is the sound of hearts drifting apart. A whisper is enough in love — don't increase the distance between you.

stories.title: Your friends
paragraphs: One day, a young man decides to get married. After spending a week preparing for his wedding, one evening he says to his father, “Dad, I have a request for you. I can’t do it all by myself. Please take this list and call all my friends on it and invite them to my wedding.” “I’m sorry, son!” his father replies.
On the day of the wedding, the boy approaches his father angrily: “Dad, I asked you to call all my friends!”
— Son, I did as you asked.
— I had fifty people on my list, but I only see fifteen here, — the boy said, expressing his concern again.

— Son, I called all fifty people one by one. I told each of them that I was calling on your behalf, that you had a problem right now, that you needed the help of your friends, and I asked them to be here at this time, at this place. Don’t worry, son. Your true friends are here with you today!
Moral: A true friend is one who is there for you when you are in trouble. It is not the many acquaintances that are valuable, but the few friends who stand the test.

stories.title: A Generous Man
paragraphs: A generous man was once asked:
“Do you expect the poor to be grateful to you for everything you share with them?”
He replied:
“I am like a ladle in a cook’s hand. Although the food is served with the ladle, it is the cook—not the ladle—who gives it.”
Moral: Those who do good should not consider themselves the true owners of what they give. They are only instruments; the true Giver is God.

stories.title: A Mature Person
paragraphs: A time comes when you value the sincerity of old friends more deeply, stop chasing meaningless acquaintances, and choose distance from ignorance and relationships that harm your peace of mind. That is when you realize that you have grown inwardly mature.
Moral: Maturity is the ability to step away from harmful relationships and protect one’s inner peace. Knowing whom—and what—to keep at a distance is also a form of wisdom.

stories.title: A Meaningless Question
paragraphs: One day, a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, visited a rabbi in New York and asked for help studying the Talmud.
“Do you know Aramaic? No? What about Hebrew? Were you at least taught the Torah as a child?”
The young man answered no to every question.
“But I defended a dissertation on Socratic logic! I would like to study the Talmud to fill some gaps in my education.”

“The Talmud is one of the greatest works of human thought, but you are not yet ready to study it. Still, since you insist, I will give you a logic question. If you answer correctly, I will teach you. Two people climb down the same chimney. One emerges with a clean face and the other with a face covered in soot. Which one will go and wash?”
“You call that a logic question?” the Berkeley graduate asked confidently. “The person with the dirty face, of course!”

“Wrong. The person with the clean face will see the other’s sooty face, assume that his own face is dirty too, and go to wash. The person covered in soot will see a clean face in front of him and suppose that he has remained clean.”
“A very clever answer! Could you give me another chance?”
“All right. Two people climb down the same chimney. One has a dirty face and the other a clean one. Which will go and wash?”
“But we have just discussed that. The person with the clean face will go.”

“Wrong again. Both will wash. The person with the clean face will see his companion’s dirty face and think that he is dirty too. The other will notice that his companion looked at him and then went to wash, so he will realize that his own face must also be dirty.”
“I truly had not considered that. May I have one more question?”
“Very well. I will ask for the last time: two people climb down the same chimney. One has a clean face and the other a dirty one. Which will go and wash?”
“Now it is clear: both of them will go!”

“No. Neither will go. The person with the dirty face will see a clean face before him and assume that he is clean as well. The person with the clean face will notice that his companion is not going to wash and conclude that there is no need to do so.”
Growing desperate, the young man begged the rabbi for one more question. The rabbi began:
“Two people climb down the same chimney. One has a dirty face and the other a clean one…”
“Neither of them will wash!” the young man answered hastily.

“Wrong again,” the rabbi said calmly. “As a specialist in Socratic logic, think for yourself: how could two people climb down the same chimney together and only one of them emerge with soot on his face? Can you not see that the question itself is meaningless? If you spend your life searching for answers to meaningless questions, neither your answers nor your life will acquire meaning.”
Moral: An answer to a meaningless question cannot lead to truth. A well-formed question is already half the answer.

stories.title: Attitude Toward a Problem
paragraphs: Is there a problem in your life?
If not, there is no reason to worry.
If there is, can you solve it?
If you can, there is no reason to worry.
If you cannot, there is still no reason to worry.
Moral: Either there is no problem, or there is a solution. Persistent worry is useless both for what can be changed and for what cannot.

stories.title: Avoid These Questions
paragraphs: Do not ask an unemployed person, “Are you still without work?”, an employee, “How much do you earn?”, a childless person, “You still have no children?”, or a single person, “When are you getting married?”
Nor should we embarrass someone by asking, “You did not know that?” What seems like ordinary curiosity to us may touch another person’s deepest wound.
Moral: Some questions wound the heart. Every painful question left unasked may lift a burden from someone’s shoulders.

stories.title: Be Sure of Your Purpose
paragraphs: Two men were struggling to move a heavy chest through a doorway. After a long effort, they stopped, exhausted and drenched in sweat.
One said:
“What a heavy chest! We still could not get it inside.”
The other asked in surprise:
“Weren’t we supposed to take it outside?”
Moral: Clarify the goal before beginning the work. Otherwise, you may labor for hours while directing all your strength the wrong way.

stories.title: Being cool-headed
paragraphs: Try to assess the situation you find yourself in calmly, without panicking, so that you can make the best decision and turn the situation to your advantage.
Moral: The best decision is made with a calm mind, not in a panic. Cool-headedness can turn even a difficult situation into a good one.

stories.title: Being Human
paragraphs: “It is easy to become a scholar, but difficult to become a true human being,” we often hear. What, then, does being human mean?
It means living with virtue, wisdom, civility, justice, honor, and dignity.
Being courteous, perceptive, respectful, and humble—showing regard for others without praising oneself.
Thinking before acting, maintaining balance, remaining consistent, and standing upright in adversity.
Keeping one’s word; refusing to worship money or position; neither stealing nor taking what belongs to another.
Rejecting lies and slander, never betraying others for personal gain, and defending what is right.
Remaining free of hypocrisy and hatred, refusing to turn people against one another, and knowing how to love.
Moral: True worth lies not in knowledge alone, but in humanity. A heart capable of respect also makes room for love and justice.

stories.title: Being self-confident
paragraphs: Value yourself!
Do not allow weakness!
Add strength to your strength!
Do not lose hope!
Be knowledgeable!
Be determined!
Be of good intentions!
Protect your dignity!
Be faithful!
Moral: Value yourself, do not lose hope, protect your dignity. Self-confidence is a person's strongest support.

stories.title: Don't do these
paragraphs: Don't talk about your wealth in front of the poor, your health in front of the sick, your happiness in front of the distressed, your freedom in front of the prisoner, your strength in front of the weak, your children in front of the childless, or your parents in front of the orphan.
Moral: Don't remind the other person of something they don't have. They don't need reminders, they need understanding.

stories.title: Don't open your mouth
paragraphs: If you're not going to open your mouth to say something nice, don't open it at all.
Moral: The power of words lies in using them appropriately and for good. If you don't have anything worth saying, silence speaks louder.

stories.title: Don't say "I didn't deliver, I couldn't do it"
paragraphs: Days replace each other. Some end their days happy, some sad. But no matter what, don't say "I didn't deliver, I couldn't do it" for the things you couldn't do today. Most importantly, don't despair. The next day, as soon as the sun rises, the whole day is yours.
Moral: Every day is a new page. You can't change yesterday, but how you write today is in your hands.

stories.title: Education or character
paragraphs: The king asks his minister:
— Minister, is education important or character?
The minister answers without thinking:
— Character, my king.
The king sends a proclamation to the country, orders to find the best animal trainer and bring him to him. They find such a person and bring him. The king asks the man:
— How long can it take you to train a cat to serve the assembly with a bowl in its paw?
— Six months, my king.
Six months pass. The man is called to the palace with the cat he has trained. The king asks:
— Did you teach it?
— I did, my king.
The entire palace gathers. The cat begins to serve them with a bowl in its paw. When the cat approaches the minister, the king asks:
— Minister, is education important or character?
Before the minister can answer the king, he takes out a mouse he has been holding ready in his pocket and drops it on the ground. Seeing the mouse, the cat drops its paw and runs after it.
The vizier answers the king:
— Character, my king.
Moral: Education does not change character; when the opportunity arises, the true nature is revealed. Knowledge is good, but character is more important.

stories.title: Everything is in our own hands
paragraphs: (From Indian folklore)
A young boy gets the idea of ​​“playing a game” with an old monk. He catches a bird. He takes the bird in his hand and hides it behind his back, and asks the monk:
— O wise old man, tell me, is the bird in my hand alive or dead?
But he thinks to himself: if the old man says “it is alive”, I will strangle the bird and kill it; if not, “it is dead”, I will open my hand and let the bird fly away, and thus scare it away.
The wise old man thinks for a while and says:
— My dear son, the answer to your question is in your own hands.
The boy stops and lowers his head.
The old man continues:

— War and peace, punishment and pardon, good and evil - all this is in your own hands. The path of a person’s life is determined not by his mind, but by his intentions. Remember that every person is capable of doing both good and evil. But there is always a choice, and this choice is in our own hands.
Moral: Both good and evil are human choices. Our destiny is determined not by our minds, but by our intentions.

stories.title: Explaining a problem
paragraphs: The person who explains their problem simply is a problem solver; the person who explains it beautifully is a "literary person", the person who explains it with a "lover", and the person who covers it with a smile is a "sage".
Moral: People carry their problems in different ways: some talk, some write, some keep quiet and smile. The deepest problems are often hidden in the deepest silence.

stories.title: Giving up
paragraphs: "It is a beautiful quality to give up!"
From those who do not know the value of things,
those who trample on sincerity,
those who change for profit,
from arrogant and boastful people,
those who are envious, gossipers,
those who make a habit of lying,
those who do not know what decency is,
those who nullify their values,
those who turn a blind eye to ignorance,
those who despise their homeland, deny their nation,
those who forget their native language,
those who are deprived of maternal love, paternal honor, and filial love...
"It is a beautiful quality to give up!"
From those who think they are irreplaceable...!
Moral: Giving up on some people is not weakness, but self-respect. Walking away from those who do not know their worth is a beautiful quality.

stories.title: He wouldn't give so little
paragraphs: A king gives a gold coin to a beloved child he meets, but the child doesn't take the money. When the king asks why he didn't take it, the child says:
— When I go home, my mother and father ask, "Where did you steal this money?"
— You say that the king gave it to you, — says the king.
— Then they won't believe it at all. They say that if the king had given it to him, he wouldn't have given so little, — replies the child.
The king likes this answer very much and he gives the child a bag of gold.
Moral: Great things begin in the family, in proper upbringing. A child who grows up honestly becomes an honest person tomorrow.

stories.title: Honey or dry bread
paragraphs: It is better to sit with a scholar and eat dry bread than to sit with an ignorant man and eat honey.
Moral: The person you sit with will either elevate you or degrade you. The simple bread of a scholar is better than the sweetness of an ignorant man.

stories.title: How can I get rid of my thoughts?
paragraphs: One day, a man came to visit one of the scholars of his time and asked:
— How can I get rid of the painful thoughts that I am a prisoner of?
Instead of answering him, the scholar stood up, hugged a nearby pole and began to shout with all his might:
— Separate me from this pole, save my life from it!… —.
The man, looking at him in surprise, asked:

— Why are you doing this? I thought you were a wise man and came to ask for help. But I see that you do not look like a wise man. You yourself held the pole, it did not hold you. Let go of it, and your life will be saved!
The scholar let go of the pole and said to the man:
— You yourself answered your own question. It is not you who holds thoughts, but you! Let them go so that your life will be saved.
Moral: You yourself hold the thoughts that oppress you; it is in your hands to let them go. Change your perspective, and your burden will lighten.

stories.title: I am now aware
paragraphs: From someone who has fallen hard in life:
I no longer try to make anyone love me. I am aware that those who don't like me can always find an excuse.
I now know my worth and I am aware that I don't have to prove myself to anyone.
I am now aware that I don't want to give my life to people who are complacent, arrogant, and conceited.
I am now aware that those who want something have a purpose, and those who don't want something always have a "but".
I no longer share my secrets with someone who gossips, because I am aware that a gossiper cannot keep a secret.
I no longer try to convince or lead stubborn people, because I am aware that it is impossible to turn a stubborn person from his or her path.
I am now aware that I want people who lie, make empty promises and don't keep their promises out of my life.
I am no longer able to forgive, to be cruel and harsh. I am aware that I should value people who are only able to apologize when they make a mistake.
I am now aware that I am happier with the person I am "myself" with.
Moral: True maturity is not about changing others, but about knowing who to let into your life and who to stay away from.
