stories.title: I was busy cleaning
paragraphs: Today I was busy cleaning...
And in my whole body...
I cleaned all my muscles, nerves, veins, even my blood...
I threw away all the garbage that had accumulated deep down...
First of all, I threw away the disappointments... I didn't even look at what they were when I threw them away.
You should have seen this...
How much space they occupied inside me...
In their place, I carefully placed forgiveness. I diligently sowed the seeds of forgiveness on every disappointment...
I threw out my jealousy...
How jealous I am...
It was very easy. I was happy...
It was as if I had found something I had lost...
Thank God there was no grudge or hatred in my heart...
I don't know how I cleaned it...
It was my turn to be afraid...
At first I was even afraid to take it out...
How I got used to living with them...
I couldn't understand how I could get used to so much pain and anxiety...
Every day new fears, caused by new worries, were accumulating inside me...
How much I had postponed my happiness and hopes...

If I had given them this attention at that moment, if I had thought about them every day and added a hope, if I had given them without receiving, if I had loved them without expecting, if I had realized the love and strength inside me first of all, I wouldn't have needed such cleanings...
I had difficulty cleaning my fears...
They were intertwined like chains and almost locked together... But I expelled them without regretting that I had once kept them alive inside me like a nightmare.
I know that if I got angry with my fears, if I shouted at them, they would come back and attack me.
Today I was busy cleaning...
I planted joy, I planted trust, I planted love...
I planted giving without receiving, loving without being loved, sharing...
I planted madness, naturalness, forgiveness inside me...
I planted love in every cell of my body...
I planted enthusiasm, excitement, silence...
All the best ideas come to me in silence...
I planted acceptance...
Not bowing down, but accepting as it is...
Moral: True cleanliness is in the heart: throwing away disappointment, fear, and resentment and planting love, forgiveness, and hope in their place. The one who cleans his inner world finds peace.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: I Would Not Trade It for Anything
paragraphs: A day,
a beautiful day,
a sunny day —
I would not trade for anything.
For its sake I do not love war,
for its sake I do not love oppression,
for its sake I do not love lies.
I know they cannot live in the sun,
I know they cannot live side by side with love —
neither injustice,
nor fear,
nor hunger…
Necati Cumalı
Moral: On a beautiful, sunny day there is no place for strife, oppression, or lies. In the light, injustice, fear, and hunger cannot live.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: It was not your right
paragraphs: In the Battle of Çanakkale, only the wounded who could survive were given morphine injections. One of the seriously wounded brought to Dr. Tarık Nusret was his own son. Seeing the impossibility of saving his son's life, the father did not give him an injection. Two hours later, hugging the lifeless body of his martyred son, the father whispered in deep shock: "Forgive me, my son, it was not your right."
Moral: Sometimes the greatest justice is when a person goes against his own interests. A father who knows the truth will not give his son such an unfair share.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Lying
paragraphs: — Are you lying?
— Yes.
— What kind of lie is that?
— I only tell that lie to myself. That is, every day I tell myself that “you are stronger than everyone, more educated than everyone, more capable than everyone,” etc.
— Maybe this is true?
— No, such a claim cannot be true. Because there are people stronger than me, and there are people more capable than me.
— Then why do you tell yourself this lie?
— Believe it or not, this lie gives me great motivation. It encourages me to be stronger, more educated, and to work harder on myself.
Moral: Sometimes the kind words you tell yourself — “you can do it” — become the force that drives you forward. A person is as strong as he believes in himself.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: May your face always smile
paragraphs: A person who sells vinegar with a smile will have more customers than a person who sells honey with a frown.
Moral: A smiling person is more loved than a frowning one. A smile is the cheapest but most powerful charm.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Never complain about any day you live
paragraphs: Never complain about any day you live:
Good days make you happy,
Bad days give you experience,
The worst days teach you a lesson,
The best days give you memories.
Moral: Every day has its share: Good days make you happy, Bad days give you experience, and the worst days give you a lesson. Never complain about any day.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: No one listens to a person who complains constantly
paragraphs: A wise man taught a group of people who complained about the same problems over and over again. He told a funny joke; everyone laughed heartily. He told the same joke a second time; only a few people laughed. When he told the same joke a third time, no one even moved their lips.
Complaining about the same problems over and over again instead of finding a solution is similar. No one listens to a person who complains constantly.
Moral: Repeated complaints, like repeated jokes, quickly become boring. Find a solution to the problem; no one will listen to you if you whine over and over again.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Not every pain is told to people
paragraphs: Not every pain is told to people.
The day will come, they will hit you with that pain.
Moral: Don't tell every secret to everyone. One day they may hit you with that pain - choose who you tell.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Other People's Opinions
paragraphs: One day, the human being lost the comma (,). What he said got mixed up. Another day, he lost the period (.). His thoughts got long and he couldn't separate them. Another day, he lost the exclamation mark (!). He lost his joy, his anger, all his emotions. Then he lost the question mark (?). He forgot to ask questions, he had to accept everything as it was, without questioning. Another day, he lost the colon (:). The ability to explain and explain disappeared.
When he reached the end of his life, he had only one quotation mark left - and it contained only other people's opinions.
Moral: A person who loses his own values ​​and roots one by one is filled with foreign ideas. If you don't protect your spiritual roots, you will eventually cease to be yourself.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Our qualities can be our enemies
paragraphs: The enemy of a peacock is its own tail...
It is its sweet tongue that traps a nightingale.
It is its fancy fur that traps a fox...
Some of the qualities we see and love in ourselves can actually be our weakness and disaster...
Moral: Sometimes the trait we boast about is our weak point. The peacock's tail betrays the nightingale, the tongue - do not rely too much on your superiority.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Phrases to avoid
paragraphs: Avoid these phrases, especially in the family, and never use them against your spouse:
“Don’t talk nonsense!”

This phrase makes your spouse feel that their thoughts and feelings are worthless, misunderstood, and belittled. Instead, if you gently say, “I don’t think like you, I don’t completely agree with you on this issue,” you will show that you take their opinion into account and maintain respect between you.
“Don’t exaggerate!”

This phrase may sound like a sign that your spouse’s view of events is wrong; he or she will feel criticized. Instead, by asking, “Can you explain a little more clearly why you are worried and what you are feeling?” you will take a step towards eliminating the misunderstanding that has arisen.
“Look at his or her husband (wife)! He or she does this, and you do that?”

This phrase is very dangerous because when you say it, you are bringing third parties into your family relationship. Comparing your spouse to someone else will make them distrust you. They will think that you are thinking the same thing, and they will feel hurt and unloved. Instead of making comparisons and analogies, clearly state your expectations.
“You don’t understand!”

This is an insult—you are putting your spouse down. If you think that they won’t understand you on this topic or don’t want to share your opinion, it is more appropriate to say, “I don’t want to talk about this, don’t be offended, let’s talk about something else” or “This probably doesn’t interest you.”
“Don’t go there, don’t talk to her, don’t do this, don’t wear that, don’t talk like that, bring this, take that!”

Your spouse is not your subordinate. It is better to respectfully discuss with them what you don’t want or don’t like and to avoid conflict. Instead of using impassioned statements, use requests (please, please, etc.).
Moral: Words can hurt the person we love the most. In the family, we should use the language of respect and requests, not orders and insults.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Strength and Pain
paragraphs: My God! Give me either strength for the pain I suffer, or pain as much as I can bear.
Muhammad Fuzuli
Moral: A person should either ask for strength to bear his pain, or pain according to his strength. Do not fall under a burden that exceeds his strength.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The Flower of Honesty
paragraphs: A prince was preparing to ascend the throne. But according to the rules, he had to get married first. In order to choose a suitable candidate, he had the most beautiful girls in the country summoned to his presence.

The daughter of one of the servants in the palace was also in love with the prince. She also told her mother that she wanted to go to the prince's presence. Although her mother tried to dissuade her daughter from this idea, the girl did not change her mind and insisted on going to the presence.
The expected day came. The young beautiful girls who gathered at the palace wore their most elegant clothes, decorated themselves, and did their best to impress.

The prince gave each of the girls a seed, instructed them to plant it in a pot and return to him in six months. He said that he would choose the one who grows the most beautiful flower and marry her. The girls took the seed and returned home excitedly.

The girl in the palace also planted the seed she had received in the pot. Despite her diligent care, not a single sprout grows in the soil. She tries every way, consults with gardeners, but still nothing. When six months are up, the girl is forced to come to the palace with an empty pot. Unlike her, the other girls come with pots full of beautiful flowers.
The time of the selection comes. The prince enters the hall, walks among the girls, and looks at the pots one by one. Finally, he announces in a loud voice that he has chosen the servant's daughter.
Everyone is stunned. The other girls protest this decision: how can a girl who comes with an empty pot be chosen as a candidate for the bride?
The prince explains the reason for his decision as follows:

— This young lady grew and brought me the most valuable flower. The name of that flower is the flower of honesty. All the seeds that I distributed to you were fake, it was impossible for them to bloom.
Moral: The most valuable decoration is honesty. A person is exalted not by his appearance, but by having a true word and a clear conscience.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The Goose to Be Taken
paragraphs: On a very cold winter day, the king decided to leave the palace in disguise and take his chief vizier with him. After walking for a while, they came across an old man working on the edge of a stream. The man was dipping the skins in his hands in water and beating them.
The king greeted the old man:
— Assalamu alaykum, o piri-fani.
— Assalamu alaykum, o sardari-jahan, — and the old man accepted the greeting. The king asked:
— What did you do at six?
— Unless you add six to six, it doesn't make thirty-two, — he replied.
The king asked again:
— Did you never get up at night?
— We got up, my king... but it was good for the people...
The king laughed and asked his last question:
— If I send a goose, would you go?
— Of course, I will go, and without shouting, — the elder replies.
The king and the chief vizier leave the man and continue on their way. The king asks the chief vizier:
— Do you understand what we are talking about?
— No, my king, — the chief vizier replies in a distressed manner.
The king gets angry:
— If you do not understand what we are talking about by this evening, I will have your neck cut off.
After the frightened chief vizier takes the king to the palace, he rushes back to the edge of the valley and sees that the man is still working there.
— What did you talk about with the king? — the chief vizier addresses the elder.
The man looks at the chief vizier from head to toe beautifully:
— Forgive me, I will not tell the weather. Give me a hundred gold coins, and I will tell you, — he says.
The chief vizier gives the hundred gold coins.
— You greeted the king as “sardari-jahan”. How did you know that he was a king?
— I am a tanner. No one but the king could wear the fur he is wearing.
The vizier scratches his head:
— What did he mean by “if you don’t add six to six, it won’t be enough for thirty-two”?
The man also takes a hundred gold coins to answer this question:

— King, didn’t you work during the six months of heat, and now you are working on this winter day? I said: If we don’t work not only during the six months of heat, but also in the six months of winter, we won’t be able to find bread.
The chief vizier continues:
— What did he mean by “didn’t you ever get up at night?”
The man takes another hundred gold coins:
— King, don’t you have any children? He asked. Yes, but they are all girls; they got married, they are destined for someone else, I said.
The chief vizier lowers his head:
— And he said, “If I send a goose”… what did he mean?
The man laughs and says to the chief vizier:
— You find her too, — he says.
Moral: A wise word is revealed to those who understand it. Not everyone understands what they hear — some answers a person must find for themselves.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The strongest shield
paragraphs: The strongest shield in life is distance.
Moral: Sometimes the strongest way to protect yourself is to keep a healthy distance. Too much closeness to everything and everyone burns you.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The three best things
paragraphs: Father:
— Son, we should strive for these three things in life: to eat the best food, to sleep in the best bed, and to live in the best house.
Son:
— Father, but we are poor, how can we do this?
Father:

— If you eat when you are hungry, this will be your best food. If you sleep tired after working hard, this will be your best sleep. If you give people a place in your heart, this will be your best home.
Moral: The best food is found in hunger, the best sleep after hard work, and the best home is found in hearts. Happiness is not in opportunity, but in perspective.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Think, Speak, Act Positively
paragraphs: Think positively, because your thoughts become your words.
Speak positively, because your words become your actions.
Act positively, because your actions become your habits.
Develop positive habits, because your habits become your values.
Develop positive values, because your values ​​become your destiny.
Moral: Thoughts become words, words become actions, actions become habits, and habits become destiny. The beginning of a positive destiny is positive thinking.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Try to think like this
paragraphs: Don’t say, “I’m not good at this job.” Say, “Maybe there’s something I don’t know? I’m sure if I refresh my knowledge and work on it, I can do it.”
Don’t say, “I’ve given up on this job.” Say, “Maybe I can solve this problem in a different way? I’ll try, maybe it will work.”
Don’t say, “This job is too hard.” Say, “It’s hard, but not impossible; it just takes a little extra time and effort.”
Don’t say, “I’m satisfied with the work I’m doing, I can’t do better.” Say, “I can work on myself, improve, and achieve better results.”
Don’t say, “I made a mistake, I wish I hadn’t.” Say, “It’s not the end of the world; mistakes help me learn.”
Don’t say, “He’s so smart, I can’t be like him.” Say, “I can learn how he did it and achieve the same success.”

Moral: Changing your mindset is the first step to changing your life. Saying “I can't” closes the door, saying “I can learn” opens up new possibilities. Failure is not the end, it is an opportunity for growth.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Turning difficulties into opportunities
paragraphs: Sometimes in life, things go very smoothly, and sometimes we face unexpected difficulties. The important thing is to be able to turn the difficulties we encounter into opportunities.
Moral: The same difficulty breaks one and strengthens another. It is up to a person to turn difficulties into tools, not weapons.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Who Handles Honey Licks His Finger
paragraphs: A beekeeper filled containers with the honey he had collected and brought them to a grocer to sell. They struck a bargain on the price and began to weigh the honey.

Because the grocer had only a one-kilo weight, he broke off pieces of honeycomb by hand and weighed the honey kilo by kilo. But before placing each piece on the scale, he never failed to lick his honey-smeared fingers.

Once, twice, three times… The beekeeper saw that some of the honey never reached the scale — it stayed on the grocer’s fingers and went to his tongue. He frowned and showed his displeasure. The grocer paid no attention and kept weighing, licking his fingers as he went.
At last the beekeeper’s patience ran out:
— Uncle, this won’t do — you’ve licked away half the honey!
Still licking his honeyed fingers, the grocer smiled quietly and replied:
— Brother, I mean no harm. Who handles honey licks his finger.
Moral: Even a small share in a job usually brings some gain from it.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Words for the mouths, not dust for the feet
paragraphs: Words for the mouths, not dust for the feet!
Moral: Preserve your dignity: live in such a way that you neither fall into disrepute nor become as worthless as the dust underfoot.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: You can't go down a well with his rope
paragraphs: Once upon a time, there was a master named Ali who was busy making rope from flax fibers. Since he didn't do his job well, the ropes he made often turned out rotten. He was even called "Master Ali, the rotten rope." Master Ali's ropes often broke and caused many accidents.
One day, a sheep fell into a deep well. An acquaintance, intending to go down the well to get his sheep out, asked the sheep's owner for a rope, but he didn't like the rope he was given:
— I know this rope. This is Master Ali's work. You can't go down the well with his rope, he complained.
— Don't be unfair. Why, you can go down the well with Master Ali's rope; but I can't say whether you can get out of there with the same rope, I can't say," the sheep's owner replied with a smile.
Moral: A person gains or loses trust in his name by the quality of his work. Once trust is shaken, it is very difficult to restore it.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

categories.title: Word, silence, and communication
categories.blurb: The power of speech, the wisdom of silence, and right conversation.

stories.title: Communication
paragraphs: If you often interact with the elderly and children, you will see experience in one and innocence in the other.
Moral: Experience is learned from the elderly, innocence from the child. Every age has a value to give to a person.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Language
paragraphs: Language is a flower, it grows in the mouth,
if you don't water it and protect it, it will wither and disappear.
Moral: If the language is not protected, it will wither and disappear like a flower that is not watered. Keeping your mother tongue alive means using it lovingly every day.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Silence
paragraphs: The answer to some questions is silence.
Either it's not the time for an answer,
or the interlocutor doesn't deserve an answer!
Darvish Jalal Ruhavi
Moral: The most correct answer to some questions is silence — either it's not the time, or it doesn't deserve the answer in front of you.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Silent corridor
paragraphs: There were two organizations working together — one was the sponsor, the other was the project development agency.

The project team worked tirelessly for months, carefully polishing the documents, and one day, when everything was ready, they sent the materials to the sponsor and began to wait for a response. Days passed, weeks passed. The result — silence.
The uncertainty within the team grew, spreading like a shadow along the corridor:
“Have the documents arrived? Have they been reviewed?”
No one had any clear information. And requests to the sponsor only brought vague, vague answers.
A few months later, the team decided to go directly to the sponsor’s office to clarify the matter. There, the truth finally emerged:
“Yes, the documents arrived. But we did not accept them. Because the submission form was incorrect and the official procedure was not followed.”
The team froze in place.
“Why didn’t you tell us that?” they asked.
“We could have fixed everything in a short time.”...
Frustrated, the employees returned to the office and complained to their management:

“If we had been actively monitoring the process, checking in on the status regularly, and communicating clearly, this misunderstanding would never have happened. We wasted time, wasted energy, and lost trust—all because the hallway between us was silent.”

Moral: When communication is unclear, even the best work can go unnoticed. When there is no consistent follow-up, even the strongest partnership can falter. In collaboration, the greatest enemy is often not failure—it is silence.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

stories.title: Speaking the right words
paragraphs: He who knows how to speak the right words will never have to apologize.
Moral: He who speaks the right words will never have to apologize later. The right word at the right time is precious.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Tell what you know
paragraphs: Tell what you know, but don't teach wisdom. Listen carefully to what is said, but don't assume everything is true.
Just as being silent does not mean that you know nothing, talking too much does not mean that you know much. It is foolish to belittle a person, and to extol him excessively is cowardice.
Moral: Speak correctly, listen correctly, and you will be able to remain silent. Neither humiliate nor exalt a person - see him as he is.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The Conversation of the Candles
paragraphs: Four candles were burning in a room. The atmosphere was so quiet that you could hear the candles talking to each other.
The first candle said: “I am FAITH! But no one is helping me to burn. I think I will soon go out.”
And so it was. Its flame began to fade rapidly, and finally FAITH went out completely.
The second candle said: “I am FAITH! What a pity, I am no longer needed by anyone. That is why there is no point in me burning anymore.”
As soon as he finished speaking, a light breeze blew out FAITH completely.

The turn came for the third candle. He said in a sad voice: “I am LOVE! I have no strength left to burn anymore. People have forgotten me, my value has disappeared. Even my closest people have forgotten to love.”
LOVE could not stand it any longer and went out.
At that moment, a child entered the room and saw that all three candles were not burning. “Why don't you burn? Weren't you supposed to burn forever?” he began to cry.
Then the fourth candle spoke: “Don't be afraid, as long as I burn, we can light the other candles again. I AM HOPE!”
The child was happy and with shining eyes, he took the HOPE candle in his hand and lit the other candles one by one.
Moral: When faith, loyalty and love go out, it is hope that lights them up again. If we keep the light of hope alive, the other values ​​will also come alive.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The Knower and the Unknower
paragraphs: (Chinese Proverb)
The one who does not know and knows that he does not know — yearns for knowledge. Teach him!
The one who knows and does not know that he knows — is asleep. Wake him up!
The one who does not know and does not know that he does not know — is ignorant. Stay away from him!
The one who knows and knows that he knows — is a leader. Follow him!
Moral: Teach the one who yearns to learn, awaken the one who is heedless, stay away from the ignorant who thinks he knows everything, and follow the one who really knows.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: The Shepherd's Word
paragraphs: Once upon a time, in a village, there lived a poor but honest shepherd named Hasan. One day, the village chief called him and said:

— Hey Hasan, I have heard that you are very familiar with the pastures of the mountains. I will entrust you with the herd this summer. If my animals return healthy and fat in the fall, I will give you a cow.
Hasan agreed. He grazed his herd all summer, rain or shine, and guarded it without blinking an eye at night. When fall came, the herd returned to the village fatter and healthier than before.
Hasan came to the chief, hoping to receive the promised cow. The chief smiled mockingly and said:
— I had no intention of giving you a cow, that word was just said to encourage you to work. If you are already poor, what will you do with a cow?
Hasan's eyes filled with tears. But he answered calmly and with dignity:
— You are right, chief, I am poor. But I have a conscience and I am the master of my word. You may be rich, but if your word is worthless, then you are truly poor.

These words spread from mouth to mouth in the village. The master's name fell out of respect, and people began to avoid doing business with him. But he understood, albeit late: the value of a person is determined not by his wealth or position, but by his loyalty to his word.
Moral: A person's true wealth is not his wealth, but his word, conscience, and trust.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: What is a word?
paragraphs: A word is a wound;
A word is a pearl.
Moral: A word can be both a wounding thorn and a precious pearl. What makes the difference is how you use it.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: Words and silence
paragraphs: Sometimes a person says more by keeping quiet. Because words are not just sounds — they are a mirror of intention.
If a word will break a heart, if a sentence will extinguish hope — it is not worth saying.
If the words you are going to say will not warm a heart, if they will not cause a smile — be silent.
Remember... not every word blooms. Some are like thorns — they hurt the one who touches them.
Silence is wisdom. Sometimes it is the most valuable answer.
If a word is born from the heart, it turns into wisdom; if it comes out of the mouth without thought, it causes harm, wounds.
Silence. Because silence also speaks — sometimes more deeply, sometimes more honestly.
Moral: Not every word blooms; some hurt like thorns. Silence is wiser than words that will not bring good.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: You need to call the shepherd
paragraphs: A student who wants to complete his education after many years turns to his master to receive his blessing.
His master:

— Yes, but I have one condition. I will ask you a question to see if you have properly learned the knowledge I have given you over the years. If you answer the question correctly, I will know that my efforts have not been in vain, and I will give you my blessing.
The student confidently says:
— Come on, my master, ask.
His master:
— My son, imagine that you are going to your village and on the way a pack of rabid dogs belonging to a shepherd attacks you. You are in danger. What will you do to save your life?
— I will bend down and pick up a few stones from the ground and throw them at the dogs, and I will chase them away.
— But, my son, if you throw stones at one, you throw stones at two — you will not be able to handle them all. They will join together and tear you apart.
— Then I will run away.
— Be sure that they will run away from you quickly and catch you. So what?
The student realizes that he is helpless and asks his master for help.
His master:
— My son, there is only one way out of this situation: you must call the shepherd and ask him to stop his dogs. The dogs will freeze in place as soon as they hear the shepherd's voice.
Moral: Not every problem can be solved by force. Sometimes taking a step back and looking at it differently is the shortest way out.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

categories.title: Wisdom and life lessons
categories.blurb: Meaning, choices, and ways of thinking.

stories.title: A Different Path
paragraphs: One day, a cow returning to its shed had to cross an untouched forest. Unable to choose a sensible route, the animal wandered uphill and downhill, creating a long, twisting, and difficult trail.

The next day, a dog came to the same place. To reach the other side of the forest, it followed the cow’s trail. Then came a flock of sheep. Seeing a ready-made path, the shepherd led the flock along it.

Before long, people began using the trail as well. They complained about its difficulty as they turned left and right, ducked beneath branches, and twisted their way through the bushes. Yet no one thought to look for a better route.

Through constant use, the trail gradually became a road. Unaware that the other side of the forest could be reached in only half an hour, people and heavily burdened animals spent three hours following the cow’s winding path.

Years passed. The small road first became the town’s main route and eventually its most important street. Although it was the least efficient route imaginable, everyone merely complained about the traffic.
Watching it all, the old and wise forest pitied the people who blindly followed the familiar road without ever asking whether it was the right one.
Moral: The path everyone follows is not always the best one. Sometimes those who step beyond habit and search for a new route reach their destination more quickly and easily.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: A Human Being Emerged
paragraphs: I joined thought with the heart—and love emerged.
I gathered love through labor—and loyalty emerged.
I divided bread according to conscience—and justice emerged.
I brought love, labor, conscience, loyalty, and justice together—and a human being emerged.
— Yaşar Kemal
Moral: When love, labor, conscience, loyalty, and justice come together, a true human being is formed. Humanity is the union of these values.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: A Life Lesson
paragraphs: While teaching his cub about life, a father wolf pointed to some sheep:
“Their meat is delicious.”
Then he pointed to the shepherd:
“But his staff can be very bitter. Be careful.”
Seeing the dog beside the shepherd, the cub exclaimed happily:
“Father, look! That one resembles us.”
The father replied:
“Run the moment you see it, my son. We have suffered most from those who look like us but are not truly one of us.”
Moral: Sometimes the greatest harm comes from those who resemble us while concealing different intentions. Recognizing hypocrisy in time is the first step toward protecting oneself.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: A More Effective Way
paragraphs: A hunter walking through a forest came upon an unusual scene. A woodcutter had been hacking at a fallen tree for a long time with enormous effort. His face was drenched in sweat and his whole body was tense.
The hunter approached and asked:
“Why is the work going so slowly and painfully? Your axe is completely blunt. Why not sharpen it?”
The woodcutter stared at him in surprise:
“What are you talking about? Where would I find time to sharpen my axe? I still have twenty more trees to cut!”
Moral: Hard work is valuable, but unexamined effort can be wasteful. Sometimes a short pause to sharpen the tool makes all the work that follows faster and easier.

stories.title: A Windmill Turning in Still Air
paragraphs: If a windmill turns when the air is still, someone must be blowing on its sails.
Eskimo proverb
Moral: No outcome arises without a cause. The force behind an event may be invisible, yet its influence becomes clear in the result.

stories.title: At the Bookstore
paragraphs: After a long search, a medical student found the book he needed at the Bilge bookstore in Bursa. When he saw the price on the back, his smile vanished: he could not afford it.
Hiding his disappointment, he leafed through the pages, found the section assigned by his professor, and—seeing that the owners were busy with customers—read it quickly before leaving.

For the next month, the student returned every other day and studied among the shelves. One week before his final examinations, he came again, but the book was gone. He searched every shelf; it seemed to have vanished.
As the pale-faced young man was about to leave, the owners stopped him:
“Please sit down. We have something to tell you.”
One bookseller reached beneath the counter and produced the book:
“A customer recently asked its price and appeared ready to buy it. I removed it from the shelf and kept it for you. You may continue reading it here.”
After completing his studies and becoming a doctor, the young man never forgot the two booksellers. He never charged patients who could not afford treatment.
Moral: A small act of kindness can leave a lifelong mark on the heart. Those who receive kindness often carry it forward to others.

stories.title: At the Doctor’s Appointment
paragraphs: I was waiting for my turn at a doctor’s office. Having missed breakfast at home, I bought a sandwich and apple juice from the café and began to eat.
A boy sitting near the window was watching me closely. His expression seemed to say, “I am hungry too.” Feeling sorry for him, I returned to the café and bought him a sandwich and juice.
The boy ate eagerly, while I felt pleased with what I believed was a good deed.
At that moment, his mother emerged from the registration room. Seeing the scene, she hurried over in alarm:
“What have you done? The doctor told me to bring him fasting. I took time off work, and we traveled a long way. Now we will have to begin everything again tomorrow.”
The woman could not hold back her tears. I stood frozen: while believing I was helping, I had undone an entire family’s effort.
Moral: Judgment based only on emotion and assumption can lead us to the wrong decision. Asking about the situation before helping is itself part of compassion.

stories.title: Blind people with eyes

stories.title: Blind Well
paragraphs: One day, a villager's donkey falls into a blind well (a well whose water has dried up). Hours pass; finally, the owner and his neighbors, hearing the donkey's painful cries, rush to the rescue. He says, he says, and finally they come to the conclusion that it will be impossible to get it out of the well, and they see the only solution in filling the well with earth. Each takes a shovel in his hand and begins to carry earth from the surrounding area and pour it into the well.

The poor animal shakes off the earth that has fallen on it and throws it under its feet, and thanks to this earth it gradually rises, finally managing to climb to the mouth of the well. The people are very surprised when they see the donkey come out of the well safely.
Moral: Shake off the earth that has fallen on it and throw it under its feet, and rise. The way out of helplessness is not in whining, but in shaking and struggling.

stories.title: Diderot effect
paragraphs: One of the 18th century French writers, the enlightener Denis Diderot, falls into a huge debt swamp. His miserable situation reaches the ears of the Russian Empress Catherine.

The Empress makes Diderot a kind offer to get out of this swamp: she buys his library for money and gives it back to him. Moreover, she pays Diderot 25 years of salary in advance for working in that library. Of course, paying this advance at such an unexpected moment meant making a fortune for Diderot. Now Diderot was free from all debts and relieved.
One day, a friend gives him a red velvet robe (luxurious outerwear). It all starts from there...
Denis puts on the robe. While working enthusiastically at his desk, he suddenly thinks that this beautiful velvet robe and the table do not match.
Intoxicated by the cash in his safe, he immediately goes to change the table and buys a magnificent one. The dress and the table now match each other...
But then he sees that the old carpet on the floor does not suit either the dress or the table. He runs out and buys a carpet that suits his money and himself.
Still, there was a feeling of unease inside him. The armchairs, cupboards, chairs, pictures on the wall, and the decorations in the room no longer match each other, they seem old...
Everything is starting to sink in...
Time comes, time goes... Diderot changed everything in the house, from the needle to the thread.
It did not take Diderot long to realize the situation. He realized that the reason for his return to the starting point was his own inexhaustible greed.
As a result, the author wrote his famous work on this subject, "I Regret Parting with My Old Dress." Then he wrote a short sentence that will go down in history:
"While I was the master of my old dress, I became the slave of the new one."

Moral: After a person acquires a new thing, he feels the need to change the rest - this is called the "Diderot effect." There is no end to greed; it is better to be the master of the old than the slave of the new.

stories.title: From the memories of a woman from Istanbul
paragraphs: It was 1919. Istanbul was completely under British occupation. I had just finished high school.

I was a beautiful girl, and ambassadors came to our house. One day, a young man who introduced himself as a lawyer came to our house with his ambassadors. I saw this handsome, tall boy and liked him. We got engaged. I loved my fiancé... I wanted to build a happy home, so I wove small towels by lamplight until morning and prepared my dowry.
One day, a rumor spread in the neighborhood.
They said, “Ayesha's fiancé was not a lawyer at all, he was crying all day long by carrying a coffin in front of the mosque.”
I was devastated. My father and I went to the mosque, watched from a distance, and saw that he was really carrying a coffin.
I was shocked. We returned the engagement, and we broke up.
Five years passed. I was married, I had a child. Our country was already free.
One day I met him in the city. My son was with me.
He stopped when he saw me. He said hesitantly, “If you have time, I would like to offer you a cup of tea.” I agreed. We went into an office.
It was a law firm; his name was written on the sign on the door. His assistants were working inside.
“Are you really a lawyer?” I asked.
“Yes,” he said.
“But if you are a lawyer, why were you carrying a coffin in front of the mosque?”
He bowed his head and said, “Forgive me.”

“Istanbul was under occupation. We were surrounded by British soldiers everywhere, they were checking everything and everyone very carefully. And we were sending coffins full of weapons to Anatolia, to help the National Forces, under the guise of funerals. It was a vital task for the country. I couldn’t tell you that…”
Moral: Don’t judge by appearance; behind every behavior there may be a truth that you don’t know. Our freedom is owed to the sacrifice of the selfless.

stories.title: Hayat’s Life Story
paragraphs: When my mother left our home, my father, and us, I was six and my brother was eight. Even at that age I understood why she left my father, but I could not understand why she left us. Would a mother abandon her children?
My father used to beat my mother. He beat me and my brother too. I came to believe that all men beat their wives and children…

Only after my mother left did I learn that a home without a mother is nothing but four walls. Just as no one said in the mornings, “Wash your hands and face and come — breakfast is ready,” I learned that no one asked “Are you hungry?” even if you went days without food. Of all I learned, this burned me most: when there is no mother’s scent, children grow up in an instant, whatever their age. I grew up at six.

About ten days after my mother left, the police came to our house. They said she had taken her own life. In her hand she had been clutching an envelope. On it was written: “To be given to my daughter and my son.”
I could not read then — how was I supposed to read it? My brother read it. I cried as I listened. My brother cried too.

When my mother left us, she had gone to her father’s house. Her father flew into a rage. Apparently a woman was supposed to stay in her own home; even if her mouth were full of blood, she was supposed to say, “I drank red sherbet.” My mother begged my grandfather: “Let me stay with you for a month; then I will find a way, take my children, and begin a new life.”

Oh, no, no, no! A woman living alone? She would cheapen my grandfather’s honour for a penny; he would not be able to show his face; better if his daughter were dead. That evening my mother, without thinking, put the clothesline around her neck. My grandmother told me this years later on her deathbed, when I was nineteen.

When my father heard of my mother’s death, he was not upset at all. He said he would put us in an orphanage. From then on we would live there; that would be our home. Brother and sister might be parted, forget each other, and years later fail to know each other — so we were both to keep Mother’s letter.

But before I could ask how the two of us would keep one letter, my brother cut it in half with scissors. He gave me the beginnings of the sentences. Since I had the openings, once I learned to read I would have to guess the rest. My brother had already memorized the letter anyway.

When my aunt heard we were to be sent to an orphanage, she came. She told my father: “A girl is not given to an orphanage. I will take Hayat and raise her myself.” Living with my aunt, I understood why: a girl meant an unpaid servant ordered about the house. Not once did my aunt call me by my name. My name became “Come-here”: “Come-here, fetch water… Come-here, wash these dishes…”

Once a month my brother visited me at my aunt’s. He said he was fine in the orphanage. I said I was fine too — I did not want to upset him. Did he also say “I’m fine” so I would not worry? I never dared ask.

I had started school. I was the first in the class to learn to read. How could I not — I was going to read my mother’s letter. The part I still had began: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I…” Every night in bed I tried to finish that sentence:
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I love you so much.”
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I miss you terribly.”
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I am waiting for you.”
According to the words I added, I built dreams. In my dreams I was very happy. Does anyone ever dream of bitterness?
I finished middle school. My aunt said I would not go to school anymore. But I wanted to study — to stand on my own feet and live under one roof with my brother.

That summer the wife of Uncle Hasan, the neighbourhood grocer with three children, died of cancer. I was heartbroken. What would the three children do — how would they find a mother’s scent? Why did mothers die? Would those three forget their names as I had, and become “Come-here” too?

While I was grieving for Uncle Hasan’s children, it came out that I was betrothed to him. It turned out I had been sold for eight bracelets and three thousand liras. Because I was too young for a civil marriage, forty days later our religious marriage was performed.

I was fifteen. I was Uncle Hasan’s wife. I had three children — two, five, and six. And my aunt insisted we must have a child of our own… I was supposed to have a child so my place would be secure and Uncle Hasan would not look at other women.

The first slap from Uncle Hasan came because I called him “Uncle Hasan.” Does a woman call her husband “uncle”? When I lost my mother at six, I learned to keep silent. So I did not ask, “Does a man call a fifteen-year-old girl his wife?” — I stayed quiet.

When Uncle Hasan hit me, all three children clung to their father’s legs: “Don’t hit Sister Hayat — she plays with us, she tells us stories,” they begged. I was those children’s older sister. What I called stories were my dreams.

When Uncle Hasan left the house, I stood before the mirror — I would learn to say “Hasan.” Every time I said “Hasan,” I saw in the glass his thinning hair, the glasses slipped down his nose, his swollen belly. Every “Hasan” made me ashamed, as if I had sinned, and I could not call him that. While I practised, Uncle Hasan’s six-year-old son came: “Sister Hayat, Mother used to call Father ‘Bey’ — you say ‘Bey’ too,” he encouraged me.

“Bey” — of course, “Bey” would be better. I bent and kissed dark-eyed Sami, who listened to my dreams as if they were fairy tales. I called five-year-old Elif and two-year-old Zahra and began to tell them a story. That day I began: “Once upon a time there was a six-year-old girl named Nagil. Nagil had lost her mother. She searched everywhere; when she could not find her, she went to the land of dreams. There Nagil was so happy that she never returned to the real world.”
In my tale Nagil was always happy, always smiling. Every day I told the children that story. We were very happy.

Uncle Hasan was good too. I now called him “Bey.” From time to time he grew angry, but I understood why: instead of a woman he had bought, for eight bracelets and three thousand liras, a storytelling sister.

My brother came to visit. Each time he wanted to give me his half of Mother’s letter. I would not take it. I was afraid that if I read the other half, I would fall from the land of dreams into a cruel real world and be unhappy. All my dreams were built on that other half.

By forty, the children who had listened to my stories had grown. Sami had become a doctor, taken a post in another city, and left our house. When he felt low he would call: “Sister Hayat, tell me a story.”
Elif had become a teacher and married. I had a granddaughter. They badly wanted to name her Hayat; I would not allow it. Elif said, “Then let her name be Nagil.” So my granddaughter’s name was Nagil.
My youngest, Zahra, became a veterinarian. “Sister Hayat, whenever an animal is restless I tell it a story, and it calms down,” she would say. Zahra married too, and I had a grandson.
When I turned forty-five, Uncle Hasan — my Bey — passed away. I grieved deeply. His last words were “Forgive me — make it lawful.” With all my heart I forgave him. He was a good man.
But my claim —
against those who see no wrong in marrying off fifteen-year-old girls, and those who support them;
against the blind minds who call it dishonour when a daughter they know is beaten every day seeks divorce, and those who support them;
against those who show no mercy to children left helpless and hopeless like wounded birds, and those who support them —
I do not forgive!
Moral: Blind custom and a false idea of “honour” can destroy a woman’s life, a child’s life. Those who look away from early marriage, violence, and neglect are partners in that oppression.

stories.title: If I don’t do it these days, the world won’t fall apart
paragraphs: When I asked one of our employees what stage of the implementation of a task entrusted to him was, his answer deeply disappointed me:
“If I don’t do it these days, the world won’t fall apart…”

I thought for a moment: Yes, the world won’t fall apart. But what about the trust between us? Won’t that fall apart too? Wouldn’t this relationship harm our cooperation, mutual respect, and the common work we do?

The issue wasn’t that the task was delayed by a few days. The issue was a person’s attitude towards the commitment they took on. Because responsibility is not only about doing the job, but also about keeping your word, justifying the trust of the other party, and ensuring that people can rely on you.

I think it’s not right to approach any commitment you take on in such an irresponsible way. What was even more regrettable was the way this approach was expressed. To me, such an answer sounds at least rude and shows that the other party's time, effort, and trust are not sufficiently valued.

I must admit that these words broke my heart. At that moment, I realized that our cooperation could not continue as before. Because the foundation of any professional relationship is trust. When trust is shaken, cooperation is also seriously tested.

What disappointed me most was that my colleague realized the wrongness of what he said, neither apologized for it nor fulfilled the task. As a result, my trust in him was shaken, so I was forced to provide a solution to the problem in another way.

This incident once again showed me that the most valuable resource in organizations is time, not money, nor technology. The most valuable resource is the trust that people have in each other. It can take years to earn trust, but sometimes it can be lost in just one sentence.
Moral: Trust is the most valuable asset of organizations. It takes years to earn it, and losing it is like a sentence - those who keep their word protect this wealth.

stories.title: If the door in front of you doesn't open, it's not your door
paragraphs: This story takes place between a company manager and his employee. One day, Jamal comes to his boss, Salim bey, and tells him that he has heard that there will be a promotion at work, and that he has expectations of his own. Although Salim bey says that he is satisfied with Jamal's work, he tells him that he is fired, saying, "You are not a good fit for us." Jamal has to leave the company in disappointment.

Two years later, they meet again. After greeting each other kindly and checking in on each other, Jamal tells his former boss that he has started a new company and that his business is going well. Salim bey says that he is very happy.

Jamal expresses his gratitude to Salim bey as follows: "Actually, I would like to thank you for not wanting me to stay in that company for which I was not a good fit, but for releasing me. This has meant a new opportunity for me, it has encouraged me to do a job that I really like, and I am very happy with my situation now."
Moral: Every closed door can actually be a sign of a better path. Sometimes, the deprivation of "good" leads to "better."

stories.title: It is futile
paragraphs: It is futile to advise a fool, to argue with an ignorant person, to befriend a hypocrite.

stories.title: It Won’t Go to Waste
paragraphs: A kindness done from the heart,
a deed kneaded with love,
a word spoken in sincerity,
conduct wrapped in courtesy,
a smile coloured with affection,
a step taken for truth and justice,
respect shown to moral values —
never goes to waste; besides lighting the path of those around you, it also helps your own life become bright, sound, and beautiful.
Moral: Kindness, words, and deeds from the heart never vanish; they light others’ way and brighten your life.

stories.title: Lecturer and mehter
paragraphs: A lecturer is invited to a village to educate the population. The man enters the hall and sees that only one person is sitting inside. After greeting, he addresses this man: “No one else has come. What do you say, should we go to the lecture or not?”
The only “listener” says:
— Teacher, I am a mehter, I have twenty horses. If all the horses run away and only one remains, I will still feed it, give it water and feed.
The lecturer begins his speech and speaks at length. After finishing, he asks the mehter:
— How was it, did you like my lecture?

The mehter replies: “I am a horse breeder, I did not understand anything from what you said. But I can only say that I will feed the water and feed of twenty horses to one horse and not make it break.”
Moral: Speaking well is not about talking too much, but about the idea being understood and assimilated by the listener.

stories.title: Life is short

stories.title: Liver
paragraphs: Where do the expressions using the word “liver” come from—“jan-jiyar” meaning a very close, sincere, and kind friend; “jiyarguşam” meaning a very beloved child; “agqıyar” meaning a coward, a coward, a helpless person; “jiyarparam” meaning a very beloved person, etc.—originate?

Ancient people were impressed by the warm and bloody appearance of the liver, so they considered warm blood to be life, and its absence to be death. For this reason, the liver has long been considered the center of life.

For example, the Babylonians believed that the human soul resided in the liver. Since the liver was thought to primarily represent emotions in some cultures, the liver came before the heart in idioms and writings.

In ancient Greece, virtue and related qualities such as courage and determination were attributed to the liver. If a person had a healthy liver, he was considered virtuous—he was perceived as someone who followed his principles, overcoming all obstacles.
Moral: Language does not arise by chance; behind every word there is a history, a belief. Our words are the memory of our past.

stories.title: Living in the past

stories.title: Newton's 2nd Law

stories.title: Nothing Is Ever Truly Lost

stories.title: Pawn and king
paragraphs: Don't look down on a pawn!
One day, it will become a KING.
Don't trust it just because it is a king!
One day, it will become a MATCH.
Moral: Don't look down on anyone because they are small, don't brag about your position. A pawn can become a king, and a king can become a checkmate.

stories.title: Planting millet in the bottom
paragraphs: One day, the king went on a walk with his courtiers. In a village on the way, he saw an old man planting seedlings in his field. He called out to the elder from a distance:
— Father, why are you busy planting these seedlings? Mashallah, you have not lived your life; you will probably not be able to eat the fruit of these seedlings.
The elder replied to the king:

— It is not necessary for us to eat the fruit of these seedlings, my son. Just as we ate the fruit of the seedlings planted by those before us, those after us will also eat the fruit of the seedlings we plant.
This answer pleased the king and he ordered the elder to be given a bag of gold.
The elder pointed to the bag full of gold and said:
— Did you see, my son? The seedlings we planted have already borne fruit.
This answer pleased the king and he ordered the elder to be given another bag of gold. The old peasant was not an ordinary man - he was a wise and wise man:
— My son, the saplings that everyone else plants bear fruit once a year, but the saplings we planted have already borne fruit twice.
The ruler, who liked this answer, ordered the nobleman to be given another bag of gold. But this time the vizier intervened and tried to dissuade the ruler from his thoughts:
— Oh, my sultan! We must leave here as soon as possible. If this nobleman leaves like this, instead of planting saplings in his field, he will plant millet in the state treasury.
Moral: A person does not live only for himself. We ate what those who came before us planted; we must plant for those who come after us.

stories.title: Properties of water
paragraphs: Look at the properties of water:
— if it makes friends with a tree, it keeps it alive;
— if it comes into contact with fire, it extinguishes it;
— if it encounters impurity, it purifies it;
— if it mixes with flour, it turns it into dough, making it ready for baking;
— if it unites with the sun, a rainbow is formed;
— if it flows, it brings life;
— if it stagnates, it turns into a swamp and begins to smell.
The human heart is also like water: it is very lively in communication, but lifeless in solitude.
Moral: The human heart is like water: it comes to life in communication, stagnates and withers in solitude. It is other people who keep a person alive.

stories.title: Teacher, Hello — Do You Remember Me?
paragraphs: — Teacher, hello! Do you remember me? You were once my teacher at school.
— Yes, I remember. You were my pupil in primary school. I’m glad to see you again after so many years. What do you do?
— I’m very glad to see you too. I have become a teacher like you.
— Wonderful. Why did you decide to become a teacher?
— Because you once inspired me as a teacher; you were an example in life. So I decided to become a teacher too — to help children grow and to inspire them to succeed.
— I’m glad you think so and chose teaching. But you said I inspired you and was an example. What exactly do you mean?

— When you taught us, one boy in the class had been given a fine watch by his parents. My parents could not afford one for me. I liked the watch very much, and one day at the long break I stole it from his pocket. After the break he told you it had been stolen. You asked the class to return it. When no one spoke, you closed the door and said you would search all the boys’ pockets. I thought to myself that this would be the most shameful moment of my life.

The boys lined up along the wall; you told everyone to cover their eyes with their hands. One by one you checked every pocket. But after you took the watch from my pocket, you went on checking the others, and in the end you told no one who had stolen it. All year you said not a word of it to me or to my parents. You simply returned the watch to its owner. That day you did not let my dignity be crushed; you kept me from being branded a “thief” or a “liar” for a childish act, and you forgave me.

That event was a great lesson for me. I understood that a true teacher is not only one who gives knowledge, but one who instills right values — who does not merely punish a mistake, but teaches learning from it, and who binds the pupil to life. At that very moment I decided that one day I too would be a teacher like you.
The teacher listened and was astonished. The young man asked:
— Don’t you remember this? Have you forgotten that you took that watch from my pocket?
— I remember the incident; I simply did not know the watch had come from your pocket.
— How could you not know? You found it in my pocket yourself!
— Because when I checked the pupils’ pockets, I had closed my eyes too…
Moral: To protect a person’s dignity without shaming them — by closing your eyes — is true teaching. A person whose dignity is kept learns from the mistake and rises.

stories.title: The dead are the survivors
paragraphs: When one of two people who love each other with all their heart dies, the real "dead" is the one who survives.
Moral: When one of two people who love each other with all their heart leaves, the real "dead" is the one who is left behind and yearns. Love is even deeper in separation.

stories.title: The most beautiful places in the world
paragraphs: The most beautiful places you can be in the world are in the thoughts, prayers and hearts of your loved ones.
Moral: The most beautiful place a person can be is in the hearts and prayers of their loved ones. The true place is not an address, but love.

stories.title: The road to the cotton field
paragraphs: It was a time when we didn't know how to read or write properly. A teacher came to our village. He didn't just say that a teacher had come, but someone who would become a brother and father to us. When he learned about the miserable condition of our school and us students, and that we had to work in the cotton field after graduating from school, his eyes filled with tears.

There was a road in our village. Aydin teacher asked us where it went. We said that that road went to the cotton field. There was another road that extended from the village. He also asked where it went. Since we had never left our village in our lives and thought that the world consisted only of our village, we could not answer this question.
That day, he also asked us what we wanted to be when we grew up. We all remained silent because we didn't know what to answer...

Our teacher taught us how to read and write in a short time. Days passed, and we were already writing and reading comfortably. One day, Aydin teacher brought us many letters. He said that these letters came from doctors, engineers, scientists, and people with various professions. According to him, those people would become our pen pals. Those people whom we had never met for years wrote letters to us. In their letters, they talked about their professions, the meaning of life, and the importance of science and education. Until we received those letters, we had never even dreamed of studying science or having a profession other than cotton growing.
Because we thought that there was always only one path in front of us - the path leading to the cotton field.

Thanks to our pen pals, our lives changed. We learned where the other path led. Thanks to the great effort of teacher Aydin, we achieved great success years after graduating. Now some of us are preparing to become doctors, some are engineers, and some are teachers.
Years later, another letter came to us:

“My children... Always have dreams. They will take you where you want to go. All you have to do is make an effort, work hard, and be determined to achieve your goals. I congratulate you all from the bottom of my heart. I knew you would succeed and succeed”.
“Your pen pal, teacher Aydin.”
We were all in shock. After all, it was our native teacher Aydin who wrote the letters that changed our fate for years.
Moral: A teacher not only showed the way to children, but also created new paths for them. For a person who can dream, the world no longer consists of just one path.

stories.title: The secret to living well and living long
paragraphs: Half your food, double your walks, triple your laughter, and set no limits on your love.
Tibetan proverb.
Moral: Eat little, walk a lot, laugh a lot, love endlessly. The secret to a long and happy life lies in simplicity and love.

stories.title: There is no need to be smart when everyone is crazy
paragraphs: One day, a wise man receives news from above: "O man, from tomorrow the taste of water will change, and those who drink it will go crazy." The man quickly runs home, fills the jugs and bowls he can get his hands on with water, and sits down. The next morning, he sees that everyone is really starting to go crazy, and he only drinks from the water he has collected. This goes on for a week or two. The man can't stand it anymore and goes outside. As soon as he says a few words to those he meets, everyone mocks him: "Man, are you crazy? Go to a madhouse!" The poor man returns home, breaks the bowls and jugs, drinks from the ordinary fountain, the water that everyone drinks, and goes to bed.
Moral: The crowd may condemn you for knowing the truth. Protect your mind, but don't tire yourself out by trying to prove your worth to the public every moment.

stories.title: This boat is also empty
paragraphs: My master used to say:
When I was young, I often went to the lake, I used to dream and think in solitude. I had a small boat. I would sail in that boat for hours, finding peace in the world of thoughts.
One day, early in the morning, when the sun broke, I was sitting in my boat as usual, deep in thought.

Suddenly, someone's boat crashed into my boat and shook my entire dream world. I became very angry. I opened my eyes with the intention of cursing the owner of that boat and saw that the boat that crashed into me was empty. There was no one in the boat to whom I could vent my anger. So I closed my eyes and plunged into the world of beautiful dreams again. When the sun rose, I felt that my soul had regained complete peace.
The empty boat was a lesson for me. Since then, whenever someone tries to hurt me, I simply say to myself:
— This boat is also empty.

Moral: If a person wants to maintain his peace, he should not look for evil intentions behind every incident. Sometimes what worries us is just a coincidence; it is our choice whether to magnify it and turn it into anger.

stories.title: Three Questions
paragraphs: The king called the vizier to him and said:

— I am asking you three questions. If you do not find the answer by tomorrow, you will be expelled from the palace. The first: What does God eat? The second: What does God cover? The third: What does God do?

No matter how much the vizier racked his brains, he could not find the answers to the questions. In the evening, he returned home in a state of dismay. He had a clever and shrewd servant. The servant saw that his master was in a bad mood and asked the reason, and the vizier told him what had happened to him.
The servant said:

— I know the answers to all three questions. But I will tell you two now and one tomorrow. Know that what God eats is the sorrows and sorrows of his servants. What God covers is the faults of his servants.
The next day, the vizier went to the king and told him these two answers. The king said:
— That is true. But did you find these answers yourself, or did someone teach you?
The vizier tells the truth:
— My wise and clever servant taught me.
Hearing this, the king orders the vizier to take off his robe and give it to his servant. Thus, the vizier takes off his robe and puts it on his servant, while he himself puts on his old clothes.
The vizier, stunned, asks the servant:
— And what is the third answer? What does God do?
The servant smiles and says:
— Don't you know yet? God makes the vizier a servant and the servant a vizier in an instant!
Moral: A vizier today can become a servant tomorrow, so no one should be confident in his seat!

stories.title: Three Scenes
paragraphs: A young man on a journey encounters three strange scenes on his way.

The first strange scene he encounters is this: several people were sowing wheat in a field. The wheat grains sprout and grow as soon as they hit the ground, and at that moment they produce a harvest, but instead of harvesting the harvest, the farmers burn the field.

The second strange scene was this: a man tries to lift a large stone from the ground, but he cannot. He can lift it only after placing another on top of that large stone. When he places a third stone, he lifts it more easily. No matter how much the young man looks, he cannot understand anything and continues on his way.

The third strange scene he encounters on the road is this: a man is riding on the back of a sheep, and several men are climbing on its shoulders. The sheep runs away quickly; no matter how many men run after them, they cannot catch up.

No matter how much the young man ponders what he sees, he cannot understand any meaning and arrives at a city. He sees a radiant old man near the entrance gate and greets him. The old man accepts the greeting, stops him and starts a conversation. The boy tells what he saw along the way, and the old man explains them as follows:
— Do you know who those farmers, the wheat field and the people who burned it are? Those who first do good, and then talk about the good they have done here and there, belittling its value.

— The meaning of the scene of the man lifting the stone is this: committing a sin for the first time is very difficult for a person. But if a person does not repent after committing a sin, subsequent sins are very easy for him. A sin without repentance is an open door for another sin.

— As for the sheep and the people on its back, do not forget that the sheep is an animal of paradise and carries those who ride on its back to paradise. The first to ride on a sheep are scholars. Those who hang on the shoulders of scholars are believers from all walks of life. Those who run after them are unbelievers and irreligious.
Moral: Goodness that is talked about and its value is reduced to nothing, sin without repentance, and following a true leader—each of them is a hidden lesson in life.

stories.title: Three statues
paragraphs: There were good friends between the rulers of two neighboring countries. One day, one of the rulers decided to send the other a birthday present. He invited the best sculptor of his country to his presence and instructed him to make three statues of gold, one inch high, exactly like each other. But there would be a difference between these statues that only the ruler and the sculptor knew.

The statues were ready and were sent to the neighboring ruler on his birthday. The letter accompanying the gift said: “I congratulate you on your birthday with these three golden statues. At first glance, the statues may seem exactly the same. But one of them is more valuable than the other two. When you find that statue, let me know.”
The ruler, who received the gift, first weighed the statues on a scale. It turned out that they weighed the same, down to the gram. Other investigations were also carried out, but without results.
The ruler summoned all the people in his country who knew art to his palace. Everyone carefully examines the statues, but cannot find a difference between them. Days pass, and no solution is found.

Finally, one day, the ruler is informed that there is someone who can solve this problem. He is immediately found and brought to the palace. The man carefully examines the statues and asks for a thin wire. He puts the wire in the ear of the first statue - the wire comes out of the other ear. Then he puts the wire in the ear of the second statue - the wire comes out of its mouth. Finally, he puts the wire in the ear of the third statue, but the wire gets stuck inside. Thus, the difference between the statues is revealed.
The ruler writes a reply to his neighbor who sent the statues and sends it:
“These three statues symbolize three different types of people. What he hears:”
— he takes it from one ear and gives it from the other;
— he immediately lets it out of his mouth;
— he is able to keep it in his heart.
The most valuable person is the one who can keep what he hears as a secret in his heart and only tells it when it is appropriate and at the right time. Thank you very much for this valuable gift.
Moral: The most valuable person is the one who can keep what he hears as a secret in his heart and only speaks when it is appropriate. Keeping your word is also a form of wisdom.

stories.title: To be full or to be lost
paragraphs: We are full by sharing,
We are lost by dividing.
Yunus Emre
Moral: We become stronger when we are divided, but we are lost when we are divided. To preserve unity, we must keep our knowledge and spirituality healthy.

stories.title: To seek
paragraphs: To seek something where it is not is not to seek, but to deceive oneself — like seeking loyalty in disloyalty, literary shamelessness, and mercy in dishonesty.
Moral: To seek something that is not where it is not is to deceive oneself. Do not expect everything from everyone — know a person as much as he or she can give.

stories.title: Two Cups of Water
paragraphs: In ancient times, there was a ruler who was famous for his wealth. This ruler would take a part of his wealth with him wherever he went and boast about it. The ruler had a wise teacher whom he trusted the most. One day, the ruler asked him: “You are a wise man. Tell me, what do you think of my rule and wealth?”

The wise man looked into the ruler’s eyes and said: “Suppose, my ruler, you are in a very hot, endless desert. Would you give half of your wealth to someone who gives you a cup of water so that you don’t die?” “Of course I will,” the ruler replied. The wise man said: “Suppose, after a while, your thirst increased a little. Would you give the other half of your wealth for the next cup of water?” The ruler thought for a moment and said: “Of course I would give it to you so that you don’t die.”
The wise man smiled and said: “My lord, do not boast too much, for the value of your wealth is only two pots of water.”
Moral: The value of wealth depends on the circumstances: in the desert, all your wealth is worth only two pots of water. Do not boast about your wealth - its value is fleeting.

stories.title: What do I need?
paragraphs: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566; ascended the throne in 1520 and ruled until the end of his life) raised the Ottoman state to the highest possible level of his time, but from time to time he wondered: “I wonder if one day the sons of Osman will also face a decline, will it collapse?”

As in many matters, he decided to reveal this anxious thought to his foster brother, the famous scholar Yahya Efendi. He wrote and sent the following letter to Yahya Efendi, whose discovery and miracle he believed in: “You are knowledgeable about divine secrets. Please clarify these for us. In what case does a state collapse? What will be the fate of the sons of Osman? Can a day come when this state will go bankrupt?”
Yahya Efendi, who read this letter from the powerful sultan of the time, Suleiman the Magnificent, responded very briefly: “What do I need, my Sultan!”

The sultan, who read this answer in amazement in the Topkapi Palace, could not make sense of it, and his anxiety increased even more. Because a person like Yahya Efendi would not give such a simple answer to a serious issue. “I wonder if there is a meaning in this answer that we do not know?” the sultan thought and stood up and went to Yahya Efendi’s court in Beşiktaş. This time, the sultan repeated his request in a reproachful manner, saying: “Brother, what can I do, answer my letter. Take the matter seriously.”
Yahya Efendi:
“My Sultan, is it possible not to take your request seriously? I have thought about your request carefully and expressed my opinion clearly.”
“Okay, but I did not understand anything from your answer. You simply said what I need. This seems to mean that you are not involving me in these matters.”
Yahya Efendi engraved these instructive words on the pages of history:

“My Sultan! If oppression spreads in a state, if injustice rises to the throne and those who hear it say, 'What do I need?' and then the shepherds, not wolves, eat the sheep, those who know the truth remain silent and hide it, if the cries of the poor, the needy, the destitute, and the destitute rise to the heavens and no one hears it except the stones, then the end of the state is in sight. In such cases, the treasury of the state is emptied, the trust and respect of the people are shaken. The sense of obedience that is the means of order disappears, and the sense of respect for the people disappears. Collapse and bankruptcy are thus inevitable...”

The old sultan, who began to cry while listening to what was being said, bowed his head and confirmed these things. Then he left, thanking God that there was a scholar in his country who could give him such advice.
Moral: A society that sees oppression and says, “What do I need?” falls into decline. Turning a blind eye to injustice is also complicity in injustice.

stories.title: What does it mean to be late?
paragraphs: Being late means not being able to do something, an action on time. Especially in our relationships and behavior with the people around us.
Expressing our love to someone, receiving our share of love from someone, forgiving those who have broken our hearts, apologizing for those we have hurt is valuable and beautiful when it is in time.

We are human beings. Each of us can make a mistake or act wrongly at any time. The important thing is not to delay in admitting and correcting the mistake we made, apologizing, and making amends. Life is short.
Let us not delay so that we can live a life full of justice and happiness, where there are no "wishes" and many "good things".
Moral: Expressing love, forgiving, and apologizing on time is beautiful. Life is short - let us not postpone the affairs of the heart.
