stories.title: What is important in life?
paragraphs: The teacher enters the classroom, greets the students, and takes a glass jar out of her bag and places it on the table:

— We all have only one life, and we can achieve everything we want in this life — if we use our time wisely. — Then she fills the jar with golf balls and asks the students: — Do you think the jar is full?
— Full, — everyone answers in unison.
The teacher takes a handful of large pebbles from her bag, adds them to the jar, and asks again:
— Now, is the jar full?
— Yes, — the students answer.
The teacher pours some more sand into the jar and asks again:
— Is the jar full?
The students confirm that the jar is full this time.
Having finished her demonstration, the teacher explains to the students the meaning of what she has seen:
— Imagine that this jar is a symbol of life:
the golf balls represent the things you value most in life — your family, friends, and loved ones;
the large pebbles represent other important factors—your wealth, possessions, and occupation;
and the sand represents other things you may need but are not so important.

If I filled the jar with sand first, there would be no room for golf balls or pebbles. Life is like that. If we fill it with small, unimportant things and spend all our time and energy on them, we will not have time for the most important things.
Moral: Fill the jar of life with the most valuable things first—family, love, and health. If you get caught up in the little things, there will be no room for the important things.

stories.title: What we learn in life
paragraphs: In this life, you constantly learn:
from whom to be patient, from whom to love, from whom to be loyal, faithful, and moral; from whom to know what hypocrisy, deceit, malice, and betrayal are.
Moral: Life teaches us something from every person: from whom to be loyal, from whom to be treason. Both are lessons.

stories.title: Where does this road lead?
paragraphs: A young man walking along the road meets an old man sitting by the side of the road and asks:
— Uncle, where does this road lead?
— Nowhere, my son.
— How do you mean? A road that leads nowhere?
— By God, I have been here for fifty years; this road is still where it was. It is the people who come and go.
Moral: The road is still where it is, the people who come and go. Know not where the road leads, but where you are going.

stories.title: An Organization Without an Action Plan
paragraphs: An organization without an action plan resembles a ship whose destination is known but whose nautical chart, route, and crew responsibilities have not been defined. Such a ship may occasionally reach port through good fortune, a capable captain, or favorable weather. That outcome, however, would be the product of circumstance rather than systematic management. Lasting success is achieved not by chance, but through thoughtful planning and disciplined execution.

Over time, an organization without a plan also begins to lose its members. People are sustained not only by ideas, but by the hope of seeing those ideas put into practice. When hope fades, people leave; when people leave, the organization gradually weakens and eventually ceases to function.
Moral: A goal provides direction; a plan defines the path toward it. An organization may advance by chance without a plan, but lasting success requires deliberate and consistent action.

stories.title: At the Fish Shop
paragraphs: After work, a man was walking toward the bus stop when he passed a fish shop. Remembering how much his wife and daughter loved fish, he went inside to surprise them with dinner.
He asked the seller for one kilogram, then changed the order to two. At that moment, an elderly woman in a worn coat approached timidly:
“Son, would you buy some fish for me too?”
Without hesitation, the man told the seller:
“Make it four kilograms—two for me and two for her.”
He then asked whether she had bread. When she said no, he hurried to the shop across the street, bought four loaves, and gave her a share.
“Is there anything else you need?”
The woman took an empty medicine bottle from her pocket. They were eye drops she had last been able to buy two months earlier; without them, her sight was worsening.
The man went to the pharmacy. The fish seller, who had watched everything, offered the woman a chair. Returning with the medicine, the man was heartened by the seller’s compassion as well.
He gave the woman the medicine and then all the money left in his pocket. Blessing him, she made her way home.
As the man headed toward the bus stop, he remembered that he had not paid for the fish. His pockets were empty. The seller simply smiled:
“Go, brother. It is freely given.”

With no bus fare, the man walked home. He called his daughter, told her he had bought fish, and promised to arrive soon. As he walked through the rain, he thanked God for the chance to help; the tears on his cheeks mingled with the rainwater.
Moral: Do not wait for great means before doing good; kindness depends not on wealth, but on a generous heart. A person rich in spirit finds a way to help even while possessing little.

stories.title: Baklava
paragraphs: When I was a child, our family had very little money. One day, my father brought home some baklava, and we enjoyed it with tea that evening.
The next day was a holiday. My mother packed one piece of baklava, a few olives, and some bread for me to take to school.
My classmates had many different foods. A boy I disliked saw my modest meal and laughed:
“Did you bring that baklava for the mice?”
When the whole class laughed, I ran home in tears and shouted at my mother:
“Why did you give me only one piece? Everyone else had so much food—you humiliated me!”
My mother answered sadly:
“My child, that was the only piece that belonged to me.”

Her words shattered me. She had saved her sole piece of baklava for me instead of eating it herself. I was too ashamed even to embrace her. Ever since, I have asked forgiveness whenever I remember my behavior; baklava became the one sweet I could never eat again.
Moral: Mocking another person’s poverty is among the gravest wrongs. Never forget that a mother may surrender her own share—even her final bite—for her child.

stories.title: Chief Accountant and CEO
paragraphs: The chief accountant says to the CEO:
— Suppose we spent time and money on the development of our employees, but despite this they left our company. What do you think would happen?
CEO:
— Suppose we spent all the time and money we had on them, and they chose not to leave the company. What would happen then?
Moral: An investment in a person is not a loss. He who considers not spending to be saving is choosing tomorrow's big loss over today's small comfort.

stories.title: Do you have money?
paragraphs: Value your parents while they are alive. Never ask, "Do you have money?" Go and meet all their needs within your means. No one can take their place.
Moral: Value your parents while they are alive, meet their needs with deeds, not words. No one or nothing can take their place.

stories.title: Everyone Has Work to Do
paragraphs: I am very lucky to have wise teachers. One of them was my literature teacher, the esteemed Baladadash. He would say that if someone asked you for something or assigned you a task, even if for a trivial reason, you should never leave it unanswered.

Everyone has work to do. A person bothers you not because he is idle, but because he needs you. Never ignore an appeal to you; do not keep that person waiting by staying silent. If you will not be able to help, say so openly. Leaving people without an answer destroys their trust in you.
Moral: It is a very painful feeling to live knowing you are regarded as unreliable and untrustworthy.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

stories.title: Former Minister at Seminar
paragraphs: A former minister was invited to a seminar. When it was his turn, he stood up on the podium with a plastic cup in his hand and began to speak. But it was clear that his mind was elsewhere. Suddenly, he raised the plastic cup, looked at it, and took a deep breath. He turned to the hall and said:

— Do you know what I think? Last year, I spoke on this very podium. The only difference was that I was a minister then. When I came here, I had a business class ticket, a limousine and escort cars were waiting for me at the airport. They took me to a hotel. I rested in a luxury suite, and the next day I came here in the same limousine. A special welcome was arranged. While I was waiting for my speech, they offered me coffee in an expensive porcelain cup. Then they seated me in a specially designated place. But today I am not speaking to you as a minister. I flew here yesterday with a ticket I bought with my own money.

No one met me at the airport. I took a taxi to the hotel, and no one accompanied me to my room. When I came here this morning, they checked my ID against the list and let me in. Then I sat down in the first place I found in the hall. I wanted coffee, so they showed me the coffee machine in the hallway. So I went out and filled this plastic cup that you see here.

The seminar participants had already started laughing. The former minister continued: “I think that last year’s coffee in an expensive cup was not for me, but for my position.” The hall erupted in applause. As soon as the applause died down, he said:

— I want to share with you this important lesson that I learned: all praise, all services rendered are only for your rank, role, or position. None of them belong to you. Instead of the expensive cup that you used while you were in office, when you leave office, you will be given a plastic cup — that is, what you deserve.
Moral: The respect shown to you is often for your position, not for yourself. Therefore, do not brag about your position — your true value will be seen when you leave.

stories.title: Garden and gardener
paragraphs: The teacher addresses his students:
— Imagine that a gardener is taking care of the garden. Did you imagine it?
— We did, — the students answer.
The teacher says in a serious voice:
— Remember what I am going to say now: it is not true to say that the garden grew thanks to the gardener, but it is also not true to say that the garden grew by itself.
Moral: It is neither true to deny the hard work of others nor to belittle one's own. A person grows neither entirely by himself nor entirely thanks to someone else.

stories.title: Grocery store and supermarket
paragraphs: An elderly woman had a grocery store in our neighborhood. One day, a supermarket opened opposite her store. Both began to write and hang the prices of groceries on the sign in front of their shops. When the supermarket posted “Butter — 70 dollars,” the woman posted “We have butter — 60 dollars.” The next day, the supermarket posted “Butter — 50 dollars”; the aunt immediately updated her sign: “We have butter — 40 dollars.”
One of the residents of the neighborhood, concerned about this situation, turned to the woman:
— Aunt, it’s better if you don’t compete with this supermarket. They have wide means, and if the price drops they won’t suffer, but you will go bankrupt.
The woman replied without losing her composure:
— I don’t sell butter at all… Let people at least buy it cheaply.

Moral: A person who lives by the question “Whom did I help?” rather than “What did I gain?” is different. The one who gives without expecting anything in return is actually the one who gains the most.

stories.title: Henry Ford's Choice
paragraphs: It is said that one day Henry Ford, the founder of the Ford Motor Company, invited two young friends who wanted to work for his company to dinner. Both young men graduated from the same university and were very talented and educated specialists.

The dinner was over, the party ended. As they left the restaurant, Ford told one of the young men that he had hired him, and wished the other good luck and said that he could not give him a job. The disappointed young man gathered all his courage and asked Ford:

— Mr. Ford, we have not talked about cars or engineering skills all evening, we have only touched on general topics. But you offered my friend a job, and deprived me of this opportunity. Why did you make such a decision?
Ford replied:

— Look, young man, there are two reasons for this. First: I have observed the behavior of both of you throughout the meal. I noticed that your friend added salt after tasting the food, while you added salt first and only tasted it afterwards. I value those people who decide to make changes only after experimenting and measuring.

— The second reason is this: your friend was very polite to the waiters, and you ignored the waiters and only showed politeness to me. And people should be treated the same, regardless of their position.
Moral: A person's character is shown in his small actions: in his impulsive decisions and in his attitude towards the weak.

stories.title: His Hand Is at Work
paragraphs: A man bought ten eggs for ten kopecks and sold them for nine. When acquaintances asked the purpose of this strange trade, he replied:
— Never mind the loss; seeing that I trade, everyone takes me for a merchant — everyone sees that my hand is at work.
Moral: Wasting time on empty work for the sake of appearances is the real loss. Looking busy does not bring real benefit.

stories.title: Hot bread
paragraphs: The smell of hot, fresh bread spread throughout the street.
The old man approached the baker. He needed to buy hot bread for his grandson. The child had been asking for fresh bread for days.
People were standing in line to buy bread. He took his place in line.
There weren't many people, and his turn came quickly.

He took out some change from his pocket. If he had a lot of money, he would have bought two loaves of bread. He handed the money to the baker. But the baker didn't take money from the grandfather and gave him a package.
— Take it, uncle, and enjoy it.
There were three loaves of bread in the package.
— Son, I was going to buy one loaf.
— Take all three, uncle, and eat them later.
The grandfather slowly approached the baker and whispered in his ear:
— Son, I only have money to buy one loaf of bread.
The baker smiled:
— Uncle, this is our share. Today is Friday; we get three hot loaves of bread every Friday. Enjoy it.
— May God be pleased with you, my son.
— Amen!
He had just left the bakery when someone called out to the grandfather:
— Uncle, oh uncle!
The grandfather turned and looked:
— Here, my son.
— Uncle, this is my mother's zakat; I would be very happy if you accept it.
The young man put an envelope in the old man's pocket.
— May God accept it, my son. May God be pleased with your mother.
As they passed by the market, a woman called out to him:
— Uncle... Wait a minute, please wait.
The old man stopped and looked in the direction from which the voice came. A young woman handed him two full bags:
— Uncle, this Ramadan we are giving food to everyone who passes by, please accept it. What can I do, don't let us down, take these bags.
— May God accept it, my daughter.
— Amen, uncle!
The old man reached home with difficulty, exhausted.
— Welcome, father.
— Where is your mother, my daughter?
— In the kitchen. She said I will cook eggs, Orkhan loves kaygana (a local egg scramble) very much.
— Take these and give them to your mother, my back is broken.
— Grandpa, did you buy hot bread? — the grandson said.
— Yes, I bought a lot.
— Long live grandpa!
— Dad, you didn’t have money in the morning, not even to drink tea.
— God gave it to you, my daughter.
His wife entered the room:
— How much did you buy, man?
— These are your share, wife.
The man told what had happened one by one.
The adhan was called. They opened the iftar with kaygana (a local egg scramble). The hot bread was perfect. There was butter and cheese in the bag. It went very well with the tea.
— Yes, it was very good, thank God. May God accept it. The halva was also very tasty.
When his grandson got up from the table and said:
— I'm going to go to my room and pray a little more, — the grandfather was surprised:
— Do it before you go to bed, my son, it's still early.

— I did it at this time yesterday. I asked God for warm cheese and bread. Look, today it came. Now I'll go and pray that He will send you money to fix your teeth. Your teeth are rotten, and you chew hard with these teeth.
His mother smiled:
— I wish your late father could see these days.
— My father comes to me in my dreams every night anyway and sees these things. In fact, he told me to pray.
The old man suddenly remembered his jacket. He went to the hanger, put his hand in his pocket and took out the envelope. There was a large amount of money in the envelope.
His eyes filled with tears.
— What happened, man, why are your eyes wet?
— My Lord has sent everything that our grandson has in his heart, wife. Just look at this money — we can both get our teeth fixed before the holiday. Thank God!
Moral: A sincere child's prayer, the kindness of a few kind-hearted people can solve a family's problems. In a society that is able to give, no one goes hungry.

stories.title: Loan book
paragraphs: A plain-clothed stranger enters a neighborhood shop. After looking at the seller and the counter for a while, he says:
— Brother, if I ask you for a loan of bread, tea, or eggs, will you give it to me?

— There is a man who has been carrying bread for free for three months. To be honest, I don't believe he will pay this fee. But what can I do, he takes care of three orphans, let alone leave their children hungry. God is great, he will provide for us too. I don't want the fee for the bread I gave you. Take it and go, you will be happy. — A smile spreads across the stranger's face and he says in his heart: "I think I found what I was looking for."
— How much debt do you have in that loan book?
The seller asks, somewhat surprised and somewhat annoyed:
— What are you doing?
The man who came continued the conversation calmly, somewhat reassuringly:

— Look, brother, I beg you, don't get angry. I'm not such a vain person that I'd come here and spoil your nerves, take up your time. I'll buy that notebook of yours. Please, count all the debts in it right now and tell me.

The seller looked at the man in front of him, and then at the overflowing notebook. Seeing that the man in front of him was stubborn, he didn't resist; he added up all the debts recorded in the notebook and told the man the amount received. The man who came took a wad of money from his jacket's breast pocket, put that amount in front of the seller and said:

— Brother, may God be pleased with you. If you trust this community so much, if you don't leave an orphan hungry out of consideration for God, then you are a good person. I have paid everyone's debts. Let this be my share of Ramadan to this community. Now give me that notebook. I will take him and bury him, and I believe that list will be my help on the Day of Judgment. — The man took the notebook and left the store.

When the shopkeeper counted the money in front of him and put it in the cash register, he still couldn't fully understand what was happening. It was as if he had been hit by frost. He looked out the small window of the shop. There was no stranger in sight. Everyone was hurrying home because it was almost time for iftar. At that moment, the seven-year-old daughter of Suraiya, whose husband had died of tuberculosis, appeared at the door and said shyly:

— Uncle Ahmed, my mother says to give me one loaf of bread and three eggs for iftar. We will give you the money when my uncle comes to us next month. — The shopkeeper seemed to wake up from a dream at the girl's words. As usual, she reached under the counter to take out the notebook. She paused for a moment, smiled, and said:
— Come, my daughter, take the eggs, the bread, and the butter. Tell your mother that that uncle came and went...
Moral: A kindness done silently is the highest kindness. Forgiving a person's debt and not leaving an orphan hungry is the true richness of the heart.

stories.title: Mercedes
paragraphs: Mercedes was not the surname of its founder or the name of a large automobile company. It was the name of the daughter of a father who was passionate about cars.
The father believed that the name of his daughter would bring him success.
And so it happened...
The car he named "Mercedes" won consecutive victories in the races it participated in.
Thanks to these successes, countless Mercedes cars have been produced since 1902.
The father's love for his daughter turned the Mercedes name into the brand of one of the largest automobile manufacturers in the world.
Mrs. Mercedes, who had two unsuccessful marriages, lived in Vienna. In 1929, at the age of thirty-nine, she died of cancer and was buried in Vienna.
Moral: A name given with love, a work done with love can change the world. A father's love immortalized a name.

stories.title: Pay rent for water
paragraphs: A man buys a well from a villager. When he wants to draw water from the well, the seller does not allow him: “I sold you the well, not the water in the well,” he says. An argument ensues. He says, so does the judge—in the end, they have to go to the judge.
The judge says to the seller: “Since the water is yours, you cannot keep it in someone else’s well! Either take your water and go, or pay rent to the owner of the well for keeping it there.”
Moral: He who wants to take his rights by crooked means falls into his own trap. Justice weighs the rights of both parties.

stories.title: Scarf seller
paragraphs: The freezing cold of the night had enveloped the city. The ground was icy and slippery. My breath felt as if it would freeze. I was trying to walk very carefully so as not to fall. I approached the bus door, said “thank goodness,” and managed to get there safely. At that moment, a child approached me with the scarves he was trying to sell. I had no strength to pay him any attention; my only concern was to get on the bus as soon as possible.

The child: — Will you buy one, sister? — he said, holding out a scarf. To get rid of him, I said: — No, I don’t want one. — Take it, sister, take it, you’ll need it, — he said. To escape the situation, I said: — I don’t have any money. — Never mind, sister, you take it — I don’t want money; let it be from me, — he said. — That won’t do; I don’t want it, I already have a scarf, — I said, and threw myself onto the bus. At that moment I was thinking only of myself; I did not care about the child at all. I hurried toward my seat.

Before sitting down, I put my hand into my coat pocket to take out my phone. My hand touched a package. I took it out and looked. I was very surprised to see a package with a scarf inside. So the child had slipped the package into my pocket without my noticing.

I immediately threw myself out of the bus door onto the street. The child selling scarves was still in the same place, trying to sell the scarf in his hand to people boarding the bus. I approached this child who paid no mind to the cold — his nose bright red, his pitch-black eyes shining like stars in the night, his innocent smile showing his white teeth, about twelve or thirteen years old, wearing a thin coat, without gloves, trying to earn money in the night cold with bare hands. I put my hand on his shoulder and showed him the scarf: — What is this?
The child smiled and said: — It’s nothing, sister; you’ll need it — let it be from me.
— If you do that, how will you earn money? Aren’t you sorry for yourself in this cold? — I said.
— It’s all right, sister, — he said with loving eyes.
I held out the money.
— No, sister, I don’t want it; let it be from me, — he said again.

Yet if he had looked at me and said, “Sister, you said you had no money — where did you get this?”, I would have sunk into the ground from shame at that moment. But he was a straightforward, innocent, pure child, with an untainted heart, who considered everyone as pure as himself.
— Take this, — I said, looking firmly into his face. Seeing my determination, he took the money and with his other hand began to take change from his pocket to give me back.
— No, I don’t want it; keep the change, — I said.
— Sister, this is too much; that won’t do, — he said, and hurriedly tried to separate the money; some of it fell to the ground.
— It’s all right; may you be well — keep it from me, — I said with a smile.
Embarrassed, with that smile that melts the ice, the child said: — Thank you, sister; may God be pleased with you.

“Thank you too! Thank you too, child of my poor country — big-hearted and content!” I said in my heart, and went and sat down. Outside, ice-cold air still covered this child’s small, beloved city — a city in which there are still children who remain pure in their innocence, whose trust in people has not been damaged, who turn winter into spring with their laughter, and who try to earn something to support their families.

We set off. In the darkness of the night, that city and that boy selling scarves were left behind. With a bitterness that had settled into my heart, I thought of the souls cast out of their homes in this cold. Various emotions I could not name rose inside me; something knotting in my throat took my breath away, and tears kept looking for a chance to fall from my eyes.
Our bus continued on its way, winding through the snow-covered mountains.
Moral: Sometimes the most helpless person shows the greatest generosity. The pure heart of a child turns material poverty into wealth.

stories.title: The Weight of Butter
paragraphs: A baker regularly bought a certain amount of butter from a peasant. One day he noticed that the weight of the butter he received was decreasing day by day. He accused the peasant of cheating him and complained to the judge.

When the peasant was summoned before the judge, he replied: “Actually, I don’t have any scales. I put the butter I want to sell in one hand and the one-kilo loaf I buy from the baker every day in the other, and I measure the butter against that.”
Moral: As you treat others, you often receive the same measure in return. The bread you give comes back to you as butter.

stories.title: We Are Rich
paragraphs: Near the end of the fourth century, Emperor Nintoku of Japan climbed a high tower one day and surveyed his country. Seeing not even a wisp of smoke rising, he realized his people were in poverty and that no one could cook at home.

He at once issued a decree ordering the people to work only for themselves for three years. He also sent the palace workers home. Working for themselves and paying no tax, the people came to abundance after three years.
Three years later Nintoku climbed the tower again, saw smoke rising on every side, and was sure that hearths were burning across the land. Joyfully he said to the lady beside him:
— Now we are rich!
But the empress pointed to the palace, neglected for three years — roof leaking, flowers withered — and asked:
— Do you call this wealth?
Nintoku’s answer has been remembered by the Japanese for centuries:
— Our people’s poverty is our poverty, and their wealth is our wealth.
Moral: True wealth is not in the treasury, but in the people’s well-being. A leader’s greatness lies not in the post, but in the meaning given to that post.

stories.title: Why am I poor?
paragraphs: Once a poor man met Buddha and asked him:
— Buddha, why am I poor?
— Because you don’t give anything from your wealth to anyone.
— How can I do that? I have nothing to give to others!
— You have five riches that you could share with others, but you don’t.
— Please explain those five riches to me.
— Okay.
1. You could give others a smile with your face, but you don’t.
2. You could look at others with compassion and love with your eyes, but you don’t.
3. You could say good words to others with your tongue, but you don’t.
4. You could wish others happiness with your heart, but you don’t.
5. You could do good deeds for others with your hands, but you don’t.
Moral: There is always something to give: a smile, a kind word, a compassionate look, a helping hand. A person is as rich as they share.

stories.title: A bell to hang from the cat's neck
paragraphs: A group of mice gathered together and looked for ways to get rid of a cat that had become a nuisance to them.
Many ideas were put forward, but none were accepted. Finally, a young mouse suggested hanging a bell from the cat's neck.

The essence of the plan was this: as the cat with the bell hanging from its neck approached the mice, they would hear the bell and run away, thus saving their lives. This proposal was met with great enthusiasm and applause by all the mice.
At this moment, the old mouse, who was silently watching what was happening in a corner, spoke up:
— This is a very clever proposal, and if it were implemented, I have no doubt that it would be successful. But one question makes me think: well, tell me, who would hang the bell from the cat's neck?
Moral: It is easy to make a plan, but difficult to carry it out. Even the brightest idea that is not implemented is worthless.

stories.title: A woman whose house was robbed
paragraphs: In ancient times, the house of an old woman living in a city was robbed. The woman came to the king in a state of dismay to complain. The king listened to her and angrily asked: “Then why did you fall into such a deep sleep that you did not even notice that a thief had entered your house?” The woman replied: “Thank God, king, we thought you were awake, so we slept peacefully in our house.”
Moral: The peace of the people comes from the trust they have in the state. If the people know that their leader is awake, they will sleep peacefully in their own homes.

stories.title: Homeland and land
paragraphs: If you add water to the land, you get mud, if you add blood, you get a homeland.
Moral: What turns the land into a homeland is the blood shed for it. Homeland is not just a place, it is a sacredness for which sacrifices are made.

stories.title: Nazim Hikmet in Bursa Prison
paragraphs: Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet was serving a sentence in Bursa Prison. One day, an inspector from the Ministry of Justice came to inspect the prison. He asked the prison chief to call Nazim Hikmet — he wanted to meet with him.

Nazim was called. He entered the room... They had a short conversation. But the ministry employee did not offer the poet a seat. After the conversation, he said: "You can go." Nazim Hikmet turned around and asked the inspector as he was leaving the door:
— Do you know Omar Khayyam?
— Of course. Is it okay not to know him?
— And can you tell me who the king was during Omar Khayyam's time?
The inspector was surprised by this unexpected question and could not answer.
Nazim Hikmet said:
— You see, you remembered the artist, but not the king. The time will come when they will neither remember the Minister of Justice nor you. But they will always remember my name.
Saying this, he leaves. The inspector realizes his mistake. Even though he calls him, the poet does not return...
Moral: As time passes, those in positions of authority are forgotten, but those who create true value are remembered. Positions are temporary, deeds are permanent.

stories.title: Sharing justice
paragraphs: Either no one should cry,
or these always laughing people should not laugh;
or no one should have this disease called money,
or the moneyed nation should learn to share;
or no one should say what they love,
or they should give the definition of this true love;
or these holidays should not be experienced at all,
or there should be no one who does not eat meat during the holidays.
Moral: Humanity is created when joy, bread, and love are shared. If one side laughs and the other side cries, there is no justice there.

stories.title: The just verdict of the Frankfurt judge
paragraphs: This incident was recorded in the city of Frankfurt in 1506. A merchant lost his bag with 800 guilders on the road. By chance, a carpenter passing by found the bag. The carpenter, who was extremely religious, did not tell anyone that he had found the bag, thinking that it was impossible not to notice that so much money was lost, so the owner would definitely look for it.

One day, the carpenter went to church to worship. After the service, the monk announced to the congregation that a merchant who had come to Frankfurt had lost his 800 guilders and promised a reward of 100 guilders to whoever found it.
Hearing this, the carpenter took the money he had found, went to church, and handed the bag over to the monk.

The merchant was informed that his money had been found; he went to church and took the bag, but refused to pay the carpenter the 100 guilders he had promised—he gave him only 5 guilders. The carpenter asks the merchant to keep his promise. The greedy merchant claims that he has 900 guilders in his wallet, not 800, in order to avoid giving him 100 guilders, and that the carpenter took money from the bag. The monk intervenes in the argument to defend the carpenter: he says that he knows him, that he is an honest man, and that he would never do such a thing. The argument becomes heated. The monk takes the merchant and the carpenter to the city court.

The trial begins. The judge asks the merchant to swear by placing his hand on the Bible that he has lost his 900 guilders. The merchant, without hesitation, places his hand on the Bible and swears. The judge also asks the carpenter to swear by finding the 800 guilders. The carpenter also places his hand on the Bible and swears.
Everyone is impatiently waiting for the judge's decision. The judge says that everything is clear as day and explains his decision as follows:

— The carpenter found 800 guilders, and the merchant lost 900 guilders. Therefore, the money that the carpenter found does not belong to the merchant. Therefore, since the owner has not been found, these 800 guilders are given to the carpenter. The merchant can continue to search for the 900 guilders he lost.
Moral: Greed traps a person. The stingy person who denies the truth eventually becomes a victim of his own lies; justice is on the side of the righteous.

stories.title: The Skins of the Lambs
paragraphs: “It is better to shear the wool of rams than to skin lambs.”
This saying is associated with Azmzadeh Asad Pasha, who was the governor of Damascus province during the Ottoman period. The story goes like this:

One day, Asad Pasha’s treasury was empty and he was in great distress. His advisors advised him to impose an additional tax on the weavers of Damascus as a way to fill the treasury. Asad Pasha, who listened to the advice, asked: “How much income would we get if we imposed such a tax?”
“We will buy fifty or sixty bags of gold,” they said.

Asad Pasha objected: “These people are already struggling to make ends meet. How will they pay this tax?” The advisors said: “They will sell the gold and jewels in their houses, Pasha,” and tried to persuade him.
Asad Pasha says: “I will get this amount in a better way.”
The advisors are silent.
The next day, the Pasha sends an invitation to the Mufti and offers to meet secretly at night. At night, the Mufti comes to visit the Pasha. The Pasha says:

— Mufti Effendi! According to the information we have received, you are acting contrary to the Sharia in your personal life, drinking alcohol secretly at home. I must report this situation to Istanbul. However, I thought I would inform you in advance.

Hearing this, the Mufti Effendi begins to beg the Pasha. In order not to inform Istanbul, he offers him a thousand mecidiyes. The Pasha does not accept. The Mufti offers twice as much. The Pasha does not accept again. In the end, they agree to six thousand mecidiyes.
The next day, Asad Pasha invites the Ghazi and tells him: “Gazi Effendi, we have learned from reliable sources that you are taking bribes and using your position for your personal gain.”

This time, the Ghazi Effendi begins to beg the Pasha. He, like the mufti, bargains with Asad Pasha: “Oh, my lord, do not remove me from my post, or I will be disgraced among the people.” They also agree to six thousand mejidiye gazi.
Then Asad Pasha invites the treasurer, the chief of security, the merchants and the wealthy to a meeting one by one.

At the end of this operation, Asad Pasha collects exactly two hundred bags of mejidiye gold. Then he calls his advisors and asks: “Have you heard that I imposed a tax on the people of Damascus?” “No, we have not heard,” they say.
The Pasha says: “Despite not imposing a tax, I have collected not fifty, but two hundred bags of mejidiye gold.”
— How did you do this, Pasha?
The Pasha replies: “It is better to shear the wool of rams than to skin lambs.”
Moral: It is more just to take the unjust profit of the wealthy than to rob the poor. The burden should be placed on the strong, not the poor.

stories.title: The story of the Bedouin whose camel was stolen
paragraphs: A Bedouin walking in the desert with his camel came across a man who was barely standing, his lips parched with thirst. The man begged the Bedouin for water to drink. The Bedouin got off his camel and gave him water. The man drank the water, then suddenly pushed the Bedouin away, mounted the camel, and started to run away.
When the Bedouin realized that he could do nothing to save his camel, he shouted after the thief:
— Take the camel, it is yours. But never tell anyone about this story.
Surprised by the Bedouin's strange request, the thief stopped for a moment, looked back, and asked why.
— If you tell, this story will spread everywhere, and no one will ever help the needy people he meets again, — the Bedouin replied.
Moral: Sometimes hiding your own harm is to protect the faith of others in the goodness of others. One bad news can close the door to thousands of good things.

stories.title: The world can be conquered with this nation
paragraphs: One day, the king changed his clothes and went to the city to observe how the people lived. He began to inspect the city markets to learn about the quality of the goods, their prices, and the mood of the shopkeepers.
The king entered the first shop at the beginning of the street. He greeted and said:
— Give me half a batman of butter, half a batman of honey, and some cheese.

The shopkeeper, who greeted the customer with a smile, politely accepted the greeting and gladly took half a batman of butter. While giving the butter, he addressed the man in front of him, not knowing that he was the king, as follows:

— My lord, if you wish, I can also give you honey and cheese. However, by selling this butter, I have already made a siptah — the first sale of the day. If you buy your other requests from my neighbor across the street, who has not yet made a siptah, I will be very pleased.

The king, who was very happy with this, paid for the butter and went to the shop opposite. From there, he also asked for half a batman of honey and cheese. After the old owner of the shop had tasted the honey:
— Thank God, thanks to you we have also tasted it today. But I ask you this: do not buy the cheese from me, but from the shop next door. It has not tasted it yet, — he said.
The king, who was very impressed by what he saw, went to the shop next door and made his purchase, and said:
— With such high morality in this nation, the whole world can be conquered, — he said and left the market happy and satisfied.
Moral: Real power does not lie in weapons, but in the honesty and halalness of the people. Not buying land, but conquering hearts is the real victory.

stories.title: Why injustice when there is justice?
paragraphs: Haji Bektaş Veli:
Why hatred when there is love?
Why war when there is peace?
Why quarrel when there is brotherhood?
Why enmity when there is friendship?
Why intolerance when there is tolerance?
Why captivity when there is freedom?
Why injustice when there is justice?
Moral: It is man's own fault to choose hatred, strife and injustice when love, peace, brotherhood and justice are possible.

categories.title: Aging and time
categories.blurb: The seasons of life and what time changes.

stories.title: Aging
paragraphs: Aging is like climbing a mountain: the higher you rise, the more tired you become and the shorter your breath, yet the wider your view of the world grows.
Moral: Growing older is not merely a loss of strength; through experience and wisdom, it is also the ability to see a broader landscape.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: For those who have reached sixty...
paragraphs: It is time to use the money you have saved up so far. Use it and enjoy it. For those who are not aware of the sacrifices you have made to get it, do not save it. This is the ideal time to enjoy peace.

Do not worry about the financial situation of your children and grandchildren, and do not be upset that you have spent your money on yourself. You have taken care of them for years, taught them everything you could. You have given them education, food, shelter and support. Now it is their duty to earn their own money. Let them find their own way.
Now lead a healthy life without much physical exertion. Exercise moderately, go for a walk every day, eat well and sleep well.

At this age, it is easy to get sick and difficult to stay healthy. Therefore, you should keep yourself in good shape, pay attention to your medical and physical needs. Contact your doctor; get check-ups even if you feel fine.

Do not stress over small things. You have already overcome a lot in your life. You have had both good and bad memories. Don't let the past hold you back and the future scare you. Feel good now. Minor troubles will soon be forgotten.
Regardless of your age, always live your love. Love your partner, love life, love your family and remember: as long as your mind and compassion are in order, you are not old.

Don't stop going to the hairdresser, take care of your nails, visit a dermatologist and dentist, use perfumes and creams. When you are well-groomed on the outside, this feeling also seeps into you, you feel proud and strong.

Don't lose sight of age-appropriate fashion trends, but maintain your own style. Read books, flip through newspapers, watch the news. Go online, find out what people think. Make sure you have an active email account and use at least a few social networks.

Respect the younger generation and their opinions. They may not agree with you, but the future is theirs and they will direct their lives in the direction they want. Do not criticize, give advice and try to remind them that yesterday's wisdom is still valid today.
Never use the phrase "in our time...". Now is your time. Be a part of this time as long as you live.
Try to stay away from negative people and spend your time only with people who give you a good mood, positive energy.
Do not give up your hobbies. You can travel, walk, cook, read, dance. If you want, you can keep a cat or a dog.

Get out of the house, meet people you have not seen for a long time, experience something new or old anew. The main thing is to get out of the house from time to time. Go to museums, walk in the park.
Try to always be polite, do not complain and criticize unless necessary. If someone has broken your heart, forgive them. Apologize to the people you have broken your heart to.

Don't carry your pain with you. It will only hurt you. It doesn't matter who is right. They say that holding a grudge is like poisoning yourself and waiting for someone else to die. Never accept that poison. Forgive, forget and move on with your life.
Laugh, be happy. Enjoy a peaceful life at this age of your life... Be happy!
Moral: The era of self-sacrifice will end one day; in the autumn of your life, give yourself the right to live. A happy person spreads happiness to those around him.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: What has changed after sixty
paragraphs: I asked one of my friends, who is in her 60s and approaching 70, what changes she has noticed in herself. She replied:
I stopped telling the elderly, “You told me that story.” After all, these conversations help them revive their good memories and relive those wonderful moments.
I learned not to correct people even when they make mistakes. After all, it is not my job to make everyone perfect. Being present is more important than perfection.
I give a lot of compliments. After all, this is pleasant not only to the person in front of me, but also to my own soul.
I learned not to worry about a wrinkle or a stain on my clothes. Ultimately, a person’s value comes from within, not from their appearance.
I learned to stay away from people who are strangers to my world. After all, they are not able to establish and maintain good relationships; and I learned that too.
I learned not to be ashamed of my feelings. After all, it is my feelings that make me human.
I learned that it is better to put my ego aside than to destroy relationships. After all, ego leads me to loneliness, and relationships help me not to be lonely.
I learned to do things that can make me happy. After all, I am responsible for my own happiness.
I learned not to help without being asked. After all, a person who needs help may not want this help to come from me.
I learned not to complain about my health, my neighbors, my relatives, my retirement! After all, despite all the difficulties, I must be grateful that I am alive and that my loved ones are with me.

I stopped saying phrases like “when I was your age…” to young people; and I never use expressions like “I gave you my best years…”. After all, every time has its own rules, and it is not right to apply the criteria of the past to the present.

I began to pay more attention to my wife, not forgetting that she was once young, strong, and full of joy — even though she is now a wrinkled, helpless, and sad old woman. After all, maybe she is the only person who really needs me right now.
I stopped blaming myself for everything. After all, I have done everything I can in life for myself and for my children.

And finally: I learned to ask my Lord for strength to change the things I can, patience to change the things I cannot, and wisdom to know the difference between the two. After all, as a human being, I am not capable of everything.
Moral: Age teaches a person the greatest wisdom: peace is better than perfection, and understanding is better than being right.
Stories are taken from open Internet sources; illustrations were created with AI.

stories.title: A Fly in a China Shop
paragraphs: A fly could never destroy a china shop by its own strength. But if it flew into a bull’s ear, the frightened animal might panic and wreck the entire shop.
The fly represents superstition, falsehood, and prejudice. The bull represents an ignorant person who acts without thinking.
Moral: A small lie whispered into an ignorant ear can cause enormous destruction. Knowledge, critical thinking, and strong moral values are our best protection against it.

stories.title: Elephant and Rope
paragraphs: A traveler passes by an elephant enclosure and is surprised to see that these giant animals are tied to a stake by a front leg with just a short rope. There is no chain or cage. It would seem natural that the elephants could easily break the rope at any moment and escape, but they did not seem to be trying to escape. The man approaches a nearby trainer and asks why these magnificent animals stand there obediently and do not try to run away.
The trainer explains:

— When elephants are young, a short rope is enough to tie them and hold them. As they grow, these animals gradually begin to believe that they cannot break the rope and escape. They think that this rope will still hold them and will not let them go free.
The man is amazed to hear this. Imagine: these animals remained bound to the spot where they stood, believing freedom was impossible, even though they could break free at any moment.
Moral: Often it is not the rope that binds us, but the distrust born of past failures. It is impossible to be free without overcoming the fear of “what will people say.”

stories.title: The donkey's law
paragraphs: One day, a donkey becomes the king of the forest. A few days later, he makes a law: everyone must go to bed at six in the evening and wake up at six in the morning. For twelve hours, there must be complete silence in the forest, and anyone who breaks the law must be punished.
In this way, for a while, the forest is quiet.

One day, a rooster wakes up at five in the morning and begins to crow. The world in the forest clashes with each other. A court is immediately set up and the rooster is executed by the donkey's verdict. After that day, no one touches the law for fear of the king.
Years pass, the donkey grows old and weak. He retreats to a corner of the forest and awaits his death. The lion comes to him, takes stock of his condition, and then asks:

— You are already living your last days. We want to know: what was the wisdom of that law that ordered you to go to bed at six in the evening and get up at six in the morning? How many times have we tried to revolt and abolish it, but we held back because it would disrupt order in the forest. We said to ourselves that perhaps there is some wisdom in this law that we do not understand.
The donkey smiled and replied:
— Indeed, I myself have been wondering about this for years: why did the wild animals of the forest obey this law that I derived from my donkeyness like sheep?

Moral: What keeps a meaningless law standing is not the power of the one who gave it, but the silence of those who obey. Behind an order there is not always wisdom — sometimes only donkeyness — so do not hesitate to ask, for an unanswered question can turn even the oldest nonsense into law.

stories.title: The Hunter's Tale
paragraphs: Until the lion learns to write, every storyteller will write the hunter's tale.
African Proverb
Moral: He who tells the story becomes the hero. If you don't learn to write your own truth, you will always be told by others.

stories.title: The Lion's Track
paragraphs: A cowardly, yet arrogant hunter, following a lion, reaches a forest and asks the woodcutter who comes across him:
— Brother, have you come across a lion or its track around here?
Woodcutter:
— I saw the lion himself; if you want, come and take you to where he is.
The pale hunter:
— No, my dear, thank you. I was actually looking for the lion's track, not the lion itself.
Moral: A person is known not by his pretensions, but by his behavior in the moment of trial. Many people "look for a lion" from afar, but when they come face to face, most of them retreat.

stories.title: The tortoise's wrong calculation
paragraphs: They ask the tortoise:
— How long will it take you to reach this nearby village?
— Taking into account the rain, mud, wind, and ups and downs, it's a three-day journey, but I'll make it in six days... — the tortoise replies.

After six days, they look and see that the tortoise has not yet reached the village. They search and finally find him halfway along the way: — Well, you couldn't make it three days' journey in six days? — they ask in surprise.

The tortoise replies in disappointment: — Never mind, friends. I calculated the rain, mud, wind, and ups and downs, but unfortunately, it didn't occur to me to calculate the bad people. As soon as I started to move, they caught me and turned me upside down.
Moral: You can calculate every difficulty in life, but not people with bad intentions. May God not let you face those who prevent you from moving forward, but those who support you.

stories.title: Two donkeys
paragraphs: Two donkeys are walking along a path. They see a monkey sitting in a tree. They say, let's tease this monkey: let's ask him if he has a friend or not? If he says "Yes", we say "Which fool is your friend?"; if he says "No", we say "Which fool would be your friend?" They approach the tree and ask: "Monkey, do you have a friend?" The monkey looks down at the donkeys who want to tease him and says:
— Wherever I look, they are all donkeys; who should I be friends with?
Moral: A trap set to humiliate someone often explodes on the head of the one who sets the trap. The one who wants to tease himself becomes ridiculous.

stories.title: Water-carrying ant
paragraphs: According to legend, Nimrod (a Biblical character, the ruler of the land of Shinar) wants to punish the prophet Abraham, whom he considers an obstacle to his cruelty, by throwing him into the fire. He builds a huge bonfire in the middle of the square. All living things that see the bonfire run away.
Meanwhile, an ant with a drop of water in its mouth starts running towards the bonfire in a hurry.
Seeing it, another ant asks:
— Where are you running in such a hurry?
— Haven't you heard that Nimrod is going to throw the prophet Abraham into the fire? — the water-carrying ant does not hide his concern.
— You probably haven't seen that bonfire. It's a huge bonfire, there's no other way but to run. Will you put out that bonfire with this drop of water in your mouth? — the second ant asks mockingly.
The water-carrying ant replies:
— Even if I can't put it out, at least it will be clear whose side I'm on.
Moral: Even if you can't, at least stand by the truth. Being there for your loved one when they're in trouble is a value in itself.

stories.title: A Magnificent Lesson
paragraphs: As a child, Mehmed the Conqueror, son of the Ottoman Sultan Murad II, would not sit quietly in class and was constantly disruptive. Whenever his teacher, Akşemseddin, corrected him, the boy replied:
“You cannot tell me what to do. I am the sultan’s son!”
The teacher was deeply troubled. He hesitated to complain to the ruler, but one day he gathered his courage, appeared before Murad II, and explained what had been happening.
The sultan thought for a moment and whispered a plan into the teacher’s ear. Akşemseddin protested that it would be impossible, but Murad II insisted:
“It will be done.”
The next day, young Mehmed again misbehaved and answered his teacher with the same threat. At that moment, the sultan opened the door and entered the classroom.
Following the plan, Akşemseddin pretended to be furious. He reprimanded the sultan for entering without permission, even slapped him, and ordered him to leave immediately.
Murad II lowered his head, apologized, and left. Seeing that even his powerful father had to obey the teacher’s rules, the prince was stunned.
A short while later, someone knocked. This time the sultan asked permission to enter and apologized again.
The plan worked. From that day forward, Mehmed no longer disrupted his lessons. For the sake of his son’s upbringing, Murad II had set aside even a ruler’s pride.
Moral: In education, personal example is stronger than any lecture. A responsible parent may even set aside personal pride to help a child find the right path.

stories.title: Albrecht Dürer
paragraphs: In a small village near Nuremberg lived a family with ten children. Their father worked eighteen hours a day to support the household. Despite their hardship, the two eldest sons, Albrecht and Albert, dreamed of becoming renowned artists. They knew their father could not afford to educate them both at once.

After long discussions by candlelight, the brothers decided to draw lots. The winner would study at the academy in Nuremberg, while the other worked in a nearby mine to support him. After four years, they would exchange places.
Albrecht won the draw. He left for the academy, and Albert began working in the mine.
For four years, one brother studied art while the other labored underground. Albrecht’s work soon attracted wide attention; some said that it surpassed the work of many of his teachers.
By the time he completed his studies, Albrecht was earning a good income. He returned home joyfully and told his brother:
“Dear brother, now it is your turn. Go and pursue your dream; this time I will support you.”
Albert held out his hands and answered softly:
“No, brother. It is too late. During these four years, the mine has crushed my hands and every finger. I can no longer draw.”
Albrecht took his brother’s hands in his own and wept.

Centuries later, the works of Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528) continue to be displayed in leading galleries around the world. The famous drawing associated with his brother’s sacrifice is known as Praying Hands.
Moral: Behind success there often stands an unseen sacrifice. To recognize and honor that sacrifice is one of the finest expressions of humanity.

stories.title: Sinan Brought Water to Istanbul but Died in a House Without It
paragraphs: During the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, rapidly growing Istanbul suffered a severe water shortage. The solution became associated with the great architect Koca Sinan (1489–1588).
One day, the sultan summoned him and asked:
“Chief architect, people pay dearly even for a packhorse’s load of water. Can Istanbul be supplied with enough water?”

Sinan requested permission to survey the surrounding country. With his assistants, he examined wells, valleys, and streams from Çekmece to Beşiktaş and calculated where dams and aqueducts could be built.
When he returned, he told the sultan:
“It can be done, but at a heavy price: sacks filled with gold would have to be placed end to end.”
The sultan replied:
“Tell me only that it is possible. If necessary, I will place the sacks not end to end, but side by side.”
Sinan began work and created a magnificent system culminating in forty public fountains across the city. Taps were fitted so that the precious water would not be wasted.

The sultan declared the public fountains the property of the people and prohibited secret pipes into private homes. In recognition of Sinan’s service, however, he verbally allowed a private line to the architect’s house.

Years passed. Suleiman and those who knew Sinan’s service firsthand died. One day, the elderly architect was summoned to the palace, where the council was investigating a complaint about the private water in his home.
Sinan explained that the sultan himself had granted permission. When asked for a written decree, he admitted:
“At the time, I was ashamed to ask the Ruler of the World for a document. I have no written order.”
After a long debate, the council decided not to punish Sinan for his past use of the water, but ordered the private line cut off.
Near the end of his life, Sinan fell gravely ill. When those beside him tried to moisten his lips, the tap was dry. The great architect said:
“We did not serve for profit, but for God’s pleasure. We await our reward in the hereafter and do not grieve that this world has denied water to our home.”
Moral: Do not place excessive trust in fame, worldly privilege, or human remembrance. True service is rendered not for personal gain, but for what one knows to be right.

stories.title: Three important things for a city
paragraphs: There are three important things for every city: sewage, bath and library. Because sewage cleans the dirt of the city, bath cleans the body, and library cleans the soul.
Fatih Sultan Mehmet
Moral: A city must keep both the body and the soul clean. The library cleans the soul, bath cleans the body, and sewage cleans the city.
